Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [Sad 2]. ﴿Bal﴾ here is for idrab. Is it the idrab of nullification (ibtali) or of transition (intiqali)?

* Students: Nullification.
* The Shaykh: What is the difference between them? Nullification is the cancelling of what preceded, as if he wiped it out and brought something in its place; transition is the affirmation of what preceded but moving from one thing to another, and what came before this idrab remains, not nullified.

He said: (﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ from the people of Makkah). The author's restriction of "those who disbelieve" to the people of Makkah is open to question, and it is better to take the general meaning. Taking the Quran as specifying some individuals of a general term is neither sound nor good, because it is a deficiency in the interpretation unless there is evidence for it. If evidence exists, the evidence must be followed; but if no evidence exists, what is obligatory? What is obligatory is to take the general meaning, because it is more comprehensive and richer in meaning. So "those who disbelieve" includes the people of Makkah and others until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿In arrogance﴾, and it is not the arrogance of domination like the "might" in His saying: ﴿But might belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]; rather, it is the arrogance of pride, haughtiness and obstinacy. For this reason he said: (zeal and pride against faith). This is a blameworthy might, because it is a might that prevents its possessor from accepting the truth, whereas the might that is the might of victory is support for its possessor, and there is a great difference between them.

He said: ﴿in arrogance and opposition﴾, that is, antagonism (mushaqqah). So shiqaq is a verbal noun of shaqqa, like qital is a verbal noun of qatala, and the meaning is antagonism. Antagonism toward whom? Antagonism toward Allah and His Messenger; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal 13]. Here the author said: (opposition, enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ), and this too is open to question. Why? Because he restricted opposition to the Prophet ﷺ, although the disbelievers oppose Allah and His Messenger; they are in pride, haughtiness, zeal and antagonism toward Allah and His Messenger. That is, they turn away from what Allah and His Messenger commanded, as if they were on one side, while what the revelation brought is on another side. ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. Someone might say: they are also in opposition among themselves, especially the Jews, for Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You think they are united, but their hearts are divided﴾ [al-Hashr 14].

He said: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾ [Sad 3]. (﴿How many﴾ means many). Among you (meaning many) with the accusative? [Students:] Yes.
* The Shaykh: (Many ﴿We destroyed before them﴾, that is, a multitude of nations).

The saying ﴿How many We destroyed﴾: the author estimated it with his statement "many," so "how many" is here a kathrah (multiplicative) construction. It is in the accusative as a direct object preceding ﴿We destroyed﴾; ﴿before them﴾ is related to ﴿We destroyed﴾; and ﴿from a generation﴾ is a specification (tamyiz) for ﴿how many﴾, because "kam" is an ambiguous noun that requires a specification, that is, something that explains and specifies it. If it were said only ﴿How many We destroyed before them﴾, the sentence would not be clear: destroyed what? But when ﴿from a generation﴾ is added, the sentence becomes clear; for this reason we say that ﴿from a generation﴾ is a specification of what? Of ﴿how many﴾, governed by ﴿from﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 4):

﴿How many generations did We destroy before them?﴾ "Before them" refers to the disbelievers who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). His words ﴿generations﴾ mean nations (ummah). The meaning is that Allah destroyed many nations before these people, and whoever destroyed many nations before these people is certainly able to destroy them too. However, the destruction of the earlier nations was by a punishment from Allah, while the destruction of those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ) was at the hands of the believers. The fighting and warfare that took place between the Messenger (ﷺ) and them was a punishment upon these deniers, and it was carried out at the hands of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Fight them, and Allah will punish them by your hands, and disgrace them, and give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people. And He will remove the rage of their hearts. And Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills, and Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ [at-Tawbah 14–15]. There is no doubt that the punishment of enemies at the hands of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions is more healing to the hearts of the believers than if the punishment came directly from Allah the Glorified and Exalted. This is something observed: when your enemy is defeated by your hand, it is more healing for your heart, more life-giving for your soul, stronger and more honourable than if Allah destroyed him by a punishment from Himself. For this reason the destruction of those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ) came at the hands of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Companions, and Allah knows best.

(...) returns to the words according to their wording, and it is permissible for it to return to the words according to their meaning. Have you not seen the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat 9], and He did not say "fought" in the dual form (iqtatalā)? Had He said iqtatalā, the pronoun would have referred to the wording. But when He said iqtatalū (plural), it referred to the meaning, because the ṭā'ifah (group) is a collective. So here ﴿they called out﴾ means the generation (qarn), and the pronoun refers back to it according to its meaning.

As for His words ﴿they called out﴾, the author says: (at the time the punishment descended upon them). But whom did they call out to? Does the meaning mean that some of them called out to others, seeking help from one another? But this is not possible? Or does the meaning mean that they called out to Allah, that is, they invoked Him to rescue them? Or does the meaning mean that both occurred from them?

The principle we have in tafsir is that whenever a word is suitable for two or more meanings, it is taken to include all of them together. Based on this, ﴿they called out﴾ has its object omitted for generality: some of them call out to others, "O so-and-so, help me, help me." Likewise they call out to Allah, since Allah says: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir 84]. But Allah said: ﴿And no time was there for escape﴾. ﴿Lāta﴾ here is the negative (lā) to which the feminine ta' has been added to mark the feminine form of the word, just as the ta' of feminine is added to (rubba) and (thumma) to mark the feminine form of the word. You say: "Rubba rajulin laqītuhu" and "Rubbat rajulin laqītuhu," and you say: "Qāma Zaydun thumma qāma 'Amrun," and "Qāma Zaydun thummat qāma 'Amrun." So here it is the negative (lā) to which the ta' has been added. Why? To mark the feminine form of the word. This negative lā functions like laysa, and its subject is omitted in this verse, and its predicate is ﴿a time of escape﴾. The estimate is (i.e., it is not the time of escape). The author explained it by its meaning. So you say: (lā) is in the sense of (laysa), its subject is omitted, estimated as "al-ḥīn" (the time), and its predicate is present, which is His words ﴿a time of escape﴾. Generally, the predicate of (lā) is a time expression. This is the usual case; it does not come except as a time expression.

The poet said:
"The transgressors regretted, but there is no time for regret ..........................."
meaning: and the hour is not an hour of regret.

As for His words ﴿escape (manāṣ)﴾, manāṣ means flight and deliverance. That is: it is not the time of flight and deliverance, because after the punishment descends, faith does not benefit a soul.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (it is not the time for escape), and the ta' is added (for the feminine form of the word), and the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿they called out﴾. Based on this, it is in the accusative position, because a circumstantial clause is always in the accusative position. That is: they called out in a state where there is no escape from what has befallen them. For this reason the author estimated it as: (i.e., they sought help, and the situation is that there is no flight and no refuge).

This is what the author estimated for the phrase ﴿and no time was there for escape﴾. That is, it is a circumstantial clause, and thus it is restricted to the circumstance of their calling out. However, it is permissible for it to be a resumptive clause (isti'nāfiyyah), so that ﴿they called out﴾ stands alone, and then Allah the Mighty and Majestic informs that this time is not a time of escape.

The difference between our saying "resumptive" (istinā'iyyah) and "circumstantial" (ḥāliyyah) is this: if it is circumstantial, it becomes a restriction on the calling out; that is, they called out in a state in which calling out does not benefit them. If it is resumptive, it is separate from what precedes it in terms of restriction: Allah informs that they called out, then He informs that they were in a state in which they were not able to flee.

The author said: (and they did not take heed, the disbelievers of Makkah). This is the outcome of mentioning that Allah destroyed many generations in the past, yet despite this, the people of Makkah did not take heed from it. Rather, they denied the Messenger (ﷺ) and harmed him, and said: he is a madman, he is a sorcerer, he is a liar, he is a poet, he is a soothsayer. Every attribute that repels people they ascribed to him (ﷺ), and they did not take warning from those who came before, but rather they added to this.

﴿And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾ [Sad 4]. ﴿They wondered﴾: wonder (ʿajab) has two causes:
The first cause: denial.
The second cause: approval, meaning one says "he wondered at such-and-such," that is, he approved of it. And "he wondered at such-and-such" also means he denied it. So it resembles the words with opposite meanings (al-addād), because in the Arabic language there are words that indicate a meaning and its opposite, which the scholars of Arabic call al-addād in language.

Wonder sometimes is approval and sometimes is denial. The saying of ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Prophet (ﷺ) liked to start with the right in his footwear and in his combing" [Narrated by al-Bukhari, with his wording (168), and Muslim (268/76), both with their chains from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) liked to start with the right in his footwear, his combing, his purification, and in all his affairs]. The meaning of "liked" here is approval.

But here, ﴿they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾ is a wonder of denial, not a wonder of approval and pleasure; rather it is a wonder of denial and rejection. This is similar to the saying of Allah in Surah Qaf: ﴿Rather, they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves, so the disbelievers said, "This is a strange thing"﴾ [Qaf 2]. Here, the similar statement came in: ﴿And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾. The ﴿that (an)﴾ here is a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah) with the implied preposition "min," meaning: they wondered at the coming of a warner. We said it is maṣdariyyah because what follows it is converted into a verbal noun, that is: they wondered at the coming of a warner from among them.

As for His words ﴿warner (mundhir)﴾: the warner is the one who informs with news for the purpose of frightening. For this reason we say that warning (indhār) is news accompanied by frightening. The Prophet (ﷺ) was a warner and he was also a bringer of glad tidings, but the disbelievers, what suits their condition is what? Warning. ﴿To warn of a severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾, and glad tidings belong to whom? To the believers.

Here He said: ﴿they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾ because this is what befits their condition.

As for His words ﴿from among themselves﴾: in lineage and in kind. He is from among them in kind, because he is a human, and Allah did not send a messenger from among the angels to humans. In lineage, because he is from Quraysh. So he was from among them in kind and in lineage, and yet they wondered.

The author said: (a messenger from among themselves who warns them and frightens them with the Fire after resurrection), that is: after they are resurrected, and he is the Prophet (ﷺ). They wondered with a wonder of denial, rejection and refusal, even though they used to describe the Messenger (ﷺ) earlier as the truthful, the trustworthy. When he brought them the message, he became in their eyes a liar and a traitor, and we seek refuge in Allah.

So then, their enmity toward him was not directed at his person, but rather at what he brought.

﴿And the disbelievers said﴾: here the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun. How would the speech have been if the pronoun were used? It would be: "And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves, and they said: This is a sorcerer, a liar." But He said: ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾. The benefit of using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is:
First: to alert the listener, because when the style of speech changes, it compels the hearer to pay attention, unlike when it is in one uniform style, where sleep may overcome him, but when it differs, he pays attention.
Second: to record the disbelief upon these people, because if He had said "they said: this is a sorcerer, a liar," we would not have known their judgment; but when He said "the disbelievers said," we know that they are disbelievers.
Third: that what drives them to this is disbelief, so it is not far-fetched that others besides them would say the same as they said, because if the cause is one, then whenever this cause exists, the effect occurs from whatever person it may be. These are the benefits of using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, as ʿĪsā said to us.

* Student: Alerting the listener.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: Informing that these people are disbelievers.
* Shaykh: Yes. The third?
* Student: Recording disbelief upon the disbelievers.
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Recording disbelief upon the disbelievers.
* Shaykh: This is what the brother said.
* Student: Giving the reason for the ruling.
* Shaykh: That is: giving the cause of this saying, that the driving force behind it is disbelief, so this extends to others; that is, every disbeliever who says this statement. Good.

﴿And the disbelievers said: This is a sorcerer, a liar﴾. ﴿This is a sorcerer, a liar﴾: to whom do they point? To the warner from among them, who is the Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿A sorcerer, a liar﴾: they combined two blameworthy attributes. ﴿A sorcerer﴾, because he captivates people's minds. ﴿A liar﴾, because what he brought is falsehood that does not correspond to reality. So the Messenger (ﷺ), who is the most truthful of creation, became in their eyes a liar. They did not say "kādhib" (liar, active participle) but "kadhdhāb" (intensive form), because kadhdhāb is an attribute of one characterized by it, as you say najjār (carpenter), ḥaddād (blacksmith), and what is similar, which are fixed attributes. They said he is a sorcerer because of the strength of his influence upon his hearers, for when people heard his recitation they were greatly affected by it. Women and children used to gather at the house of the Messenger (ﷺ) to listen to his recitation, and they were affected by this recitation. The Quraysh disbelievers would say: Muhammad has bewitched our sons and our women, and he is a sorcerer because of the strength of his influence upon them. ﴿A liar﴾ means that what he brought is falsehood with no reality. Now, who is the liar? The liar is one who informs contrary to reality; whoever informs you contrary to reality has lied to you.

He said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing﴾ [Sad 5]. This is the object of denial. ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ This interrogative carries two meanings:
The first meaning: astonished denial.
The second: a profound denial directed at the Messenger (ﷺ), in that he made the gods one god. Here He said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾, where two objects were used: the first is ﴿the gods﴾, and the second is ﴿one God﴾. That is: has Muhammad turned the gods into one god, when they worship many gods: al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat, Hubal, and other idols? How can Muhammad come and say there is no god but Allah? This, in their view, is among the greatest lies.

Further, He says: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ From the point where he told them, "Say: there is no god but Allah," meaning: how can all creation fit into one god? This is from their ignorance and dullness, that they deny that the gods could be one god. So we say to them: Who is the Creator, and how many? They say: the Creator is Allah. How many is that? What is the answer? One. If the Creator is Allah, and He is one, as you believe, then there is no strangeness in the god being Allah and He being one. And whoever encompasses creation in creating it can encompass them in worship. If the gods did not create anything by your own acknowledgement, how can they deserve to be gods? And if it is possible for creation to be confined to one, then it is possible for worship to be confined to one.

For this reason He said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing﴾: ﴿this﴾ refers to his making the gods one god; that is, indeed his making the gods one god ﴿is a strange thing﴾. ﴿Strange (ʿujāb)﴾ means wondrous, but the word ʿujāb is more emphatic than ʿajīb (wondrous), because it indicates intensity, that is: it is a thing at which a person wonders greatly and extensively. For this reason they turned away from ʿajīb to ʿujāb: ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the chiefs among them walked away, saying: "Go on, and be steadfast in your gods"﴾ [Sad 6]. ﴿The chiefs walked away﴾, and the place of walking away was not mentioned, so that it includes every place where they gather and discuss such matters. Whenever they gathered in a place and discussed among themselves what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought of monotheism, they would walk away from that place, enjoining one another in falsehood and steadfastness upon it. For this reason He said: ﴿the chiefs walked away﴾. The chiefs (al-mala') are the nobles, the great ones, and the notables. The nobles, the great ones and the notables were the ones who confronted the messengers with rejection and refusal, out of fear for their status lest it be lost by following the messengers. If you reflect on the Qur'an, you will find that those who stand against the messengers are the chiefs and the nobles, while the weak, the women, the children and the poor are the first to submit to the messengers.

Here the chiefs walk away from whatever place they are in. Every place where they gather and mention what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought of monotheism, they walk away in this manner.

As for the words of the author: (﴿the chiefs walked away﴾ from their gathering at Abu Talib's, and their hearing there that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Say: there is no god but Allah"), this is restricting an unrestricted statement. We have mentioned that interpreting the Qur'an by what is more specific is deficient, because it confines the absolute meaning to this restricted meaning, or the general meaning to the particular meaning, and this is undoubtedly a deficiency, unless evidence establishes it, in which case the evidence is followed. The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you"﴾ [Ali 'Imran 173] is general. But if we apply this statement to reality, we find that the intended "people" is specific: ﴿to whom the people said﴾ refers to a single speaker, ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾; not all people gathered against the Messenger (ﷺ), since those to whom the message had not reached did not gather against him. So interpreting "people" here as something specific is an interpretation supported by reality. But if there is no evidence, the obligation is to keep the Qur'an on its generality if it is general, and on its absoluteness if it is absolute.

Now we say: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, made the walking away from a specific gathering, namely the gathering in which they assembled with the Messenger (ﷺ) at Abu Talib's, when he said: "Say: there is no god but Allah." However, it is better that we make it general, including this gathering and others.

﴿Go on, and be steadfast in your gods﴾ [Sad 6]. ﴿Go on and be steadfast﴾: is the intended meaning here walking on foot, or walking in the sense of following a way; that is, continue on your way and be steadfast upon your gods?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verses 1–6 (part 3 of 4):

Whoever looks at the word "departed" (inṭalaqa) in ﴿And the eminent ones among them departed﴾ says: The intended meaning is walking on foot. That is, when they departed, some of them urged others to walk and move on, so that they would not return and turn back to the place they had left, as though they were departing in flight. So they advise one another to walk. If we look at the meaning, or at the general circumstances of these people, we say that the intended meaning is what? Walking along the path. That is, "Go on along your way, and let no one trouble you."

﴿And be steadfast for your gods﴾: that is, restrain yourselves for them, do not swerve from them. And this falls under the category of mutual counsel toward what? Toward falsehood.

(Some of them say to others: ﴿Walk on and be steadfast for your gods﴾, hold firm to their worship. ﴿Indeed, this﴾ mentioned, namely the monotheism, ﴿is a thing that is intended﴾.) ﴿Be steadfast for your gods﴾: that is, hold firm to them in their worship, defend them, and do not accept anything that would invalidate them. Be steadfast.

﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾. ﴿This﴾, referring to what the Prophet ﷺ brought of monotheism, ﴿is a thing that is intended﴾: that is, he who brought it intends it. This indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Its meaning is that this man has said a statement that he intends, so he is serious in his words. A thing that is intended must have its intender strive to bring it about. This is unlike the person who says a statement with the tongue and not with the heart. You will find that the one who says a statement with both tongue and heart is determined and resolved to carry out what he said, whereas the one who does not intend it has a superficial statement.

So their words, ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾: who intends it? Its speaker, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. When a statement issues from intention, this means that its speaker is resolved upon it and upon its victory, and that this statement becomes the prevailing one that people follow. This is unlike one who says a statement he does not intend, such as saying it out of courtesy, or to pass the time, or the like, for he will not have the sincere resolve to carry out what he said.

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿We have not heard of this in the latter religion; this is nothing but a fabrication. Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?  Rather, they are in doubt about My reminder; rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 7, 8].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And they marvelled that a warner from among themselves had come to them﴾.
﴿So they called out, but it was not the time for escape.﴾ What is this call?
* Student: (...) for seeking help.
* Shaykh: Yes, but whom do they call upon?
* Student: In general, they call upon themselves (...) and they call upon Allah.
* Shaykh: To seek relief?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Good. Regarding His words ﴿and it was not the time for escape﴾, how do you parse (lāt)?
* Student: Lā is a negation of the genus and it works like laysa, and the tā is an added letter for feminizing the word; the noun of (lā) is omitted, its estimated form being "al-ḥīn" (the time), and its predicate is ﴿ḥīna manāṣ﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿ḥīna manāṣ﴾. And what is the meaning of ﴿manāṣ﴾?
* Student: ﴿Manāṣ﴾ means: flight and escape.
* Shaykh: That is, flight and escape. Good, well done. Meaning, when the punishment has befallen them, even if they call out and seek help, there is no escape for them from it.

Regarding His words ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾, there is a rhetorical point in it. What is it?
* Student: In it is the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and this has several benefits:
The first benefit: alerting, because if the speech continued in one pattern here, the listener would not have paid attention.
Second: it informs that these people are disbelievers.
Third: it gives the reason that whoever says this statement is a disbeliever, so it extends to everyone who says a similar statement, that he is a disbeliever.
* Shaykh: Yes. Regarding His words ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾, the interrogative is for what?
* Student: For denunciation and astonishment.
* Shaykh: Yes. And the pronoun in His words ﴿made﴾ refers to whom?
* Student: To Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ.
* Shaykh: To Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ. Good.
How did they combine describing him as a sorcerer and a liar? Sorcery is considered from what standpoint?
* Student: The statement that God is one God.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Sorcery, because the sorcerer captivates minds (...).
* Shaykh: From the standpoint of the effect of his speech? Good. And "liar" (kadhdhāb)?
* Student: From the standpoint of his reporting contrary to reality.
* Shaykh: From the standpoint of what he reported. Good. So they described him as a sorcerer from the standpoint of the effect of his speech, just as a sorcerer affects the one who is bewitched, and as a liar from the standpoint of what he reported.
Good. Regarding His words ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is astonishing﴾, what is the meaning of ʿujāb?
* Student: It is a form of intensification, its origin being ʿajīb.
* Shaykh: In the sense of ʿajīb, but they came with...
* Student: With an intensive form.
* Shaykh: They came with an intensive form in it.
* Student: For denial.
* Shaykh: An intensification in marvelling at it.

His exalted words: ﴿Go on and be steadfast for your gods﴾: what is meant by walking? Is it walking on foot, or walking along the path?
* Student: Walking along their way.
* Shaykh: Along their way. Good. And is it not valid that it be walking on foot?
* Student: ﴿Go on and be steadfast for your gods﴾ (...) walking along the road.
* Shaykh: So it is not valid that it be walking on foot?
* Student: It is possible.
* Shaykh: How so?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, but how so? We have now understood that it is valid, but how is it so? How do they conspire, or how does one of them command the others to walk on foot?
* Student: (...) departing, (...) walking on foot.
* Shaykh: Yes, I am saying: how do they counsel one another to walk on foot? That is, why?
* Student: In flight.
* Shaykh: In flight, fearing that the gathering in which they are called to monotheism would influence them. As for walking along the path, it is clear.

Regarding His words ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾: Sami, what is the meaning of ﴿a thing that is intended﴾?
* Student: That what he brought is a thing that is intended from it; he wants us to follow what he brought.
* Shaykh: Yes. Is it intended from us, or intended from him?
* Student: He intends from us.
* Shaykh: From us.
* Student: And from us also; he wants us to follow him (...).
* Shaykh: Good. That it is intended from us is well known: the Messenger only called them because he wanted this thing from them. But how is it intended from him?
* Student: That they should leave their gods and follow him.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: It is intended from him because the one who has an intention must fulfil his intention.
* Shaykh: Yes, because among people there are those who speak words but do not care about them and do not intend what they lead to, unlike the speaker who speaks words and intends what he says. For this reason we often hear people say: "I say such-and-such and I mean what I say," meaning that he will carry it out and act upon it. So if the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, intends what he says, then it means that he will strive with all he can to accomplish it.

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: it is recommended to begin with it in important matters, and for this reason Allah begins every surah with it, and it is known that a surah is an important matter. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Every matter of importance that does not begin with the name of Allah is cut off (abtar)."[[Narrated by al-Khatib in al-Jami' (1210) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] The hadith is ḥasan.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of divinity for Allah in His words ﴿In the name of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's names, since His words ﴿In the name of Allah﴾ is a singular noun in construct, and so it encompasses every name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason some exegetes explain it by saying: "That is, I begin with every name of Allah."
* Among its benefits: seeking blessing by mentioning the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so the names of Allah are among what one calls upon Allah by, as in His words ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾, and among what one seeks blessing through and seeks help by, because it is placed before important matters. If you wish to know the extent of the blessing of this naming, look at the sacrificial animal over which the name is pronounced: it becomes good and lawful; and if the name is not pronounced over it, it becomes impure and unlawful, even though the slaughterer is one, the instrument by which it is slaughtered is one, the place of slaughter is one, and the flow of blood is one; everything is one. But when the naming was missing, it became impure carrion that is not lawful to eat. When the name is pronounced over it, it becomes good.
"When a man comes to his wife and says: 'In the name of Allah. O Allah, keep Satan away from us and keep Satan away from what You provide us,' then if a child is born to them, Satan will not harm him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6388) and Muslim (1434/116) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, with the wording: "If one of you, when he comes to his wife, says: 'In the name of Allah, O Allah, keep Satan away from us and keep Satan away from what You have provided us,' then if a child is decreed for them, Satan will never harm him."]] If he does not say this naming, he is exposed to the possibility that his child will be afflicted by Satan and harmed by him.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of mercy for Allah in His words ﴿the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, and that it is vast mercy, from His words ﴿the Entirely Merciful﴾, because ar-Rahman is an attribute that indicates breadth and fullness.
* Among them: the affirmation of the three names, which are Allah, ar-Rahman, and ar-Rahim.

Then Allah, exalted, says: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder. Rather, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾ [Sad 1, 2].
* Among the benefits of these verses: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, with letters, spoken with the Arabic letters from which people speak and form their speech, from His words ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾.
* Among its benefits: the virtue and nobility of the Qur'an, since Allah swears by it, and one does not swear except by a great thing.
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of swearing by the Qur'an. From where is this derived?
* Students: ﴿By the Qur'an﴾.
* Shaykh: This is an error. There is no evidence in it for the permissibility of swearing by the Qur'an, because Allah swears by things by which it is not permissible for us to swear, such as His words ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [ash-Shams 1], ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl 1]. So when Allah swears by something, it does not follow that we are permitted to swear by it, because Allah swears by whatever He wills. But we swear by the Qur'an on the basis of another proof, not this verse, namely that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and so it is one of His attributes, and swearing by the attributes of Allah is permissible.
* Among the benefits of these verses: that the Qur'an is a reminder in the senses we mentioned concerning the meaning of reminder. It is an admonition by which one is reminded, a reminder by which a person is reminded and learns, a reminder by which honour is attained, and a reminder of Allah by which one worships Allah through its recitation, just as one worships by the remembrance: "There is no god but Allah," "Glory be to Allah," and "Praise be to Allah."
* Among the benefits of these verses: the clarification of the zealotry and false arrogance within the souls of the disbelievers, from His words ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾.
* Among its benefits also: that the disbelievers do not (...) over their disbelief, and they persist in their transgression and arrogance, rather they try to turn the servants of Allah away from the religion of Allah, because they are in constant opposition, opposing Allah and His Messenger.
* Among the benefits of the verses: that we may say they are in constant pride and opposition against the truth, whether against Allah, or against the Messenger, or against the heirs of the Messenger, who are the scholars, or against the followers of the Messenger in general, who are whom? The believers. So they are in constant opposition to the people of truth.

Then He, exalted, says: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, and they called out, but it was not the time for escape﴾ [Sad 3].
* Among the benefits of this verse: consolation for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, that Allah destroyed the deniers before them, so it is fitting that He destroy these. We have explained during the exegesis that Allah destroyed these, but at whose hand? At the hand of the Messenger ﷺ and his companions in the battles in which they were victorious. We said that this victory, support and abandonment is more eloquent than the victory that Allah brings from Himself, because Allah punishes these by the hands of His servants, the believers, and His party.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a warning to these deniers that they will never overcome Allah in anything, just as those before them did not overcome Him: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: that denial of the messengers was widespread, because the destruction of generations was only on account of their denial. So when generations are many, it follows that denial is many; that is, when the generations destroyed are many, it necessarily follows that denial is many.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the clarification of Allah's power and greatness, in that He destroyed many nations and great generations. Allah, exalted, says: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right and said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they were rejecting Our signs. So We sent upon them a furious wind during days of misfortune, that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life﴾ [Fussilat 15, 16]. So Allah, mighty and majestic, has made clear that Allah who created them is mightier than them in strength, and that He punished them with what is the most subtle of things, namely the wind.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that destroyed nations, when punishment descends upon them, gain nothing from calling upon Allah or upon themselves, from His words ﴿and they called out, but it was not the time for escape﴾, meaning there is no escape from this punishment that has descended upon them.

Then Allah, exalted, says: ﴿And they marvelled that a warner from among themselves had come to them. And the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar"﴾ [Sad 4].
* In this is evidence of the foolishness of the Quraysh, who denied the Messenger ﷺ and found what he brought strange. The reason for this is that no one came to them who was a stranger to them, neither in kind nor in lineage. The one who came to them was of their own kind, a human like them, and of their own lineage, from Quraysh. Yet despite this they marvelled, finding what came to them strange.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of proof against these people by the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; from His words ﴿a warner﴾, meaning he has established proof against them by warning. The proof has been established for the Messenger ﷺ that he did not fall short in his message, but warned and carried out what he was to do of conveyance.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these who marvelled in denial are disbelievers, from His words ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾.
* Among its benefits: that whoever says a statement like theirs and marvels with a marvel like theirs, they are disbelievers, of whatever kind among mankind.
* Among the benefits of the verses: the clarification of the strength of the influence of the Messenger's speech upon people's souls, as in their saying ﴿This is a sorcerer﴾, and a sorcerer affects the one who is bewitched.
* Among its benefits: their lying in describing the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when they said he is a sorcerer and a liar, while in reality the liars are they, the ones who lied in what they described the Messenger ﷺ with.
* Among its benefits: that the enemies of the messengers do not oppose them with personal enmity, but they oppose them with enmity toward the message they brought.

It follows from this benefit that the disbelievers will be enemies of all who follow the Messenger: whoever follows the Messenger will find enemies among the disbelievers and the hypocrites.

It follows from this also the consolation of whoever meets enmity from the enemies of Allah when he holds fast to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger: it is said to him, "This enmity that has befallen you has befallen one better than you, so do not be surprised."

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the enemies of the messengers, indeed the enemies of the message, attach evil nicknames to whoever holds fast to the Shariah, such as what?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They attach evil nicknames to everyone who holds fast to the Sharia, from their saying ﴿This is a sorcerer, a liar﴾.

This has indeed happened. The people of negation (ahl al-ta'til), for example, describe the Salafi people of affirmation (ahl al-ithbat) as "hashwiyya," "mujassima," "mumaththila," "ra'a'," "ghawghaʾ," "hashwiyya," and similar evil nicknames, in order to repel people.

The wonder is that these people, who attach evil epithets to others, if we reflect we would find that this title they gave to those who hold fast to the Shariah of Allah applies to them. Has it not reached you the saying of the hypocrites about the Messenger ﷺ and his companions? They said: "We have never seen the like of these our reciters: more gluttonous in their bellies, more lying in their tongues, and more cowardly at the encounter than these reciters."

To whom do these three attributes apply? They apply to them. They are the most lying of people in their tongues, the most cowardly of people at the encounter, and the most gluttonous of people in their bellies; their only concern is their bellies. So whoever describes the people of evil with an attribute, his description is the first to apply to him.

* Among the benefits of these verses: those who denied the Messenger ﷺ did not establish any proof for what they denied, and they had nothing but abuse and insult. This shows the weakness of the argument of whoever opposes you. When you find that the one who opposes you has nothing but shouting, wailing, slapping the cheek, pulling out the hair and the like, know that he has no proof. He only wants to create confusion against you so that you may be defeated. Otherwise, the possessor of proof presents his proof without agitation, presents his proof calmly without stirring things up. As for cursing and reviling, this is evidence that he is defeated and forsaken, and that he wants to take this weapon as a refuge and a way out of the distress he is in, being unable to repel the proof of his opponent.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad 5].

* Benefits of this verse:
* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ used to call these people to monotheism, to the monotheism of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His divinity or in His lordship? He, with these people, debated them about divinity and called them to the monotheism of divinity (tawhid al-uluhiyyah), because the monotheism of lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah) was established among them, and they acknowledged it: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 9], ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created them?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 87]. They do not deny the monotheism of lordship, but they deny the monotheism of divinity; therefore they said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾. So the conflict between the Messenger ﷺ and the disbelievers of Quraysh was over the monotheism of divinity; as for the monotheism of lordship, they had acknowledged it.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the obligation to give priority to the most important over the less important in calling to Allah. The Messenger ﷺ, when he first called these people, called them to monotheism; he did not say: "Pray, nor give zakah, nor fast, nor perform Hajj"; he called them to monotheism. This is the manner of the Qur'an, and this is the practice of the Sunnah of the Messenger ﷺ. When he sent Mu'adh to Yemen, he commanded him that the first thing he should call them to is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obstinacy of those who denied the monotheism of divinity, in that they claimed that calling to it is a very strange matter, as shown by their saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾. As I said to you a moment ago: whoever describes the truth with the attributes of falsehood, the reality is that these attributes return to him. So which is more strange? A man who calls to the monotheism of Allah, or another who calls to associating partners with Him and denying monotheism? Which is more strange? The second. Therefore we say: the strange thing is that you deny the monotheism of Allah and claim that there is a partner with Allah; this is the strange thing. As for a man who calls to the monotheism of Allah, which is indicated by the natural disposition (fitrah) and indicated by the cosmic and legislative signs, this is not strange; rather, the strange thing is your own action.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the use of emphasizing particles in speech, and that this is one of the linguistic methods; as shown by their saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a thing﴾. They emphasized this sentence with two emphatics: inna and the lam: ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the chiefs among them went away, saying, "Walk on and be steadfast for your gods. Indeed, this is a thing that is intended"﴾ [Sad 6].

* In this also: evidence of these people's fear of the effect of the Prophet's ﷺ call upon them; and for this reason they used to urge one another to be patient for their gods, and they used to urge one another to remain and be firm in their way, and they used to urge one another to flee from the places where monotheism is called to. All of this is derived from His saying: ﴿Walk on and be steadfast for your gods﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that the people of falsehood cling to their falsehood, preserve it, and fear its shaking; as shown by His saying: ﴿And the chiefs among them went away, saying, "Walk on and be steadfast for your gods"﴾. Likewise, you will always find the people of falsehood surrounding their falsehood with a fence that prevents access to it in a way that tears this falsehood apart.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that gathering around a thing has an effect on its survival and firmness. From where is this derived? From their mutual exhortation to remain firm in what they were upon and to be patient for their gods. There is no doubt that collective action is more effective than individual action, whatever the individual may be; that is, whatever the individual's strength, there is no doubt that collective action has an effect. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ commanded us to marry the loving, fertile woman[[Abu Dawud (2050) narrated with his chain from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I have found a woman of noble family and beauty, but she does not bear children; should I marry her?" He said: "No." Then he came to him a second time and he forbade him; then he came a third time and he said: "Marry the loving, fertile woman, for I shall outnumber the nations through you."]], for the sake of the abundance of the community, since abundance has a great effect. For this reason Allah mentioned it as a favour upon the Children of Israel in His Book when He said: ﴿And We made you more numerous in manpower﴾ [al-Isra 6], and Shu'ayb reminded his people of it when he said: ﴿And remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾ [al-A'raf 86]. The common people say: "Numbers overcome bravery."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ used to say a statement and mean what he says; as shown by their saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾.
* Among its benefits also: when a person means what he says, his effect on the listener is greater; because speech, as it is by the tongue, the tongue is a means of expressing what is in the heart, and if the tongue expresses what is in the heart truly, then the means that receives this speech, which is the ear, conveys what it hears to the heart. For this reason the common people say: "What is from the tongue will not pass beyond the ears, and what is from the heart penetrates the heart." This is true: speech that comes from the heart has a far greater effect than speech that comes from the tongue. Let me give an example: if two men stood to admonish the people, one of them admonishing from the heart, so that you feel he is speaking from the heart and the effect of his words appears on the features of his face, and the other is more eloquent and more ornate and polished in his speech, but his words come only from his tongue while his heart is contrary to that, or at least he does not believe in what he says. Which of them is more effective?

The first is more effective. If a common man speaks with common speech but it is conveyed, people are affected by it more than if a man eloquent of tongue and strong in expression spoke while his heart was empty of what he says. This is an observable matter, and for this reason the disbelievers said: ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾ [Sad 6], meaning: it is said and is really intended. Because of the strength of the Prophet's ﷺ intention in what he says, they feared this intention, and said: ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended.﴾ And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. ﴿Sad. By the Quran, full of reminder﴾ [Sad 1]. The author said: (Surat Sad is Meccan). The Noble Quran includes both Meccan and Medinan revelation. The most correct view on distinguishing the Meccan from the Medinan is that what was revealed before the Hijrah is Meccan, and what was revealed after it is Medinan, even if it was revealed outside Medina. The dividing line is therefore temporal, not spatial: what came after the Hijrah is Medinan, and what came before it is Meccan.

He said: (Eighty-six or eighty-eight verses). The verses (ayat) are the separations that occur between one sentence or two sentences or more. They were named ayah because they are a miracle (mu'jizah), for the Quran, as has already been mentioned, challenged people through Allah to produce a discourse like it, even if it were brief.

He said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. This basmalah is a verse of the Book of Allah, and it is recited at the beginning of every surah except Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), for it is not recited at its beginning. That is because when the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, compiled the Mushaf, they were uncertain whether Bara'ah was a continuation of al-Anfal or a surah in its own right. So they placed a separation without a basmalah. Had they been certain that it belonged to al-Anfal, they would not have placed a separation; and had they been certain that it was independent, they would have placed the basmalah. However, we know that this ijtihad on their part matches reality and that they were certainly correct in it, because if the basmalah had been revealed between al-Anfal and Bara'ah, it would have been preserved, since Allah says: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr 9]. Since it was not preserved, by the ijtihad of the Companions, it is known that they were correct with respect to reality.

The basmalah, as you can see, consists of a preposition with its object (jar wa-majrur), a genitive construction (mudaf ilayhi), and a descriptive adjective, meaning a na't. The grammatical rule is that every prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) must have a complement (muta'alliq), that is, something it is connected to. The thing to which the prepositional phrase is connected is the governing element ('amil), and the prepositional phrase is the governed element (ma'mul). For this reason the compiler of the Jumal (Nazim al-Jumal) said:

"The prepositional phrase must have a connection
to a verb or what carries its meaning, such as the active or passive participle.
Exclude every extra particle that has an effect,
such as the bā', min, the kāf, and also la'alla."

So every original (non-extra) particle must have a connection to a verb or to something that has the meaning of a verb, such as the active participle and the passive participle.

Therefore the basmalah must have a complement. What is this complement? The most correct view on the complement of the basmalah is that it is a verb, placed later, appropriate to the context. If you wish to recite, the estimate is (bismillahi aqra'u, "In the name of Allah I recite"). If you wish to eat, the estimate is (bismillahi ākulu, "In the name of Allah I eat"). If you wish to slaughter an animal, the estimate is (bismillahi adhbahu, "In the name of Allah I slaughter"). For this reason the Messenger ﷺ said: «So let him slaughter in the name of Allah»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7400), and Muslim (1960 / 1 and 2), from the hadith of Jundub ibn Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

It is estimated as a verb because the basic element in governing is the verb; for this reason it governs its object without condition, whereas the active participle, the passive participle, the superlative and the verbal noun govern only under conditions. Good. So we estimate it as a verb, and we estimate it as placed later, so we say: "In the name of Allah I recite," for two reasons.

The first reason: seeking blessing by beginning with (bismillah).

The second reason: conveying restriction (hasr), because placing the governed element after the governing element conveys restriction, since one of the ways of restriction is to place first what should come later. Good. We estimated it as appropriate to the context, because it indicates the intended meaning more clearly than if we estimated it as a general verb, as some have said: the estimate is "In the name of Allah I begin," or "In the name of Allah I start," because "In the name of Allah I start" does not specify the action with which you begin.

So the summary is that in the basmalah we estimate:
* The student: The governing element.
* The Shaykh: We estimate it as what?
* The student: "In the name of Allah."
* The Shaykh: Yes. And what do we estimate the governing element to be? That is, what do we estimate the complement of the prepositional phrase to be?
* The student: That it is a verb placed later, appropriate...
* The Shaykh: Yes, we estimate it as a verb placed later, appropriate to the context. We estimate it as a verb. Why? Let us hear.
* The student: Because the basic element in governing is the verb.
* The Shaykh: Because the basic element in governing is that it be a verb. Good, and we estimate it as placed later.
* The student: For two reasons...
* The Shaykh: Two reasons?
* The student: Seeking blessing by beginning with "In the name of Allah." The second: restriction.
* The Shaykh: Seeking blessing by beginning with "In the name of Allah"; the second: conveying restriction. How do we say "conveying restriction"? Why?
* The student: The rule is that when the governed element comes after the governing element, it conveys restriction.
* The Shaykh: The third: we estimate it as an appropriate verb?
* The student: Because it indicates the intended meaning more clearly.
* The Shaykh: Because it indicates the intended meaning more clearly; for if you estimate "In the name of Allah I recite," it indicates the intended meaning more clearly than your saying "In the name of Allah I begin"; because "I begin" — begin with what? So it is more indicative and more specific.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Sad﴾. The author said: (Allah knows best what He means by it). This is because the word ﴿Sad﴾ is a letter of the alphabet that does not indicate a meaning in the Arabic language. A group of scholars held that the disconnected letters with which some surahs begin are symbols pointing to meanings, and each person specified them according to what he saw as appropriate. Others held that they are names of Allah or names of the Messenger, and others held what the author held, that their meaning is unknown and we do not know what they mean.

But the preponderant view is that of the imam of the exegetes of his era, Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him: that we say they have no meaning. This is because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193–195]. The clear Arabic tongue does not establish a meaning for these disconnected letters. On this basis, these letters have no meaning. That is, what is the meaning of (Sad), (Nun), (Qaf), (Alif-Lam-Mim), and the like? They have no meaning in the Arabic language, so they have no meaning in the Quran either, because the Quran is in the Arabic language.

However, this view, despite its preponderance, faces an objection: it implies that there are words in the Quran that are meaningless and have no benefit.

The answer to this is that we say: they are not meaningless in their context, for they came for a great purpose. That purpose is that this great Quran, which defeated the eloquent speakers of the language and the masters of rhetoric, did not come in letters unfamiliar to them, so that they could say, "By Allah, we do not know these letters." Rather, it came in the letters of which their speech is composed.

Those who held this view said: The evidence for this is that you hardly see a surah beginning with a disconnected letter without finding, after that letter, a mention of the Quran: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 1–2]; ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer. He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran 1–3]; ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad. A Book revealed to you﴾ [al-A'raf 1–2]; ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the wise Book﴾ [Yunus 1]. So every surah beginning with these disconnected letters is followed by a mention of the Quran, except for the saying of Allah: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum 1–3] and ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. Do people think they will be left [to say, "We believe"]?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 1–2].

This can be answered by saying: As for His saying, ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. Do people think they will be left to say, "We believe"﴾, it mentions a great attribute of those who hold fast to the Quran, namely patience over harm for the sake of Allah. As for the second, ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾, it mentions something of the characteristics of revelation, namely knowledge of the unseen, for the fact that the Romans have now been defeated and will be victorious in some years is something only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows, and it is one of the distinctive features of revelation. Whether or not this answer is sound and acceptable, an exception does not establish a rule.

He said: ﴿Sad﴾. So we say concerning it: ﴿Sad﴾ is a letter of the alphabet that has no meaning, but it was brought for the purpose of indicating that this Noble Quran, which defeated these Arabs, was composed of these letters from which their speech is made up.

He said: ﴿By the Quran, full of reminder﴾. The waw here is the particle of oath (waw al-qasam); for this reason the word after it is in the genitive: ﴿al-Quran﴾. ﴿By the Quran, full of reminder﴾. The waw is a particle of oath, which only enters upon a apparent noun, and the verb of oath is not mentioned with it. That is, the waw of oath is distinguished by not entering upon an apparent noun and not having the verb of oath mentioned with it. This differs from the ba', the ba' of oath, which enters upon an apparent noun and upon a pronoun, and the verb of oath is mentioned with it and may be omitted, and it enters upon every noun. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾ [al-An'am 109], where the verb of oath is mentioned with it. You say: "By my Lord, I will certainly do it," or "I swear by Him, I will certainly do it." Here it entered upon a pronoun. As for the ta', it is the most specific of the particles of oath; it enters only upon Allah and the verb of oath is not mentioned with it. It has been said that it enters upon Allah and upon Rabb. Ibn Malik said:

.......................... ∗∗∗ .......... "And the ta' is for Allah and Rabb."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿By the Quran, full of reminder﴾, and Allah most often swears by the waw, because it is the most common on the tongues, so it came as the most frequent in the Quran.

﴿By the Quran, full of reminder﴾. ﴿Dhi﴾ means "possessor of," and it is in the genitive, but it is in the genitive by the letter standing in place of the kasrah.

As for His saying ﴿full of reminder﴾, the author said: (that is, of clarification or honor). This means that the Quran is full of reminder, that is, full of clarification for people, admonishing them and by which they are reminded; or full of honor because of its nobility and the nobility of those who act by it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people, and you will be questioned﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44]. So it is a reminder by which what benefits people in their livelihood and their hereafter is mentioned, a reminder by which people are reminded and admonished, and it is the greatest admonition; a reminder, meaning honor for whoever holds fast to it. So it is a reminder because it admonishes people and advises them; it is a reminder because mentioned in it is what? That which relates to the welfare of people in their livelihood and their hereafter; it is a reminder because it is honor for whoever holds fast to it, based on Allah's saying: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people, and you will be questioned﴾.

He said: (The response to this oath is omitted). Why did the author say "the response to this oath"? Because there is no oath without a response, for an oath has three pillars, indeed four: the one who swears, the thing sworn by, the thing sworn to, and the formula. Every oath must include these, and they are four.

* A student: The formula, the one who swears, the thing sworn by, the response; these are four.
* Another student: The one who swears, the thing sworn to, the thing sworn by, and the formula.
* The Shaykh: Good. So every oath must have four pillars: the one who swears, the thing sworn by, the thing sworn to, and the formula.

The thing sworn to is the response of the oath. So every oath must have a response, and if the response is mentioned it is known, and if it is omitted, the context determines it. ﴿They swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths: if you ordered them, they would surely go forth﴾ [al-Nur 53]. Here the response is mentioned, or not? ﴿They swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths, if you ordered them, they would surely go forth﴾: "they would surely go forth" is mentioned. ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghabun 7]: "you will surely be resurrected" is mentioned.

In this verse the thing sworn by and the formula are present, ﴿By the Quran, full of reminder﴾, and the one who swears is Allah. What remains is the thing sworn to, which is the response of the oath. The author says: (It is omitted, and its estimate is: the matter is not as the disbelievers of Makkah said regarding the plurality of gods). This is the estimate, so the response of the oath is a negated clause: (the matter is not as the disbelievers of Makkah said regarding the plurality of gods). But the matter is that the God is one, and He is Allah. The estimate the author mentioned is not a fixed one; that is, if someone were to say the estimate is ﴿By the Quran, full of reminder﴾ that indeed your God is one, that would achieve what the author's statement achieves, that the matter is not as the disbelievers of Makkah said. Some scholars held that such an oath needs no response, because its response is known from it, like His saying: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection. And I swear by the reproaching soul. Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 1–3], and ﴿By the dawn, and ten nights, and the even and the odd, and the night when it passes. Is there not in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ [al-Fajr 1–5]; there is no response. So the thing sworn by contains the response. How does the thing sworn by contain the response in this oath clause? ﴿By the Quran, full of reminder﴾ means that you have been reminded by this Quran, and among what it reminds of is that Allah is One. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, in his book al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Quran, held this view: that the oath sometimes does not need the response to be mentioned, nor even to be estimated, because it is known from the context of the thing sworn by.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [Sad 2]. ﴿Bal﴾ here is for idrab. Is it the idrab of nullification (ibtali) or of transition (intiqali)?

* Students: Nullification.
* The Shaykh: What is the difference between them? Nullification is the cancelling of what preceded, as if he wiped it out and brought something in its place; transition is the affirmation of what preceded but moving from one thing to another, and what came before this idrab remains, not nullified.

He said: (﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ from the people of Makkah). The author's restriction of "those who disbelieve" to the people of Makkah is open to question, and it is better to take the general meaning. Taking the Quran as specifying some individuals of a general term is neither sound nor good, because it is a deficiency in the interpretation unless there is evidence for it. If evidence exists, the evidence must be followed; but if no evidence exists, what is obligatory? What is obligatory is to take the general meaning, because it is more comprehensive and richer in meaning. So "those who disbelieve" includes the people of Makkah and others until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿In arrogance﴾, and it is not the arrogance of domination like the "might" in His saying: ﴿But might belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]; rather, it is the arrogance of pride, haughtiness and obstinacy. For this reason he said: (zeal and pride against faith). This is a blameworthy might, because it is a might that prevents its possessor from accepting the truth, whereas the might that is the might of victory is support for its possessor, and there is a great difference between them.

He said: ﴿in arrogance and opposition﴾, that is, antagonism (mushaqqah). So shiqaq is a verbal noun of shaqqa, like qital is a verbal noun of qatala, and the meaning is antagonism. Antagonism toward whom? Antagonism toward Allah and His Messenger; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal 13]. Here the author said: (opposition, enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ), and this too is open to question. Why? Because he restricted opposition to the Prophet ﷺ, although the disbelievers oppose Allah and His Messenger; they are in pride, haughtiness, zeal and antagonism toward Allah and His Messenger. That is, they turn away from what Allah and His Messenger commanded, as if they were on one side, while what the revelation brought is on another side. ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. Someone might say: they are also in opposition among themselves, especially the Jews, for Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You think they are united, but their hearts are divided﴾ [al-Hashr 14].

He said: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾ [Sad 3]. (﴿How many﴾ means many). Among you (meaning many) with the accusative? [Students:] Yes.
* The Shaykh: (Many ﴿We destroyed before them﴾, that is, a multitude of nations).

The saying ﴿How many We destroyed﴾: the author estimated it with his statement "many," so "how many" is here a kathrah (multiplicative) construction. It is in the accusative as a direct object preceding ﴿We destroyed﴾; ﴿before them﴾ is related to ﴿We destroyed﴾; and ﴿from a generation﴾ is a specification (tamyiz) for ﴿how many﴾, because "kam" is an ambiguous noun that requires a specification, that is, something that explains and specifies it. If it were said only ﴿How many We destroyed before them﴾, the sentence would not be clear: destroyed what? But when ﴿from a generation﴾ is added, the sentence becomes clear; for this reason we say that ﴿from a generation﴾ is a specification of what? Of ﴿how many﴾, governed by ﴿from﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 4):

﴿How many generations did We destroy before them?﴾ "Before them" refers to the disbelievers who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). His words ﴿generations﴾ mean nations (ummah). The meaning is that Allah destroyed many nations before these people, and whoever destroyed many nations before these people is certainly able to destroy them too. However, the destruction of the earlier nations was by a punishment from Allah, while the destruction of those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ) was at the hands of the believers. The fighting and warfare that took place between the Messenger (ﷺ) and them was a punishment upon these deniers, and it was carried out at the hands of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Fight them, and Allah will punish them by your hands, and disgrace them, and give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people. And He will remove the rage of their hearts. And Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills, and Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ [at-Tawbah 14–15]. There is no doubt that the punishment of enemies at the hands of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions is more healing to the hearts of the believers than if the punishment came directly from Allah the Glorified and Exalted. This is something observed: when your enemy is defeated by your hand, it is more healing for your heart, more life-giving for your soul, stronger and more honourable than if Allah destroyed him by a punishment from Himself. For this reason the destruction of those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ) came at the hands of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Companions, and Allah knows best.

(...) returns to the words according to their wording, and it is permissible for it to return to the words according to their meaning. Have you not seen the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat 9], and He did not say "fought" in the dual form (iqtatalā)? Had He said iqtatalā, the pronoun would have referred to the wording. But when He said iqtatalū (plural), it referred to the meaning, because the ṭā'ifah (group) is a collective. So here ﴿they called out﴾ means the generation (qarn), and the pronoun refers back to it according to its meaning.

As for His words ﴿they called out﴾, the author says: (at the time the punishment descended upon them). But whom did they call out to? Does the meaning mean that some of them called out to others, seeking help from one another? But this is not possible? Or does the meaning mean that they called out to Allah, that is, they invoked Him to rescue them? Or does the meaning mean that both occurred from them?

The principle we have in tafsir is that whenever a word is suitable for two or more meanings, it is taken to include all of them together. Based on this, ﴿they called out﴾ has its object omitted for generality: some of them call out to others, "O so-and-so, help me, help me." Likewise they call out to Allah, since Allah says: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir 84]. But Allah said: ﴿And no time was there for escape﴾. ﴿Lāta﴾ here is the negative (lā) to which the feminine ta' has been added to mark the feminine form of the word, just as the ta' of feminine is added to (rubba) and (thumma) to mark the feminine form of the word. You say: "Rubba rajulin laqītuhu" and "Rubbat rajulin laqītuhu," and you say: "Qāma Zaydun thumma qāma 'Amrun," and "Qāma Zaydun thummat qāma 'Amrun." So here it is the negative (lā) to which the ta' has been added. Why? To mark the feminine form of the word. This negative lā functions like laysa, and its subject is omitted in this verse, and its predicate is ﴿a time of escape﴾. The estimate is (i.e., it is not the time of escape). The author explained it by its meaning. So you say: (lā) is in the sense of (laysa), its subject is omitted, estimated as "al-ḥīn" (the time), and its predicate is present, which is His words ﴿a time of escape﴾. Generally, the predicate of (lā) is a time expression. This is the usual case; it does not come except as a time expression.

The poet said:
"The transgressors regretted, but there is no time for regret ..........................."
meaning: and the hour is not an hour of regret.

As for His words ﴿escape (manāṣ)﴾, manāṣ means flight and deliverance. That is: it is not the time of flight and deliverance, because after the punishment descends, faith does not benefit a soul.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (it is not the time for escape), and the ta' is added (for the feminine form of the word), and the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿they called out﴾. Based on this, it is in the accusative position, because a circumstantial clause is always in the accusative position. That is: they called out in a state where there is no escape from what has befallen them. For this reason the author estimated it as: (i.e., they sought help, and the situation is that there is no flight and no refuge).

This is what the author estimated for the phrase ﴿and no time was there for escape﴾. That is, it is a circumstantial clause, and thus it is restricted to the circumstance of their calling out. However, it is permissible for it to be a resumptive clause (isti'nāfiyyah), so that ﴿they called out﴾ stands alone, and then Allah the Mighty and Majestic informs that this time is not a time of escape.

The difference between our saying "resumptive" (istinā'iyyah) and "circumstantial" (ḥāliyyah) is this: if it is circumstantial, it becomes a restriction on the calling out; that is, they called out in a state in which calling out does not benefit them. If it is resumptive, it is separate from what precedes it in terms of restriction: Allah informs that they called out, then He informs that they were in a state in which they were not able to flee.

The author said: (and they did not take heed, the disbelievers of Makkah). This is the outcome of mentioning that Allah destroyed many generations in the past, yet despite this, the people of Makkah did not take heed from it. Rather, they denied the Messenger (ﷺ) and harmed him, and said: he is a madman, he is a sorcerer, he is a liar, he is a poet, he is a soothsayer. Every attribute that repels people they ascribed to him (ﷺ), and they did not take warning from those who came before, but rather they added to this.

﴿And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾ [Sad 4]. ﴿They wondered﴾: wonder (ʿajab) has two causes:
The first cause: denial.
The second cause: approval, meaning one says "he wondered at such-and-such," that is, he approved of it. And "he wondered at such-and-such" also means he denied it. So it resembles the words with opposite meanings (al-addād), because in the Arabic language there are words that indicate a meaning and its opposite, which the scholars of Arabic call al-addād in language.

Wonder sometimes is approval and sometimes is denial. The saying of ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Prophet (ﷺ) liked to start with the right in his footwear and in his combing" [Narrated by al-Bukhari, with his wording (168), and Muslim (268/76), both with their chains from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) liked to start with the right in his footwear, his combing, his purification, and in all his affairs]. The meaning of "liked" here is approval.

But here, ﴿they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾ is a wonder of denial, not a wonder of approval and pleasure; rather it is a wonder of denial and rejection. This is similar to the saying of Allah in Surah Qaf: ﴿Rather, they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves, so the disbelievers said, "This is a strange thing"﴾ [Qaf 2]. Here, the similar statement came in: ﴿And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾. The ﴿that (an)﴾ here is a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah) with the implied preposition "min," meaning: they wondered at the coming of a warner. We said it is maṣdariyyah because what follows it is converted into a verbal noun, that is: they wondered at the coming of a warner from among them.

As for His words ﴿warner (mundhir)﴾: the warner is the one who informs with news for the purpose of frightening. For this reason we say that warning (indhār) is news accompanied by frightening. The Prophet (ﷺ) was a warner and he was also a bringer of glad tidings, but the disbelievers, what suits their condition is what? Warning. ﴿To warn of a severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾, and glad tidings belong to whom? To the believers.

Here He said: ﴿they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves﴾ because this is what befits their condition.

As for His words ﴿from among themselves﴾: in lineage and in kind. He is from among them in kind, because he is a human, and Allah did not send a messenger from among the angels to humans. In lineage, because he is from Quraysh. So he was from among them in kind and in lineage, and yet they wondered.

The author said: (a messenger from among themselves who warns them and frightens them with the Fire after resurrection), that is: after they are resurrected, and he is the Prophet (ﷺ). They wondered with a wonder of denial, rejection and refusal, even though they used to describe the Messenger (ﷺ) earlier as the truthful, the trustworthy. When he brought them the message, he became in their eyes a liar and a traitor, and we seek refuge in Allah.

So then, their enmity toward him was not directed at his person, but rather at what he brought.

﴿And the disbelievers said﴾: here the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun. How would the speech have been if the pronoun were used? It would be: "And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves, and they said: This is a sorcerer, a liar." But He said: ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾. The benefit of using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is:
First: to alert the listener, because when the style of speech changes, it compels the hearer to pay attention, unlike when it is in one uniform style, where sleep may overcome him, but when it differs, he pays attention.
Second: to record the disbelief upon these people, because if He had said "they said: this is a sorcerer, a liar," we would not have known their judgment; but when He said "the disbelievers said," we know that they are disbelievers.
Third: that what drives them to this is disbelief, so it is not far-fetched that others besides them would say the same as they said, because if the cause is one, then whenever this cause exists, the effect occurs from whatever person it may be. These are the benefits of using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, as ʿĪsā said to us.

* Student: Alerting the listener.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: Informing that these people are disbelievers.
* Shaykh: Yes. The third?
* Student: Recording disbelief upon the disbelievers.
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Recording disbelief upon the disbelievers.
* Shaykh: This is what the brother said.
* Student: Giving the reason for the ruling.
* Shaykh: That is: giving the cause of this saying, that the driving force behind it is disbelief, so this extends to others; that is, every disbeliever who says this statement. Good.

﴿And the disbelievers said: This is a sorcerer, a liar﴾. ﴿This is a sorcerer, a liar﴾: to whom do they point? To the warner from among them, who is the Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿A sorcerer, a liar﴾: they combined two blameworthy attributes. ﴿A sorcerer﴾, because he captivates people's minds. ﴿A liar﴾, because what he brought is falsehood that does not correspond to reality. So the Messenger (ﷺ), who is the most truthful of creation, became in their eyes a liar.
