The yā' here was deleted for lightness, and this is common in the Qur'an and in the Arabic language, that the yā' of the first person is deleted for lightness, as in Allah's saying: ﴿The Great, the Exalted﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 9], and ﴿And there is not for them other than Him any guardian﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 11], the presumed reading being al-muta'ali and wali.

Alright. ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted my punishment﴾: punishment is not a food that is tasted, but being afflicted by it is a tasting, and the tasting of each thing is according to its nature. If I give you something sweet and you put it in your mouth and suck it, this is tasting; if I give you meat and you chew it, this is tasting; if I strike you and you feel the blow, this is tasting. So the tasting of each thing is according to it. The tasting of punishment is not like the tasting of food and drink; rather, it is a tasting suited to it.

﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted my punishment﴾. The author says: (Had they tasted it, they would have affirmed the Prophet ﷺ in what he brought). But this affirmation will not benefit them, because if a denier affirms after the punishment has descended upon him, that does not benefit him. Allah said: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said, "We have believed in Allah alone and disbelieved in what we used to associate with Him." But their belief was not going to benefit them when they had seen Our might﴾ [Ghafir 84, 85].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 7–25 (part 2 of 7):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ [Sad 9]. This is like His saying: ﴿They said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31]. After it He said: ﴿Is it they who distribute your Lord's mercy?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32], meaning until they say: "We will place prophethood in so-and-so rather than so-and-so." Here, when they said: ﴿Was the Reminder sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [Sad 8], Allah said: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of mercy?﴾, meaning: Is it they who distribute these treasuries, so that they make the message go to so-and-so rather than so-and-so? The word "am" (أم) here means "rather" (بل), and the interrogative hamza is meant for negation. On this basis, the sense of the statement is: Rather, do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy? That is, the treasuries of Allah's mercy are not with them, so that they could say: ﴿Was the Reminder sent down upon him from among us?﴾ and ask why it was not sent down upon so-and-so or so-and-so. I told you that the parallel of this verse is His saying: ﴿They said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾, and Allah said: ﴿Is it they who distribute your Lord's mercy?﴾, so that they would make the Qur'an descend upon so-and-so rather than so-and-so.

He said: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ "Khazā'in" (خزائن) is the plural of "khazīnah" (خزينة), and a khazīnah is the place where a thing is stored. "Mercy of your Lord" means what comes by His mercy of provisions, both material and spiritual. The answer: yes or no? No, they do not have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy.

As for His saying "the Mighty", the author said: "the Overpowering" (الغالب). "The Bestower" means one who gives many gifts, which are bestowals. First, He said "your Lord's mercy", attributing lordship (ربوبية) to the Prophet ﷺ, showing special care for him and clarifying that what he received of the message was by the requirement of Allah's special lordship over him. That is why we say: the most special kind of lordship is that for whom? For the messengers. Just as the most special kind of servanthood is the servanthood of the messengers. For this reason He attributed lordship to him, because the most special lordship is Allah's lordship over His messengers, headed by Muhammad ﷺ. It is as if He is indicating that Allah's sending of the message to the Messenger ﷺ is from His mercy toward him.

As for His saying "the Mighty, the Bestower", it has a great correspondence. "The Mighty" is set against those who were in arrogance and opposition, to show that Allah's might is above their might, pride, and zealotry, and that He overcomes and subdues them.

"The Bestower" is in relation to whom? In relation to the Messenger ﷺ, meaning that He gave him prophethood.

As for "the Mighty", the author says it means "the Overpowering". This is one of its meanings, but it includes more than that. "The Mighty" includes or indicates three kinds of might: might of rank (عزة القدر), might of inaccessibility (عزة الامتناع), and might of subjugation (عزة القهر).

Might of inaccessibility means that Allah the Exalted is far removed from every deficiency and defect. He is Mighty, and every deficiency and defect is impossible for Him. Might of rank means the might of honor and sovereignty; absolute sovereignty belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and absolute might belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿To Allah belongs all honor﴾ [Fatir 10]. The third is the might of subjugation, which is the might of dominance, meaning He overpowers everyone. From the poetry of the pre-Islamic age:

"Where is the escape, when the Seeking God is pursuing? And al-Ashram is defeated, and the one who was overcome is not the victor."

So the author's explanation of "the Mighty" as "the Overpowering" is an explanation by some of its meanings, and it is a deficient explanation. We have mentioned previously that whoever explains the Qur'an by only some of what it indicates, his explanation is deficient. But sometimes the Qur'an is explained by some of what it indicates as an example, not as a restriction. Pay attention: it is explained by way of example, not by way of restriction. Like some scholars' explanation of Allah's saying: ﴿Then We gave the Book as inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants; among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir 32]. They explained "one who wrongs himself" as the one who delays the prayer past its time, the "moderate" as the one who prays at the end of its time, and the "foremost in good deeds" as the one who prays at the beginning of its time. Some explained "one who wrongs himself" as the one who does not pay zakat, the "moderate" as the one who pays zakat but does not give charity beyond it, and the "foremost in good deeds" as the one who pays zakat and gives charity. This explanation, we say, is without doubt deficient, but the explainer did not intend that the meaning is restricted to this. He intended by it what? An example. That is: the one who wrongs himself is like the one who does not pay zakat; the moderate is like the one who pays zakat but does not give charity; the foremost in good deeds is like the one who pays zakat and gives charity.

(﴿The Bestower﴾ of prophethood and other things, so they give it to whom they wish.) This is built upon the negation: Do they have the treasuries of Allah's mercy, of prophethood and other things, so that they give them to whom they wish and withhold them from whom they wish? The answer is no.

Student: O Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, regarding Allah's saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, he said: "Had they tasted it, they would have believed the Prophet," even though Allah the Mighty says: ﴿But there has become apparent to them what they had concealed before; and if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [Al-An'am 28], and this comes after His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾ [Al-An'am 27].

Shaykh: Yes, that is on the Day of Resurrection.

Student: "They have not tasted the punishment" — is this in this world?

Shaykh: Yes, in this world.

* * *

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ [Sad 9].

First, a discussion of what came before. "Ara'unzila 'alayhi" (أَأُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ) has several readings. How many?

Student: Four readings.

Shaykh: Four readings. Yes, mention them.

Student: The first, the one present now, is with the two hamzas pronounced fully (بالتحقيق).

Shaykh: Fully pronounced what?

Student: The two hamzas.

Shaykh: Yes.

Student: The second is with the two hamzas softened (بتسهيل الهمزتين).

Shaykh: Softened what?

Student: The two hamzas.

Shaykh: Wrong.

Student: The second is with the first softened and the second fully pronounced.

Shaykh: Wrong.

Student: With the second softened.

Shaykh: The second softened, good. The third?

Student: Inserting an alif between the two hamzas.

Shaykh: Inserting an alif between the first and second hamza with full pronunciation. The fourth?

Student: Inserting an alif with the second softened.

Shaykh: Inserting an alif between them with the second softened. Now, recite the full pronunciation of both hamzas with an alif between them.

Student: "Ā'unzila" (آأُنْزِلَ).

Shaykh: "Ā'unzila," good. Now, the second softened with an alif?

Student: "Āunzila 'alayhi" (آانْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ).

Shaykh: Yes. The second softened without an alif?

Student: "Aunzila" (أَاُنْزِلَ).

Shaykh: Without an alif. Good.

What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Was the Reminder sent down upon him from among us?﴾

Student: They deny this and marvel: "Was this Qur'an sent down upon him..." (...)?

Shaykh: That is, "and we were left aside, although among us is one more noble than him." Right.

His saying: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder.﴾ Here, is "bal" (بَلْ) for nullifying retraction (الإضراب الإبطالي) or transitional retraction (الإضراب الانتقالي)?

Student: For retraction.

Shaykh: Which of the two kinds? Because there is a nullifying retraction that cancels what came before, and a transitional retraction?

Student: Transitional.

Shaykh: Transitional, good. What is the connection with what came before: ﴿Was the Reminder sent down upon him from among us?﴾ and ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾?

Student: The retraction here is nullifying, to show that they are in doubt about what was sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ.

Shaykh: Good. The brother says transitional. But what is its connection with what came before, whether it is nullifying or transitional?

Student: He said: they will not believe, or they will be in doubt about what was sent down (...).

Shaykh: That is, they are in doubt about the Reminder, whether it was sent to Muhammad or to someone else. So their claim is merely a pretext. Now, His saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ "Lamma" (لَمَّا): what does it do? What does it govern in what follows it?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: I am not asking its meaning. When it enters on something, what does it govern?

Student: ﴿lamma yadhuqu 'adhāb﴾ — yes, it jussivates the imperfect verb.

Shaykh: It jussivates, and for this reason the author explained it as "lam."

Good. "Lamma" comes in Arabic in several senses; here it is for negation and jussive governance.

Student: For negation.

Shaykh: For negation and jussive governance. And others?

Student: Conditional.

Shaykh: It comes as conditional. Give an example.

Student: "I reached the town when the sun rose."

Shaykh: No.

Student: That one means "when" (حين).

Shaykh: Good, that one means "when."

Student: As for the conditional...

Shaykh: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 89]. Good.

Student: Exceptive.

Shaykh: Like what?

Student: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾ [At-Tariq 4].

Shaykh: Well done, correct. Now, His saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ indicates that they have not tasted the punishment, but...

Student: They will taste the punishment; that is, either they taste it in this world quickly...

Shaykh: No, here it indicates negation. But is it a definite negation of the thing, or what?

Student: The negation of doubt, that they (...).

Another student: The negation of something expected soon.

Shaykh: Well done: the negation of something expected soon. So they have not tasted it, but they will taste it soon.

In His saying "'adhāb" (عَذَابِ) there is a difficulty: the verb has governed it, yet it is in the genitive (مكسورة)?

Student: It is in the accusative, but it is attached to the first-person pronoun suffix (ياء المتكلم), and the pronoun ya was dropped for lightness.

Shaykh: He says: the i'rab (grammatical case) here is on the ba' (باء), as an assumed case.

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Because it is on the assumption of the first-person ya.

His saying: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ What is its connection with what came before?

Student: It is a rebuke of astonishment: do they have the treasuries of Allah's mercy, so that they give prophethood to whom they wish and withhold it from whom they do not wish?

Shaykh: Do you say this? Correct?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Good. Is there a parallel to it in the Qur'an? What is its parallel in the Qur'an (...)? Is there a verse that explains it more?

Student: ﴿They said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?" Is it they who distribute your Lord's mercy?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31–32].

Shaykh: Then Allah the Mighty said: ﴿Or do they have dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them?﴾ [Sad 10]. "Am" (أَمْ) here is for retraction, so it has the meaning of "rather" and the interrogative hamza: "rather, do they have dominion of the heavens?!" This interrogative is for negation: they do not have dominion of the heavens and the earth.

His saying: "Mulk al-samawat" (مُلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ). "Samawat" is the plural of "sama'" (سماء), which in Arabic means anything above you. Whatever is above you is a sama'. But what is meant here is the well-known, protected heavens. It is well known that they are seven heavens, as Allah stated in several verses. His saying "wal-ard" (وَالْأَرْضِ) is this well-known earth, and it is also seven earths, as is apparent from the Qur'an in His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens, and of the earth their like﴾ [At-Talaq 12]. The likeness here is in number, not in size or in quality, but in number. And the Sunnah also confirmed this explicitly, in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, it will be hung around his neck on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."[[Reported by Muslim (1610 / 137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

His saying: "wa ma baynahuma" (وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا) means what is between the heavens and the earth of great creations, such as the sun, the moon, the stars, the planets, and others that no one knows except Allah. But placing what is between the heavens and the earth as a counterpart to them indicates that what is between them is great creation, parallel to the heavens and the earth. What is between them, then? We said: the sun, the moon, the stars, and the planets, as well as the winds and the clouds, and other things that we do not know, which created beings may or may not know.

The author said: "if they claim that" (إن زعموا ذلك), that is, that they have dominion of the heavens. Do they possess that? It is impossible.

﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, made His saying "then let them ascend" an answer to an assumed condition. That is: "If they claim that they have dominion of the heavens and the earth, then let them ascend by the means that reach the sky, and bring revelation and single out whomever they wish with it."

His saying "fal-yartaqu" (فَلْيَرْتَقُوا): the fa' here is in the answer to an assumed condition, meaning: if they claim that, then let them ascend. The lam is the lam of command, and it was vowelled with sukun because it came after the conjunctive fa' (فاء العطف). The lam of command takes sukun when it comes after fa', thumma (ثم), and waw. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness﴾ [Al-Hajj 29]: this one is after thumma. ﴿And let them fulfill their vows﴾: this one is after waw. ﴿Then let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [Al-Hajj 15]: this one is after fa'. This differs from the lam of purpose, which is always kasra even if it comes after these letters, as Allah said: ﴿So that they may deny what We gave them, and so they may enjoy themselves﴾ [Al-Ankabut 66]. He did not say "wa liyatamatta'u," because the lam is for purpose. The lam of purpose is always kasra, while the lam of command is kasra except when it comes after waw, fa', and thumma. For this reason He said here: ﴿Then let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [Al-Hajj 15], where the lam is for command. The apparent meaning of the command here is a challenge: if they are truthful, let them ascend by the means. "Asbab" (الأسباب) is the plural of "sabab" (سبب), which is anything that leads to the intended goal. This verse is a parallel to His saying: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him extend a rope to the sky, then cut it off and see whether his plan removes that which enrages him﴾ [Al-Hajj 15]. That is, with something that reaches the sky, such as a rope.

So here He said: ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾, meaning: let them make means by which they ascend and reach the sky. It is known that this challenge is impossible for them to fulfill.

Then he said: "(that reach the sky, then bring revelation and single out whomever they wish with it)," based on their saying: ﴿Was the Reminder sent down upon him from among us?﴾, meaning: how was it sent down? They said: then ascend to the sky, bring down the revelation, and single out with it whomever you wish. Good.

Then the author said: "And 'an' (أن) in both places has the meaning of the interrogative hamza of denial" (الإنكار الذي بمعنى النفي). That is, they do not have the treasuries of Allah, and they do not have dominion of the heavens and the earth. Rather, they are free of all of this.

Then He, Exalted, said: "(﴿A host﴾ [Sad 11], that is, a contemptible host, ﴿there﴾, that is, in their denial of you, ﴿defeated﴾, an attribute of host, ﴿of the factions﴾, also an attribute of host.)"

﴿A host there﴾: "jund" (جُنْدٌ) is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being "they are a host." "Ma" (مَا) is indefinite and descriptive, because "ma" has several meanings, ten meanings gathered in the poet's verse:

"The carriers of 'ma' are ten, if you want to count them, so keep a sound collection of verses from poetry. You will understand the conditional of connection (شرط الوصل); marvel at its denial (نكرها) by the restrictive kaf and the negation, and the added (زيد) magnification of the verbal noun."

Who memorized them?

Student: [recites the verses above]

Shaykh: Good. Let us begin. "Sa-tafhamu" (ستفهم): interrogative. "Sharta" (شرط): conditional. "Al-wasl" (الوصل): relative. "Fa-'ajib" (فاعجب): exclamatory. "Li-nukriha" (لنكرها): indefinite, whether descriptive or described. "Bi-kaff" (بكف): restrictive (كافة). "Wa-nafy" (ونفي): negating. "Zid" (زيد): additional. "Ta'zim" (تعظيم): for magnification. "Masdar" (مصدر): verbal noun, as the masdariyyah (مصدرية). Good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 7–25 (part 3 of 7):

Here "jundun ma" (﴿جُنْدٌ مَا﴾). The author said: (contemptible). So is it a indefinite noun described by a descriptive clause, or is it the described noun? Descriptive means it is described by it, because "ma" here is an adjective of "jund." But the intended meaning is belittlement, and the evidence that this is for belittlement is His saying: ﴿مَهْزُومٌ﴾ (defeated), and the defeated is contemptible, not august. Contemptible, good.

And His saying: ﴿هُنَالِكَ﴾ (there). "Huna" indicates place, the lam is for distance, and the kaf is a particle of address. ﴿هُنَالِكَ﴾ means: in that place. The author says: (i.e., in their denial of you), so he made the locative sense here to be denial. But it appears that the matter is contrary to what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, and that what is pointed to is the sensory place, not the abstract place; that is, if they ascend through the means, they will be defeated, so ﴿هُنَالِكَ﴾ means in the place they ascend to. So if it is supposed that they ascended to the heaven, will they then have victory? Never. On the contrary, even if they thought they had reached the heaven and ascended to the heaven, that they had triumphed and had gained might, the matter is the reverse. This is what appears from the noble verse. As for making the location to be denial, this is far-fetched; rather, denial is a cause of abandonment.

﴿جُنْدٌ مَا هُنَالِكَ مَهْزُومٌ﴾. The author says: (a second adjective of "jund")? Second, and the first is ﴿مِنَ الْأَحْزَابِ﴾, which is also an adjective of "jund," meaning: a defeated host from the factions. Know that when the adjective of an indefinite noun is repeated, what follows the first adjective may be a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause. Yes: when the adjective is repeated, what follows the first adjective may be a ḥāl. So if you say: "I passed by a great, generous, brave man," it is permissible to say: "I passed by a great man, generous, brave." Yes, good. But which of them is preferable? The preferable is that it be an adjective, i.e., na't, for the coherence of the speech and its being in one pattern. Here we have three adjectives for the host: ﴿ma — mahzūm — min al-aḥzāb﴾. Which of them may be in the accusative as a ḥāl? ﴿مَهْزُومٌ﴾, but this is not possible here, because the case-marking appeared showing it is nominative as an adjective; likewise ﴿مِنَ الْأَحْزَابِ﴾ is similar: it may be an adjective, which is the original, and it may be placed in the accusative position as a ḥāl.

(i.e., like the hosts of the same kind as the factions who banded against the prophets before you; those were overpowered and destroyed, so these too will be destroyed.) Yes, meaning that these are a host among other hosts, and the other hosts, the factions who denied the messengers, what was their end? Their end was destruction and ruin, and it has passed us at the beginning of the surah: ﴿كَمْ أَهْلَكْنَا مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ مِنْ قَرْنٍ فَنَادَوْا وَلَاتَ حِينَ مَنَاصٍ﴾ [Ṣ 3].

Then Allah began to indicate the story of those hosts or those factions; so He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ [Ṣ 12]. Before whom? Before those who denied you from Quraysh and the Jews and others. ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾, and Nuh is the first messenger whom Allah, mighty and majestic, sent, by the indication of the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ كَمَا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى نُوحٍ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ [al-Nisā' 163], and the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا وَإِبْرَاهِيمَ وَجَعَلْنَا فِي ذُرِّيَّتِهِمَا النُّبُوَّةَ وَالْكِتَابَ﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 26], and if anyone had been before Nuh he would have come from their descendants. By this we know that what is found in the tree of the prophets written in some books, that Idris came before Nuh, is an error, for Idris is after Nuh without doubt.

As for the Sunnah, it is explicit in this: it is established in the long hadith of intercession that people come to Nuh and say to him: "You are the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth." This is explicit, and by it we also know that what is mentioned in history books, that Idris was an ancestor of Nuh, is an error without doubt; Idris, as it appears to us, and Allah knows best, is among the prophets of the Children of Israel.

Good. ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾. Nuh, peace be upon him, was sent to mankind when people disagreed, and the people were at first upon one religion, then they differed: ﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ وَأَنْزَلَ مَعَهُمُ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ لِيَحْكُمَ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ فِيمَا اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. Allah sent him to his people, ﴿فَلَبِثَ فِيهِمْ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ إِلَّا خَمْسِينَ عَامًا﴾, while he called them to Allah, and brought them signs and challenged them, but they, we seek refuge in Allah, whenever he called them, increased in arrogance and aversion: ﴿وَإِنِّي كُلَّمَا دَعَوْتُهُمْ لِتَغْفِرَ لَهُمْ جَعَلُوا أَصَابِعَهُمْ فِي آذَانِهِمْ وَاسْتَغْشَوْا ثِيَابَهُمْ وَأَصَرُّوا وَاسْتَكْبَرُوا اسْتِكْبَارًا﴾ [Nūḥ 7]. When Allah permitted their destruction, Nuh called upon his Lord: ﴿أَنِّي مَغْلُوبٌ فَانْتَصِرْ﴾ [al-Qamar 10], so Allah gave him victory: ﴿فَفَتَحْنَا أَبْوَابَ السَّمَاءِ بِمَاءٍ مُنْهَمِرٍ (١١) وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا فَالْتَقَى الْمَاءُ عَلَى أَمْرٍ قَدْ قُدِرَ (١٢) وَحَمَلْنَاهُ عَلَى ذَاتِ أَلْوَاحٍ وَدُسُرٍ (١٣) تَجْرِي بِأَعْيُنِنَا﴾ [al-Qamar 11–14]. And He commanded him to carry with him those of his people who believed: ﴿وَمَا آمَنَ مَعَهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلٌ﴾ [Hūd 40]. Consider, O callers, how he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years while being a messenger, and the people had not yet multiplied, yet none believed with him except a few, and even one of his own offspring disbelieved in him, namely his son who was among the drowned.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (the feminine of "qawm" is by consideration of meaning). Is "qawm" feminine, or is it the verb whose subject the people are that is made feminine? Yes, we say: thus, the verb is what has been made feminine: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ﴾. As for "qawm," there is no feminine marker ta' in it; but it is well known that when the verb is feminine, the subject is feminine; meaning, if the subject occurs with a feminine verb it is feminine, but is this word feminine in form or by consideration of meaning? The author said: (by consideration of meaning). Here we ask: how can it be feminine by consideration of meaning? Because "qawm" is a group, and every collective may be made feminine. Ibn Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"The ta' with a plural other than the sound masculine plural is like the ta' with 'iḥdā al-labin'."

("Iḥdā al-labin" is the "labina," so "labina" may be masculine or feminine, but the feminine is more preferred.) Likewise all plurals other than the sound masculine plural permit the presence of the ta' in the verb.

He said: ﴿وَعَادٌ وَفِرْعَوْنُ ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ﴾ [Ṣ 12]. ﴿ʿĀd﴾, the people of Hud, dwelt in al-Aḥqāf and were people of strength and might, among the strongest of people, so they were impressed by their strength and became arrogant, disobeyed their messenger, peace be upon him, and boasted of the strength Allah had given them, as Allah said of them: ﴿فَأَمَّا عَادٌ فَاسْتَكْبَرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ وَقَالُوا مَنْ أَشَدُّ مِنَّا قُوَّةً﴾. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ اللَّهَ الَّذِي خَلَقَهُمْ هُوَ أَشَدُّ مِنْهُمْ قُوَّةً﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 15]. Reflect on His saying: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ اللَّهَ الَّذِي خَلَقَهُمْ﴾, for in it is an indication that they are weak before their Creator. He did not say "who created the heavens," but said: ﴿خَلَقَهُمْ﴾, "who created them," so they are created, and the Creator is higher than the created and mightier than it: ﴿هُوَ أَشَدُّ مِنْهُمْ قُوَّةً وَكَانُوا بِآيَاتِنَا يَجْحَدُونَ﴾. So Allah destroyed them, and when they hoped for His mercy, Allah sent upon them a mighty wind. When they saw what the wind carried of great sand, they thought it was a cloud, and said: ﴿هَذَا عَارِضٌ مُمْطِرُنَا﴾. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿بَلْ هُوَ مَا اسْتَعْجَلْتُمْ بِهِ رِيحٌ فِيهَا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ (٢٤) تُدَمِّرُ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ بِأَمْرِ رَبِّهَا﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 24–25]. The barren wind swept over them until it would lift one of them into the sky, then drop him on his head, and they became like hollow palm trunks ('a'jāz nakhl khāwiyah) — ("a'jāz nakhl" means its roots and trunks; "khāwiyah" means overturned) — so nothing was seen but their dwellings. Yet even so, none believed with him except a small band.

He said: ﴿وَفِرْعَوْنُ ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ﴾ [Ṣ 12]. He used to drive four stakes for whoever he was angry with, tying his hands and feet to them and torturing him. Look at Pharaoh to whom Musa was sent; he was a ruler dominant over Egypt, a tyrant, obstinate, who enslaved the people of Egypt and said to them: ﴿أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَى﴾ [al-Nāzi'āt 24], and he mocked Musa and said to them: ﴿أَمْ أَنَا خَيْرٌ مِنْ هَذَا الَّذِي هُوَ مَهِينٌ وَلَا يَكَادُ يُبِينُ﴾ [al-Zukhruf 52], and he boasted of the rivers Allah had given him, saying to them: ﴿أَلَيْسَ لِي مُلْكُ مِصْرَ وَهَذِهِ الْأَنْهَارُ تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِي أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf 51]. He denied Musa and fought Musa, but not with weapons; rather with the sorcerers he gathered, for he deceived the people that Musa was a sorcerer, saying: this is a sorcerer, because he places the staff on the ground and it becomes a serpent, and he puts his hand into his pocket and it comes out white without harm; this is a sorcerer. He gathered the sorcerers, and they cast what they had of great magic that terrified the people, until Musa, peace be upon him, was awed and feared, so Allah the Exalted said: ﴿قُلْنَا لَا تَخَفْ إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْأَعْلَى (٦٨) وَأَلْقِ مَا فِي يَمِينِكَ تَلْقَفْ مَا صَنَعُوا﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 68–69]. So Allah strengthened him, and he cast what was in his right hand, the staff, which became a great serpent that swallowed the ropes and staffs with which they had filled the earth, and it appeared to the people as if they were serpents and snakes slithering; it swallowed them all. Glory be to Allah, how could this staff that was a staff swallow all of this? This is among the signs of Allah. When the sorcerers saw this, they were astonished and knew that this was not a sorcerer, because a sorcerer cannot bring about such a thing; rather it is a reality and a sign with which Allah strengthened Musa. So they all believed, all the sorcerers, and prostrated to Allah in humility and worship, and declared: ﴿آمَنَّا بِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ (١٢١) رَبِّ مُوسَى وَهَارُونَ﴾ [al-A'rāf 121–122]. So what would be the effect of these people, through whom Pharaoh had been victorious, among the people? Their effect among the people would be great and enormous. Have you seen that if a king gathered the greatest of his engineers in a vast assembly, and then they acknowledged and declared against the king's opponents, what would the people feel? Answer. Their feeling would be that the king is defeated. For this reason, when the sorcerers' faith occurred, Pharaoh resorted to force and coercion and threatened them that he would cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them on palm trunks until they tasted punishment. But with their faith they said: ﴿قَالُوا لَنْ نُؤْثِرَكَ عَلَى مَا جَاءَنَا مِنَ الْبَيِّنَاتِ وَالَّذِي فَطَرَنَا فَاقْضِ مَا أَنْتَ قَاضٍ إِنَّمَا تَقْضِي هَذِهِ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا (٧٢) إِنَّا آمَنَّا بِرَبِّنَا لِيَغْفِرَ لَنَا خَطَايَانَا وَمَا أَكْرَهْتَنَا عَلَيْهِ مِنَ السِّحْرِ وَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَى﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 72–73]. They stood firm before this obstinate tyrant, so that at the start of the day they were disbelieving sorcerers, and at the end of the day they were righteous believers. What did Pharaoh do? He remained persistent in his tyranny, we seek refuge in Allah, until Allah destroyed them by drowning, by the same kind of thing he had boasted of against his people and against Musa when he said: ﴿وَهَذِهِ الْأَنْهَارُ تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِي﴾ [al-Zukhruf 51], so he was destroyed by the water he had boasted of.

As for the author's saying: ﴿وَفِرْعَوْنُ ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ﴾ [Ṣ 12] (he used to drive stakes), and so on to the end: what appears is that this is not the reason for the description "dhū al-awtād." The real reason is that the intended meaning of "al-awtād" is the strength by which his rule was established, like the tent-pegs by which a tent is fixed. It is not far-fetched that from his tyranny he would set four stakes on which he crucified a person and tortured him; this is not far-fetched. But this cannot be praise for Pharaoh as one of strength; rather, the correct view is that what is meant by "al-awtād" here is what? The strength by which his rule was established, like tent-pegs by which a tent is fixed.

* The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ وَعَادٌ وَفِرْعَوْنُ ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ (١٢) وَثَمُودُ وَقَوْمُ لُوطٍ وَأَصْحَابُ الْأَيْكَةِ أُولَئِكَ الْأَحْزَابُ (١٣) إِنْ كُلٌّ إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ فَحَقَّ عِقَابِ (١٤) وَمَا يَنْظُرُ هَؤُلَاءِ إِلَّا صَيْحَةً وَاحِدَةً مَا لَهَا مِنْ فَوَاقٍ (١٥) وَقَالُوا رَبَّنَا عَجِّلْ لَنَا قِطَّنَا قَبْلَ يَوْمِ الْحِسَابِ (١٦) اصْبِرْ عَلَى مَا يَقُولُونَ وَاذْكُرْ عَبْدَنَا دَاوُودَ ذَا الْأَيْدِ إِنَّهُ أَوَّابٌ﴾ [Ṣ 12–17].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾.

Before we take up the discussion of His saying: ﴿أَمْ لَهُمْ مُلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ [Ṣ 10], let us ask about "am" here.

* Student: The hamza is for iḍrāb (turning away).

* The Shaykh: Is it disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah) or connective (muttaṣilah)?

* Student: Disjunctive, equivalent to "bal" and the hamza.

* The Shaykh: Disjunctive, equivalent to "bal" and the hamza. What is the difference between the connective and the disjunctive?

* The student: The disjunctive is not mentioned between two equal things, and it is used with the meaning of "bal."

* The Shaykh: And the connective?

* The student: The connective is mentioned between two equal things.

* The Shaykh: That is one difference.

* The student: And it is used with the meaning of "aw" (or).

* The Shaykh: The second difference is that the connective has the meaning of "aw" and the disjunctive has the meaning of "bal." Good. What does His saying "wa-mā baynahumā" convey?

* Student: That what is between the heavens and the earth of creatures, Allah made it a counterpart to the heavens and the earth (...).

* The Shaykh: This indicates that between them are great things. Good. The lam in His saying: ﴿فَلْيَرْتَقُوا﴾, the lam is the lam of what?

* The student: ﴿فَلْيَرْتَقُوا﴾, the lam is the lam of command, but it is brought for mockery of them.

* The Shaykh: The lam is the lam of command, but what is meant by the command here?

* The student: Mockery of them (...).

* Another student: The lam is the lam of command and the fa' is the response of the condition.

* The Shaykh: But what is meant by the command?

* Student: Mockery of them.

* Another student: Challenge.

* The student: What is meant by the command is challenge.

* The Shaykh: What is meant by the command is challenge: if they are truthful, let them ascend by the means. Good. And the fa'?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is the response of an implied condition. And the implied sentence?

* The student: If they are truthful, let them ascend by means.

* The Shaykh: If they are truthful, or if they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth, let them ascend by the means. Good. What is meant by "al-asbāb" (the means)?

* The student: The means here are what reaches the heaven.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is meant by them?

* The student: Everything that reaches to...

* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is meant by them here?

* The student: Everything that reaches the heaven.

* The Shaykh: The means that lead to the heaven. Good, is there evidence supporting what you said? Yes.

* Student: The saying of Allah, glorified and exalted: ﴿مَنْ كَانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ فَلْيَنْظُرْ هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ مَا يَغِيظُ﴾ [al-Ḥajj 15].

* The Shaykh: Well done. The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿مَنْ كَانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ فَلْيَنْظُرْ هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ مَا يَغِيظُ﴾. Good.

The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿جُنْدٌ مَا هُنَالِكَ مَهْزُومٌ مِنَ الْأَحْزَابِ﴾ [Ṣ 11]. The i'rab of "jund"?

* The student: ﴿جُنْدٌ﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject.

* The Shaykh: The estimate?

* The student: They are a host.

* The Shaykh: Good. And "mā", what is meant by it?

* The student: (...).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 38, verses 7–25 (part 4 of 7)**

* Another student: *Nakirah wasifah* (an indefinite descriptive noun).
* Shaykh: And what is the estimated meaning?
* Student: The estimated meaning is that they are defeated, that they are routed there.
* Shaykh: You said that ﴿مَا﴾ is an indefinite descriptive noun. How would you estimate it?
* Student: The estimate is that these are a defeated army.
* A student: (...) contemptible.
* Shaykh: You estimate it as "contemptible," meaning: a contemptible army there. Good. What is the referent of ﴿هُنَالِكَ﴾ ("there") in His saying?
* Student: The place is sensory (physical).
* Shaykh: And according to what the author (al-Mu'allif) said?
* A student: The figurative place is the denial (*al-takdhib*).
* Shaykh: The place is figurative, namely the denial. The second opinion is that the place is physical, meaning: if they climb up, they are a contemptible, defeated army there. Good. ﴿مَهْزُومٌ مِنَ الْأَحْزَابِ﴾ ("a defeated one among the factions"). How do you parse *mahzum*?
* Student: It is a descriptive (*sifah*).
* Shaykh: A descriptive of what?
* Student: Of ﴿جُنْدٌ﴾ ("an army").
* Shaykh: And "of the factions"?
* Student: It is descriptive.
* Shaykh: Descriptive?
* Student: Either we say it is a second descriptive, or we say it is a circumstantial (*hal*).
* Shaykh: A second descriptive or a third?
* Student: A third.
* Shaykh: A third, because the first ﴿مَا﴾...
* Student: The first.
* Shaykh: And *mahzum*?
* Student: A second descriptive.
* Shaykh: Good. As for His saying: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ ("Before them the people of Noah denied"), who is Noah?
* A student: The Prophet of Allah.
* Shaykh: The last of the prophets.
* Student: No, the first of the prophets.
* Shaykh: What is your evidence from the Book of Allah that he was the first of the prophets?
* A student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ كَمَا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى نُوحٍ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ ("Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him") [an-Nisa' 163].
* Shaykh: What is the proof in the verse?
* Student: ﴿إِلَى نُوحٍ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ ("to Noah and the prophets after him").
* Shaykh: Another proof?
* A student: ﴿وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا وَإِبْرَاهِيمَ وَجَعَلْنَا فِي ذُرِّيَّتِهِمَا النُّبُوَّةَ وَالْكِتَابَ﴾ ("We sent Noah and Abraham, and We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Scripture") [al-Hadid 26].
* Shaykh: ﴿وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا وَإِبْرَاهِيمَ وَجَعَلْنَا فِي ذُرِّيَّتِهِمَا النُّبُوَّةَ وَالْكِتَابَ﴾. Good. Is there a proof from the Sunnah?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ, as established in the hadith of intercession: (...) "They will come to Noah, peace be upon him, and say to him: 'You are the first of the messengers...'"
* Shaykh: "You are the first messenger whom Allah sent to the people of the earth." This is part of the long hadith of intercession, narrated by the two Shaykhs: al-Bukhari (4476) and Muslim (193/322), from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), and its wording is: "The believers will gather on the Day of Resurrection and say: 'If only we could seek intercession with our Lord.' They will come to Adam and say: 'You are the father of mankind; Allah created you with His hand, made His angels prostrate to you, and taught you the names of all things. Intercede for us with your Lord, so that He may relieve us from this place of ours.' He will say: 'I am not in that position,' and he will mention his sin and feel shy. 'Go to Noah, for he was the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth...'" and the hadith continues. Good. Based on this, we learn that whoever says that Idris was one of the ancestors of Noah...
* Student: He is mistaken.
* Shaykh: Mistaken and in error. Exactly.
* Shaykh: How long did Noah remain among his people?
* Student: A thousand years minus fifty years.
* Shaykh: A thousand years minus fifty years. And the result?
* Student: Only a few believed with him.
* Shaykh: Only a few believed with him. Well done. And the disbelief of those who rejected him included one of his sons. Good. We will draw a lesson from this, which will come to us, God willing, in the benefits (*fawa'id*).
* Shaykh: ʿĀd?
* Student: The people of Hud.
* Shaykh: What is the description by which they were distinguished from others?
* Student: They were extremely strong, and they became arrogant because of this strength, and they said: "Who is stronger than us?"
* Shaykh: And how were they destroyed?
* Student: Allah destroyed them with the wind.
* Shaykh: With the wind. Good. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَفِرْعَوْنُ ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ﴾ ("and Pharaoh, owner of the stakes"), what is the meaning of *dhu al-awtad*?
* Student: "Owner of the mountains."
* Shaykh: No, that is not it.
* Student: The author mentioned that it is (...).
* Shaykh: It means that they are stakes which he drives into the ground, and with which he ties the hands and feet of whoever disobeys him.
* Student: But we said that the better view is that it is explained as "strength."
* Shaykh: As "strength," meaning: the strength and might of rule and authority.
* Student: As is said of the tent-pegs.
* Shaykh: As is said of the tent-pegs that hold it and fix it in place.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿وَثَمُودُ﴾ ("and Thamud") is conjoined to ﴿قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ ("the people of Noah"), meaning: "and before them Thamud, the companions of Salih, denied." They lived in a place called al-Hijr, which is now called Mada'in Salih. Allah sent him (Salih) to them, but they disbelieved in him, and only a few believed with him. Allah gave them a great sign, which was a she-camel: they would milk her one day, and she would drink the water on another day. It was also said that each one of them would come to her, give her water, and take from her milk an amount equal to what he had given her to drink. And Allah knows best.

The point is that these people had strength; they took houses from the mountains, and their traces remain to this day. The Prophet ﷺ passed by them while going to Tabuk, and he covered his head ﷺ, meaning he covered it, and he hastened his pace, and said: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping; if you are not weeping, do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38), from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), and its wording is: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the companions at al-Hijr: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping. If you are not weeping, do not enter upon them, lest there befall you the like of what befell them."]

He says: ﴿وَقَوْمُ لُوطٍ﴾ ("and the people of Lot"). Lut was the son of the brother of Abraham. Allah sent him to his people, and they had committed the abomination, may Allah protect us, for they would approach men and leave women. Lut rebuked them for that, and said: ﴿أَتَأْتُونَ الذُّكْرَانَ مِنَ الْعَالَمِينَ (١٦٥) وَتَذَرُونَ مَا خَلَقَ لَكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ﴾ ("Do you approach males from among the worlds, and leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses?") [ash-Shu'ara' 165–166]. So you have now abandoned the lawful for the unlawful, and abandoned the pure for the vile. But they refused and were arrogant, to the extent that his own wife was one of them. So Allah commanded him to travel by night with his family, and He sent down upon his people stones of sijjil, until He made its highest part its lowest. This is clearly the correspondence (*munasabah*), for when these people turned away from the truth and descended to the lowest of morals, Allah made the upper parts of their town its lower parts.

The scholars differed about the meaning of this. Some of them said: The earth was lifted and then overturned, so its upper parts became its lower parts. Others said: Rather, it was destroyed by the stones that were sent upon them, until its upper parts became its lower parts.

He says: ﴿وَأَصْحَابُ الايْكَةِ﴾ [Sad 13] ("and the companions of the Thicket"). ﴿وَأَصْحَابُ الايْكَةِ﴾ or ﴿الْأَيْكَةِ﴾ — there are two readings.
﴿الْأَيْكَةِ﴾: the author said: (the thicket, and they are the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him). *Al-Ghaydah* is the trees that are densely intertwined with one another. They were in bliss, but they disobeyed Shu'ayb, mocked him, and said: ﴿يَا شُعَيْبُ مَا نَفْقَهُ كَثِيرًا مِمَّا تَقُولُ وَإِنَّا لَنَرَاكَ فِينَا ضَعِيفًا وَلَوْلَا رَهْطُكَ لَرَجَمْنَاكَ وَمَا أَنْتَ عَلَيْنَا بِعَزِيزٍ﴾ ("O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and we see you as weak among us. Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not powerful against us") [Hud 91]. ﴿قَالُوا يَا شُعَيْبُ أَصَلَاتُكَ تَأْمُرُكَ أَنْ نَتْرُكَ مَا يَعْبُدُ آبَاؤُنَا أَوْ أَنْ نَفْعَلَ فِي أَمْوَالِنَا مَا نَشَاءُ إِنَّكَ لَأَنْتَ الْحَلِيمُ الرَّشِيدُ﴾ ("They said: O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we do with our wealth as we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided") [Hud 87], mocking him. ﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَأَخَذَهُمْ عَذَابُ يَوْمِ الظُّلَّةِ﴾ ("But they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them") [ash-Shu'ara' 189].

The scholars said: They were struck by a very severe heat, so Allah sent a cloud that had shade. They rushed toward it, seeking its shade, but its shade was more scorching than the sun, may Allah protect us. They came from the very place where they felt safe.

Allah, exalted is He, says about these people: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الْأَحْزَابُ﴾ [Sad 13] ("Those are the factions"), meaning: those great factions who transgressed, were arrogant, and denied the messengers. The demonstrative here is in the distal form either because their rank is low and far from the truth, or because they are elevated in terms of their state of transgression and defiance. This is because *ulaa'* is not used except for something far, whether in height, in lowness, or in extent.

﴿أُولَئِكَ الْأَحْزَابُ﴾: *Ahzab* is the plural of *hizb*, and *hizb* is a group, as Allah says: ﴿كُلُّ حِزْبٍ بِمَا لَدَيْهِمْ فَرِحُونَ﴾ ("Every faction rejoices in what it has") [al-Mu'minun 53], meaning every group.

﴿أُولَئِكَ الْأَحْزَابُ﴾ may be a subject and predicate: meaning, "those are the factions who denied the messengers, so We destroyed them." It may also be that ﴿الْأَحْزَابُ﴾ is a descriptive of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾.

His saying: ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ﴾ [Sad 14]: the clause is the predicate of the subject. ﴿إِنْ﴾: he said it means *ma* (not), that is, *in* is negative. We have previously mentioned that *in* is used in Arabic in several ways: negation, condition, the lightened form of the heavy (*mukhaffafah*), and the superfluous (*zaidah*). He says: ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ﴾, meaning: "None of the factions ﴿إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ﴾ ('but denied the messengers')." ﴿كُلٌّ﴾, meaning each one of these factions denied the messengers. *Al-Rusul* is the plural of *rasul*.

Is the plural *al-rusul* distributed over the plural that precedes it in the sense of distribution by individuals, or in the sense of distribution by whole?
The meaning is that they were factions: ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ﴾, that is, each faction denied its messenger. On this reading, the plural is distributed over the preceding plural in the manner of individuals. Or it is distribution of the whole: each faction denied all the messengers.

The author followed the second view. He said: "Because when they denied one, they denied them all, since their call is one, which is the call to monotheism (*tawhid*)." So he, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the plural is distributed over the individuals in the manner of a whole: each faction denied all the messengers. What supports the view of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is the saying of Allah: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ الْمُرْسَلِينَ﴾ ("The people of Noah denied the messengers") [ash-Shu'ara' 105]. For the people of Noah are mentioned as having denied "the messengers," and it is known that no messenger was sent before Noah for us to say that they denied those before him. On this basis, the view of the author is more preponderant than the other possibility that the lexical form allows as a weaker possibility, namely that the plural is distributed over what precedes it in the manner of individuals: ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ﴾.

His saying: ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ﴾ refers to the whole considered collectively, because some of the people believed, but they were few, and the few are overwhelmed by the many. Hence He said: (﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ﴾ of the factions ﴿إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ﴾). It may also be said that no such estimate is needed, and there is no need to say that this is with regard to the majority of these peoples. For He said: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾, so His saying ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ﴾ means: among the deniers, ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ﴾ means among these deniers ﴿إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ﴾. On this view, there is no need for an exception, that is, to exclude those who believed, nor for the claim that the verse follows the majority.

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿إِنْ كُلٌّ إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ﴾ ("Each of them did nothing but deny the messengers"), the messengers who were sent to them. Here we need to distinguish between *rusul* and *nabiyyin* (prophets). First: everyone mentioned in the Qur'an as a prophet is also a messenger. The evidence is His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا رُسُلًا مِنْ قَبْلِكَ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَصَصْنَا عَلَيْكَ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَمْ نَقْصُصْ عَلَيْكَ﴾ ("We sent messengers before you; of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you") [Ghafir 78]. On this basis, everyone mentioned in the Qur'an is among the messengers, since they were related to us, and everyone related to us is a messenger.

In general terms, the scholars say, according to the well-known view among them: a *rasul* (messenger) is one to whom a law (*shar'*) is revealed and who is commanded to convey it and call to it. He is a messenger, and the messenger's duty is only to convey: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord") [al-Ma'idah 67]. As for the *nabi* (prophet), he is one to whom a revelation is made but who is not commanded to convey it. He is thus like a renewer (*mujaddid*) of this Ummah: a renewer is righteous in himself but calls to the extent of his ability. The prophet is not charged with the message; rather, revelation is made to him for what sets him right and sets others right through him, not as an obligation of messengership.

Some scholars held that the difference is that a prophet is one who renews the law of one before him and does not stand independently with revelation, so he brings the law of an earlier prophet. As for the messenger, he is one to whom revelation is renewed and who brings an independent law. This view may be considered good, based on His saying: ﴿إِنَّا أَنْزَلْنَا التَّوْرَاةَ فِيهَا هُدًى وَنُورٌ يَحْكُمُ بِهَا النَّبِيُّونَ الَّذِينَ أَسْلَمُوا لِلَّذِينَ هَادُوا﴾ ("Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light, by which the prophets who submitted judged the Jews") [al-Ma'idah 44]. But it is refuted by Adam, peace be upon him, for Adam was a prophet and was not following an earlier law. When a view is refuted by a counterexample, it is weak and not relied upon.

He says: ﴿إِلَّا كَذَّبَ الرُّسُلَ فَحَقَّ عِقَابِ﴾ [Sad 14] ("...denied the messengers, so My punishment became due"). ﴿حَقَّ﴾: means *wajaba* (became obligatory); ﴿حَقَّ﴾ means it became obligatory and established.

His saying: ﴿عِقَابِ﴾ is the subject (*fa'il*) of ﴿حَقَّ﴾ and is in the nominative case, and the sign of its nominative is the visible kasrah on its final letter, because a singular noun is put in the nominative by kasrah!
* Students: That is not correct.
* Shaykh: What is not correct? Then how did this kasrah come about? This kasrah came about for the sake of harmonizing with the elided *ya'* (the pronoun "my") for lightness. The sentence is (*fa-haqqa 'iqabi*, "so My punishment became due"), but the *ya'* was dropped for lightness. Accordingly, we say: ﴿عِقَابِ﴾ is a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma on its final letter, prevented from being visible by the preoccupation of the position with a vowel for harmony.

﴿فَحَقَّ عِقَابِ﴾: *al-'iqab* is the taking to account for a sin. For this reason it is called *'iqab*, because it comes after (*'aqib*) the crime. Every punishment for a crime is called *'iqab*.

This punishment which Allah sent down upon them is a punishment founded on justice, for Allah attributed it to Himself when He said: "My punishment" (*'iqabi*). We know that the Lord, mighty and majestic, never wrongs anyone at all, neither increasing the evil deeds nor diminishing the good deeds. But if the punishment came from other than Allah, it might exceed the crime. As for the punishment which Allah attributed to Himself, it is a just punishment.

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿وَمَا يَنْظُرُ هَؤُلَاءِ إِلَّا صَيْحَةً وَاحِدَةً مَا لَهَا مِنْ فَوَاقٍ﴾ [Sad 15] ("These people await nothing but a single blast, for which there will be no return").
﴿وَمَا يَنْظُرُ هَؤُلَاءِ﴾: *yanzuru*, when it is transitive with *ila* ("to"), means looking with the eye. When it is transitive by itself, it means waiting. When it is unrestricted, its meaning depends on context: that is, if it is not restricted by a preposition or an object, its meaning depends on the context. An example of the one restricted by *ila* is His saying: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَاضِرَةٌ (٢٢) إِلَى رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord") [al-Qiyamah 22–23]. Here ﴿نَاظِرَةٌ﴾ means "seeing with the eye," because it is transitive with *ila*, and it is attributed to faces, which are the place of the eyes. When it is transitive by itself, it means waiting, as in His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَّا السَّاعَةَ أَنْ تَأْتِيَهُمْ بَغْتَةً فَقَدْ جَاءَ أَشْرَاطُهَا﴾ ("Do they await anything but the Hour, that it come upon them suddenly? Its signs have already come") [Muhammad 18].

It may also be transitive and mean looking for lesson and reflection, as in His saying: ﴿قُلِ انْظُرُوا مَاذَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا تُغْنِي الْآيَاتُ وَالنُّذُرُ عَنْ قَوْمٍ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe") [Yunus 101].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 7–25 (part 5 of 7):

When it comes unrestricted, not transitive by itself nor by (ilā, "to"), then its meaning depends on the context, such as His saying, ﴿upon couches, they look﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 23]. Some said: ﴿they look﴾ means they await the bounty that is brought to them, and some said: ﴿they look﴾ means they look at what Allah has bestowed upon them, and among it is looking at the Face of Allah. Here, ﴿and these await not but one Shout﴾ is transitive by what?
* Student: By itself.
* Shaykh: By itself; so it means (yantadhir, "awaits"). That is, these await not, and those referred to are the people of Makkah, meaning its disbelievers, as the author said: (i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah). ﴿but one Shout﴾: ﴿Shout﴾ is a cry by which they are shouted at; ﴿one﴾ is not repeated a second time, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter﴾ [al-Qamar 46], and He also said: ﴿Indeed, all things We created with measure, and Our command is but one [act]﴾ [al-Qamar 49–50], and He said: ﴿It will not be but one shout, and at once they will all be brought before Us﴾ [Ya-Sin 53]. So the Shout is what will occur on the Day of Resurrection, as the author said: (it is the blast of the Resurrection, by which punishment descends upon them), and it is the Hour. This is the one Shout.
(﴿there is no reprieve for it﴾ with the fa' pronounced with a fatha and with a damma, meaning: return.) ﴿There is no reprieve for it﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is a negation particle, and it is not the Hijazi kind, because the Tamimis and the Hijazis agree that it does not govern, since the Hijazis make it govern only under the condition of order, i.e., the subject preceding the predicate, and here the subject did not precede the predicate but came after it; so it is a negation.
﴿Lahā﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate placed before its subject, ﴿min fawāq﴾; ﴿min﴾ is an extra preposition for emphasis, and ﴿fawāq﴾ is a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma on its final letter, whose appearance is prevented by the occupation of the position by the vowel of the extra preposition. As for morphology, the author said: (it is with fatha on the fa' and with damma), ﴿fawāq﴾ and ﴿fuwāq﴾, and its meaning is return. It was also said that its meaning is respite, i.e., it does not give them respite but seizes them swiftly. It was also said: if it is ﴿fawāq﴾ then it means return, because one says (afāqa, yufīqu) when he returns to his senses; and if it is ﴿fuwāq﴾ then it means respite, derived from the saying of people: fuwāq al-nāqah, the fuwāq of the she-camel is the interval between two milkings, or between two suckings. The interval between two milkings, when she is being milked, is a brief period; that is, a person squeezes the teat for a while, then returns and squeezes it again, and again, so the interval between two milkings is short, and likewise between two sucklings: the infant, when suckling from its mother, sucks, then sucks, then sucks. They use this to describe the swiftness of a thing and its not being delayed. We may say that the two readings combine both meanings, so the meaning becomes ﴿there is no reprieve for it﴾, i.e., there is for it neither return nor respite.
﴿And they said: "Our Lord, hasten to us our share [of punishment] before the Day of Reckoning"﴾ [Sad 16]. I seek refuge in Allah. When the Messenger ﷺ warned them of the Day of Resurrection and that punishment would be theirs therein, they defied the Messenger ﷺ, nay, they defied Allah, and said: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share﴾, meaning our portion, saying this in defiance, arrogance and obstinacy, and we seek refuge in Allah. This is like their saying: ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment"﴾ [al-Anfal 32]. This is the speech of an obstinate, arrogant person, whereas the obligation upon them was to say: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then guide us to it and grant us success in it." That is the obligation. But to say: ﴿rain down on us stones from the sky﴾ is without doubt utmost arrogance, and we seek refuge in Allah.
The author said: (They said, when there was revealed ﴿Then as for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah 19] to the end, meaning ﴿And as for he who is given his record in his left hand﴾ [al-Haqqah 25], they said: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share﴾, i.e., the book of our deeds, ﴿before the Day of Reckoning﴾), they said that mockingly.
What the author has taken is possible linguistically, but there is no evidence for it in the verse. The correct view is that the intended meaning of ﴿qiṭṭanā﴾ is our share of the punishment that you threatened us with, saying that punishment would come upon you as it came upon the factions before you. So it is as if they are saying: if the factions before us were given punishment, then let our share come to us. This is without doubt the utmost of defiance, mockery and arrogance, and we seek refuge in Allah. You marvel that a human being, one of the children of Adam, could reach such defiance, and we seek refuge in Allah. But when they obey Satan, Satan is an enemy of man who drives him to things that a person can barely believe could occur, and Allah grants success.
* * *
* Student: ﴿And they said, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share [of punishment] before the Day of Reckoning." (16) Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back [to Allah]. (17) Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise, (18) and the birds gathered; all were to him returning [in devotion]. (19) And We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech. (20) And has there reached you the report of the adversaries when they climbed over the wall into the prayer chamber? (21) When they entered upon Dawud and he was alarmed by them, they said, "Fear not. [We are] two adversaries, one of whom has wronged the other, so judge between us in truth and do not exceed the bounds and guide us to the sound path." [Sad 16–22].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. It has already been mentioned to us that Allah, glory be to Him, related that earlier nations denied their messengers and were seized by punishment. Allah mentioned that as a warning to those who denied the Messenger ﷺ and as consolation to the Messenger ﷺ. Among those mentioned was the people of Lut. What was their sin in which they stood apart from others?
* Student: The sin is the indecency, the indecency of sodomy, which spread among them, even the wife of the Prophet of Allah Lut, peace be upon him, was with them, helping them (...), this indecency, and assaulting people on their roads.
* Shaykh: No, this is not mentioned in the Qur'an.
* Student: Their gathering place.
* Shaykh: Yes, they commit the evil in their gathering place; the evil is this very thing. What was their punishment?
* Student: Their punishment, meaning their overturning; their houses rushed downward, and their land was beneath them. There are two opinions; one opinion: (...) downward.
* Shaykh: That Allah overturned their cities. The second opinion?
* Student: The second opinion: that the earth was turned over on them, making their upper part lower.
* Shaykh: This is the same as the first opinion.
* Student: And the second opinion is what (...) the lower ceiling.
* Shaykh: Correct, meaning Allah rained down on them stones of baked clay, so the building was destroyed until its top became its bottom.
The statement: ﴿Those are the factions; there is not one of them but that he denied the messengers﴾ [Sad 13–14]. How do we parse these?
* Student: ﴿Those﴾ is a subject.
* Shaykh: ﴿Those are the factions; there is not one of them but that he denied the messengers﴾.
* Student: ﴿Those﴾ is a subject, ﴿one of them﴾ is a predicate.
* Shaykh: And ﴿the factions﴾?
* Student: An adjective.
* Shaykh: An adjective of ﴿those﴾. Is there another parsing?
* Student: ﴿Those are the factions﴾: ﴿those﴾ is a subject and ﴿the factions﴾ is a predicate.
* Shaykh: ﴿Those are the factions﴾, so ﴿there is not one of them﴾ is resumptive, explaining the outcome of these factions.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There is not one of them but that he denied the messengers﴾. How do we parse ﴿in﴾?
* Student: ﴿In﴾ is negative, meaning ﴿mā﴾.
* Shaykh: Meaning ﴿mā﴾. What is the sign of negative ﴿in﴾?
* Student: It is followed by ﴿illā﴾.
* Shaykh: That ﴿illā﴾ follows it, correct. Why did He say "the messengers"? Is "the messengers" here a plural distributed in the manner of distribution of individuals or distribution of the plural?
* Student: It is possible, but the stronger view is that it is distribution.
* Shaykh: It is possible what? It is not possible.
* Student: It is possible that it is distributed as distribution of individuals, meaning that every faction denied its messenger, and this is what is meant. It is also possible that the second is that every faction denied all the messengers, and this is the stronger view.
* Shaykh: Distribution of what?
* Student: Distribution of the plural.
* Shaykh: Distribution of the plural, because the plural is distributed over each individual; meaning every faction denied all the messengers. What is the stronger view?
* Student: The stronger view is that it is distribution of the plural.
* Shaykh: Distribution of the plural. What is the evidence for its being stronger?
* Student: That Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 105].
* Shaykh: That Allah said: ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾, although no messenger had preceded Nuh, yet He said: ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾. What is the reasoning for this statement? What is the reasoning for saying that whoever denies one messenger denies all the messengers?
* Student: Because all of them are from Allah.
* Shaykh: Because all of them are from Allah and their call is one; so it is denial of a kind, not denial of a single person. Correct.
The statement: ﴿These await not but one Shout﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿await﴾?
* Student: The meaning of ﴿await﴾ is, in two senses... a word, meaning two aspects.
* Shaykh: We do not want a word; define ﴿these await not but one Shout﴾.
* Student: When it comes with the meaning of (ilā, "to").
* Shaykh: I said: recite the verse; because the one who, when asked about a specific thing, goes on giving the whole detail, indicates he does not know. Like a student asked a question who wrote the entire chapter. There was a student in an exam asked the ruling on turning the head during prayer, and he answered: The answer: it is disliked in prayer to turn one's head, to raise one's gaze to the sky, and to rest one's hand on the hip. Recite the whole section, write at the end; take what you want and leave what you want. I ask you about a specific thing and you answer the whole section. I say: what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿these await not﴾?
* Student: It means: await not.
* Shaykh: ﴿These await not﴾, well done. The word ﴿yanẓuru﴾ comes with various meanings, among them "await," as in this verse, and among them?
* Student: Among them: looking and seeing, the second meaning, if it is...
* Shaykh: Among them, that it comes with the meaning of looking with the eye.
* Student: If it is transitive by (ilā).
* Shaykh: If it is transitive by (ilā), like: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 17]. And the third?
* Student: That it depends on context, the looking of reflection, meaning.
* Shaykh: That it is the looking of reflection.
* Student: Because of His saying: ﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-A'raf 185].
* Shaykh: ﴿Say: Look﴾ [Yunus 101].
* Student: ﴿Say: Look.﴾
* Shaykh: In "dominion," and likewise the one: ﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what Allah has created?﴾. So it comes with the meaning of intellectual contemplation, and the context supports that.
The statement: ﴿There is no reprieve for it﴾. ﴿Fawāq﴾: are there two readings?
* Student: ﴿Fawāq﴾ and ﴿fuwāq﴾.
* Shaykh: Do they have the same meaning according to what the author said and what we have established?
* Student: ﴿Fawāq﴾ means return and respite.
* Shaykh: What is its meaning according to the author's opinion? Do the two words have one meaning?
* Student: According to the author's opinion, it means return only.
* Shaykh: So they have one meaning?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: So ﴿fawāq﴾ and ﴿fuwāq﴾ have the same meaning, like this? Is there another opinion?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: That ﴿fuwāq﴾ is the interval between two milkings.
* Shaykh: The fuwāq of the she-camel, meaning the interval between two milkings or two sucklings when her infant is nursing. If we take both readings, the meaning of the verse, taking both readings in the two aspects we mentioned, is:
* Student: That is, intensity of the speed of their seizure.
* Shaykh: The speed of their seizure, like this? And that it is not lifted from them. If we interpret it as return, ﴿there is no reprieve for it﴾ meaning return, in the sense that punishment is not lifted from them; ﴿there is no reprieve for it﴾ meaning no respite. So the meaning is that it is swift upon them.
Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, [saying], "Walk on and remain steadfast to your gods. Indeed, this is a thing intended. We did not hear of this in the latest religion. This is nothing but an invention."﴾ [Sad 6–7].
* Among the benefits of this verse: that these who deny the Messenger ﷺ regarding what he brought of monotheism have no proof except what their forefathers were upon; this is shown by their saying: ﴿We did not hear of this in the latest religion﴾.
* Among its benefits: that these are arrogant and obstinate; despite having no proof, they said: ﴿This is nothing but an invention﴾.
* Among its benefits also: that every person who lacks sacred knowledge resorts to what people were accustomed to. This is as it was before, for many people, when you forbid them from evil, they say: this is what people have followed. This is not a proof. Just as this was in the past, it is also in the present: among people, when I denounce an evil to them they say: this is what people still do, or they say: we have not heard of this.
From this is the saying of some common folk when they are alerted to something they did not know: they say: this is a new religion, we have not heard of this. This is not a proof. The proof is the established evidence from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ.
* Among the benefits of these verses, in His saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ [Sad 8] to the end: that these people want the Law to follow their desires; revelation comes to whom they wish and is withheld from whom they do not wish; this is by His saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the possessor of falsehood does not realize that his argument is an argument against him; for their saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ would be an argument if the Reminder had been sent down to whom they chose; for if it had been sent down to the one they named and wanted, others would have said: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾.
* A branch of this benefit: every false claimant argues with a truth, i.e., with a proof of the truth, but his use of it is false, so he has no argument. Among this is what the people of distortion argue in the matter of the attributes or other authentic texts which they do not use correctly. For example, the people of negation argue for their negation with Allah's saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 11]. It is known that upon reflection this proof is an argument against them, since negation of likeness indicates the affirmation of the basic meaning; if the basic meaning were not established, negating likeness would have no benefit. Is that not so?
Likewise, every falsifier argues for his falsehood with a valid argument, but his use of it is not correct; we find that this argument is an argument against him. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his book Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa'l-Naql, known as al-'Aql wa'l-Naql, that there is no possessor of falsehood who argues with a verse or an authentic hadith except that his evidence becomes an argument against him and not for him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those who proposed this suggestion and denied that revelation should descend upon Muhammad ﷺ are in doubt about what they claim. If they are in doubt, how do they propose? For this reason He said: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt concerning My Reminder﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those who deny the messengers are about to have punishment descend upon them; by His saying: ﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾.
* Among its benefits: that when punishment descends, it touches a person and affects him; for He expressed it by His saying: ﴿they have not yet tasted﴾.
* Among its benefits also: that words are interpreted according to context. Tasting originally refers to food and drink, but it may be used for what afflicts a person directly, and it is then called a taste.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Or do they possess the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, the Mighty, the Bestower? Or do they have dominion over the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them climb up by the means.﴾ [Sad 9, 10].

* Among the benefits of these two verses: refuting the argument of those who said: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾. This is because the sending down of revelation upon a person is part of God's favor upon him and of the treasuries of His mercy, and these proposers do not possess this, since the command and the bounty are in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two names of God, ﴿the Mighty﴾ and ﴿the Bestower﴾, and the affirmation of the attributes they contain. ﴿The Mighty﴾ contains the attribute of might (ʿizzah), which has three divisions, as we have passed over in the tafsir. ﴿The Bestower﴾ contains the attribute of abundant giving, and how numerous are God's gifts, the Mighty and Majestic. It also contains power, since only one who is able gives; it contains self-sufficiency (ghina), since one who has nothing cannot give; and it contains generosity (karam), since the miser does not give. Is the indication of "the Bestower" upon "giving" by way of the indication of…?
* Student: Correspondence (muṭābaqah).
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: Inclusion (tataḍammun).
* The Shaykh: Inclusion. The indication of "the Bestower" upon giving is by way of the indication of inclusion. The indication upon power, self-sufficiency and generosity is by way of the indication of implication (iltizām). So in this name there are the three types of indication. What are they?
* Student: (...) "the Bestower".
* The Shaykh: What are the three types of indication?
* The student: Implication, correspondence, and inclusion.
* The Shaykh: The difference between these three: the indication of a word upon its whole meaning is the indication of correspondence; upon part of its meaning it is inclusion; and upon an external necessary consequence that the word does not indicate by its own wording, but which is among its necessary concomitants, it is the indication of implication. I will give an example from a sensory matter to clarify the abstract matter. This is a house that contains rooms, sitting areas, and courtyards (barahāt, meaning ahwāsh, enclosed yards). The indication of this house upon all that is in it of rooms, sitting areas and courtyards is the indication of correspondence. Its indication upon each single room alone, each single sitting area alone, and each single courtyard alone is the indication of inclusion. Its indication that it has a builder is the indication of implication, because a house must have a builder. We say: this has been built by a builder. What is the evidence? Because the house must have a builder. So "the Bestower," for example, its indication upon the name and the attribute which is giving: is it upon the name and the giving?
* Students: Correspondence.
* The Shaykh: Correspondence. And upon the name alone, or the giving alone?
* Students: Inclusion.
* The Shaykh: Inclusion. And upon power, self-sufficiency and generosity?
* Students: Implication.
* The Shaykh: The indication of implication.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: observing that the verse-endings (fawāṣil) suit the context of the verse, because ﴿the Mighty, the Bestower﴾ is appropriate to His saying: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy?﴾.
The correspondence, or the suitability of verse-endings to the content of the verse, is a proof of eloquence (balāghah), and nothing deviates from this. For this reason, when a man recited before a Bedouin: "And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from God, and God is Forgiving, Merciful," the Bedouin was astonished how one would say "an exemplary punishment from God" and then say "God is Forgiving, Merciful"? Forgiveness and mercy do not suit exemplary punishment. So the Bedouin said to the reciter: "Repeat." He recited: "And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from God, and God is Forgiving, Merciful." He said: "Repeat, that is not how the verse goes." So he recited: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from God, and God is Mighty, Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 38]. He said: "Now it is right: He is Mighty and Wise, so He cuts off. If He were Forgiving and Merciful, He would not cut off, glorified and exalted is He." For this reason God said in Surat al-Ma'idah concerning those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption: ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is only that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment. Except for those who repent before you gain power over them; so know that God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 33, 34]. From this verse the scholars derived that if they repent before they are overpowered, the prescribed penalty (ḥadd) is lifted from them, because God said: ﴿so know that God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, meaning: if He forgives them and shows them mercy, then they are not to have the prescribed penalty enforced upon them.
In this verse, the correspondence of ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, the Mighty, the Bestower﴾ is an apparent correspondence, because God is possessor of mercy, possessor of might and dominance, and possessor of giving and bounty. So He gives to whom He wills in accordance with what His might requires from the treasuries of His mercy. However, some verses have endings that apparently differ from their content, such as the saying of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord." And I was a witness over them while I was among them. But when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things. If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 117, 118]. Here the saying ﴿indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ came as a response to ﴿and if You forgive them﴾, whereas what was expected was "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful." Some scholars raised a difficulty about this and said: how does he say ﴿and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ and not "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful"? It was answered that ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, did not limit himself to mentioning forgiveness, but mentioned both forgiveness and punishment. He said: ﴿If You punish them﴾ and ﴿and if You forgive them﴾. So the ruling was now undecided between forgiveness and mercy, if we look at his saying ﴿and if You forgive them﴾, and between might, wisdom and judgment, if we look at his saying ﴿If You punish them﴾.
