Shaykh: Then why do we not make it general, including prayer?

Student: (...) sunset?

Shaykh: Yes, because the evening remembrances take place after the afternoon, so he remembers Allah after the afternoon, and he was occupied from that.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: How?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, it is written with an alif as long as it is not joined to a pronoun. If it is joined to a pronoun, there is no need for the alif.

Student: What need, when the waw is in the position of this...

Shaykh: That is, if he said ruddū alone, he would not say hā.

Student: In ruddū, the pronoun refers to whom?

Shaykh: No, my point is: you are saying, why was no alif written after the waw? Is that what you mean or not? I am saying: the alif is not written after the waw with a pronoun. If you say ruddūhu, you do not write an alif. Ruddūhā, you do not write an alif. But ruddū Zaydan, you write an alif.

Student: And in ruddū, the pronoun refers to whom?

Shaykh: The waw refers to the addressee.

Student: To the addressee; it is for the plural.

Shaykh: Yes, and it is for the plural, addressing a group. And hā refers to the horses; that is, return the horses to me.

Student: Yes, and the waw is for the absent party.

Shaykh: No, it is for the addressee. An imperative directed to a group is not for the absent. If it were a past verb, it would be for the absent, but this is an imperative verb, and the waw attached to an imperative verb is for the addressee.

Student: I thought it was past.

Shaykh: No, if it were past he would say ruddūhā. The past is said ruddūhā.

Student: I said it could be passive.

Shaykh: No, passive would be with the object: ruddūhā.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: In any case, it is an imperative verb; he orders them to return them to him.

Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Someone asked a mufti, saying: I was a disobedient person, and I have cassettes of songs and so on. What should I do with them? Should I record religious lectures on them, or what should I do with them, or burn them? He said to him: burn them, and he cited this verse as evidence, saying: Solomon, peace be upon him, slaughtered the horses.

Shaykh: This question is ahead of its time, because it will be among the benefits, God willing.

Student: Why was it better to make the verb implicitly carry a meaning rather than the imperative verb?

Shaykh: Yes indeed, because when you make the verb implicitly carry a meaning, you gain a new meaning in addition to the original meaning of the verb. For example, if we say, regarding His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan 6], that the intended meaning is "they are quenched by it," this includes two meanings: drinking and quenching. If you say that the bāʾ in ﴿from which they drink﴾ means min (مِنْ), "they drink from it," we gain only one meaning, which is drinking.

Student: If we make the verb implicitly carry a meaning, O Shaykh, it is as if we have brought something additional.

Shaykh: No, it is not additional, because when we say yarwā (is quenched), we have brought the original meaning of "drink," since there is no quenching except after drinking. What made us bring the additional meaning, which is quenching, is that, true, quenching is additional to mere drinking. What made us bring it is that the bāʾ does not take yashrabu (drink) as its complement.

Student: Shaykh, may Allah pardon you, (...) some scholars (...)?

Shaykh: Yes, this is the amulet (tamimah). If we permit amulets with the Qur'an, some people came and included shirkī (polytheistic) things in them. What do you say? We say: the ruling revolves around its cause. If they write polytheistic things, it becomes forbidden because of shirk. But if they write something of the Qur'an, there is no shirk in it. That is, the one who writes the amulet must be trustworthy.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: He brought what?

Student: I am saying: they are common in some places in the Hijaz (...), the northern and southern land.

Shaykh: What is common?

Student: These hangings that contain shirk.

Shaykh: No, that is prohibited, this.

* * *

Student: ﴿And We had certainly tried Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he returned (in repentance). He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom not appropriate for anyone after me; indeed, You are the Bestower." So We subjected to him the wind, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed. And the devils, every builder and diver, and others bound together in chains. This is Our gift, so grant or withhold without account. And indeed, he has with Us closeness and a good return.﴾ [Sad 34–40]

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We bestowed upon David, Solomon, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah). When there were displayed before him at evening the poised, swift horses.﴾ [Sad 30–31], and so on to the end. Where is the complement of ﴿idh﴾ (when) in His saying: ﴿when there were displayed﴾?

Student: Yes, ﴿when there were displayed﴾.

Shaykh: That is, idh is a temporal adverb and needs a complement.

Student: It is omitted; its estimate is: "remember when there were displayed."

Shaykh: "Remember when there were displayed." His saying: ﴿the poised﴾, what are ﴿the poised﴾ (...)?

I loved the love of good intensely.

What is meant by "good" here?

Student: The author explained it as horses, and this is a deficiency.

Shaykh: What led him to explain it as horses?

Student: It is excused by the context, the context of the verse.

Shaykh: Where He said: ﴿the poised, swift horses﴾. And the second view, or the second possibility?

Student: That it is general, including horses and other wealth and so on, since "good" is applied to wealth.

Shaykh: What is the proof or evidence that "good" means wealth?

Student: ﴿And indeed, he is, in love of good, intense.﴾

Shaykh: ﴿And indeed, he is, in love of good, intense﴾ [al-'Adiyat 8]. And what is meant by "good" here?

Student: Wealth.

Shaykh: Wealth. What is the evidence that it means wealth? ﴿And you love wealth with immense love﴾ [al-Fajr 20].

His saying: ﴿over the remembrance of my Lord﴾. What is meant by the remembrance of his Lord?

Student: According to the author's view, he said it is the afternoon prayer, but the remembrance includes more than prayer, and includes the evening remembrances as well as prayer.

Shaykh: Well done. His saying: ﴿I have loved the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord﴾. What is the position of ʿan (over/from) here?

Student: In meaning, you mean?

Shaykh: Yes, what is the meaning of "I loved it over the remembrance of my Lord"?

Student: That is: "apart from the remembrance of my Lord."

Shaykh: That means what?

Student: That is: I loved the love of good apart from the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted.

Shaykh: What does it mean according to this?

Student: In the sense of "other than."

Shaykh: ʿan in the sense of "other than"?

Student: In the sense of "other than Allah, exalted is He"; that is, other than the remembrance of Allah.

Another student: "In exchange for his worship."

Shaykh: That is, what?

Student: Instead of mentioning his Lord.
Shaykh: "Instead of mentioning his Lord" is one interpretation. Is there another?
Student: Or that it is implied (muḍammana).
Shaykh: Implied; that is, he preferred love of good over remembering Him.

Regarding His words ﴿حَتَّى تَوَارَتْ بِالْحِجَابِ﴾ (until it was hidden behind the veil): to what does the pronoun refer?
Student: There are two opinions. The first is that the pronoun refers to the horses: he saw them moving away from him, far off.
Shaykh: He kept watching them going and coming.
Student: The second opinion is that it was hidden by the veil from the sun.
Shaykh: The sun. And what is meant by "the veil" on this view?
Student: The veil means the earth.
Shaykh: The earth, correct? He says: ﴿فَطَفِقَ مَسْحًا﴾ (so he began to strike). Is "ṭafiqa" one of the verbs of beginning?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: And where is its predicate?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: Its predicate is omitted: "so he began to strike, striking." ﴿بِالسُّوقِ﴾ (with the shanks): what does it mean?
Student: It is the plural of (sāq, shank).
Shaykh: The plural of "sāq." That is, he strikes their shanks until he hamstrings them. And "al-a'nāq" (the necks)?
Student: It is the plural of (‘unuq, neck), and he strokes their necks.
Shaykh: With his hand? He strokes with his hand like this. So the meaning of your words is that he strokes their shanks with his hand, and likewise strokes their necks.
Student: That is, striking with the sword.
Shaykh: Even on the shanks?
Student: Yes.
Shaykh: And the necks are for slaughter. Let us take the benefits.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿وَوَهَبْنَا لِدَاوُودَ سُلَيْمَانَ نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ﴾ (And We gave to David, Solomon; an excellent servant).
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: children are a gift from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the servant, and it follows from this that the servant must thank Allah, exalted is He, for this blessing.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the praise of Solomon in His words ﴿نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ﴾ (an excellent servant). Here "servanthood" is the special servanthood.
- Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of causes and means, by His words ﴿إِنَّهُ أَوَّابٌ﴾ (indeed, he was one who often turned back), for this is the cause of his being praised.
- Among its benefits: the virtue of returning to Allah and turning back to Him with the heart and with action, because Allah praised Solomon for this.
- Among the benefits of the noble verse in His words ﴿إِذْ عُرِضَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ (when there were displayed before him) to its end: the demonstration of the greatness of Solomon's kingdom, since people would present these horses to him for enjoyment, and to view and inspect them. The evidence for this is that He said ﴿إِذْ عُرِضَ عَلَيْهِ﴾, which indicates that there were people who would present these horses to him.
- Among the benefits of this verse: this custom, namely the displaying of horses and enjoying their running at the end of the day, is an ancient custom that people still practise to this day. You hardly find anyone holding a horse race at the beginning of the day; it takes place at the end of the day, and this is one of the ancient customs of people that continues to this day.
- Among the benefits of this verse: it is appropriate to select good, beautiful horses that delight the soul in seeing them and in their running, by His words ﴿الصَّافِنَاتُ الْجِيَادُ﴾ (the swift, well-bred horses standing on three legs).
- Among its benefits: it is appropriate to keep horses, since this was the practice of the messengers, peace be upon them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Good is tied to the foreheads of horses until the Day of Resurrection" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2850) and Muslim (1873/98), from the hadith of ‘Urwah ibn al-Ja‘d]. So whenever horses are instruments of war, the good is in their foreheads until the Day of Resurrection.
- Among the benefits of this verse: the mention of an example of describing Solomon as "awwāb" (one who often turns back), where He said ﴿إِنِّي أَحْبَبْتُ حُبَّ الْخَيْرِ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّي﴾ (Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord) to its end.
- Among its benefits: wealth is good, and it is so, because when a person is granted wealth he is able to enjoy fully what pertains to wealth, unlike when wealth is restricted for him, for then he cannot enjoy it.
- Among the benefits of the noble verse: turning away from the remembrance of Allah for the sake of worldly matters is blameworthy, because Solomon reproached himself for loving good and giving it precedence over the remembrance of Allah.
- Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation that the sun moves continuously and does not set; that is, it is hidden from sight in the sky, by His words ﴿حَتَّى تَوَارَتْ بِالْحِجَابِ﴾.
- Among its benefits: the affirmation that the sun is what revolves around the earth in its rising and setting, because He attributed the action to it, saying ﴿حَتَّى تَوَارَتْ﴾. If the matter were as the geographers of today say, that the earth is what revolves and the sun is hidden because of its rotation, He would have said "until you (fem.) were hidden behind the veil," or "until it was hidden," meaning [the earth] — because if you are the one who revolves while your counterpart is stationary, which one is hidden? The stationary or the revolving one? The revolving one. So when Allah affirmed that the hiding belongs to the sun, this indicates that it is the one that revolves. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَتَرَى الشَّمْسَ إِذَا طَلَعَتْ تَزَاوَرُ عَنْ كَهْفِهِمْ ذَاتَ الْيَمِينِ وَإِذَا غَرَبَتْ تَقْرِضُهُمْ ذَاتَ الشِّمَالِ﴾ [al-Kahf 17], where these are four verbs, all attributed to the sun.

In the authentic collection, it is related from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was with the Prophet (ﷺ) when the sun set, and he said to him: "Do you know where it goes?" I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Indeed, it prostrates beneath the Throne and seeks permission; permission is granted to it, and it is said to it: 'Return from where you came,' so it rises from its place of setting" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3199) and Muslim (159/250), from the hadith of Abu Dharr].

This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and it is obligatory upon the believer to follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, for this is the method in all matters. As you know, regarding the Names and Attributes of Allah we follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and as you know, regarding the legal rulings we follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Therefore, in cosmic matters too we follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, for the apparent meaning of the Qur'an comes from the All-Knowing Creator, so He is more knowing of His creation than they are. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿مَا أَشْهَدْتُهُمْ خَلْقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَلَا خَلْقَ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation) [al-Kahf 51]. If this comes from the most knowing, it is obligatory upon us to affirm it.

It is therefore obligatory for us to let the apparent meanings of the Book and the Sunnah stand as they are, until there is a clear, sensory proof showing that the wording is not to be taken in its apparent sense. Even if it were made clear, as clear as the sun, that the earth is what revolves, we would say: these verbs whose apparent meaning is that the sun revolves were expressed in terms of what we observe, so the setting is in terms of our observation, for what is observed by the senses, according to the apparent view of common people, is that the earth is stationary and the sun revolves around it. So the expression follows what people apparently observe. But when do we need to interpret verses? When something has been established by a certain sensory proof with no difficulty, because the apparent meaning is only probable in its indication, and this indication cannot be displaced except by a definitive proof stronger than it.

- Among the benefits of this verse: the earth is spherical. For when it was established that the sun is hidden by the veil, this indicates that the earth is what casts the veil over it, and as we observe, the sun descends from the high point of the sky, then descends little by little until it is at the lowest point, in the earth. This indicates that the earth is spherical. This is also a definite matter with no difficulty; it is apparent from the Qur'an and apparent also from reality. In the Qur'an Allah says: ﴿إِذَا السَّمَاءُ انْشَقَّتْ (١) وَأَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّهَا وَحُقَّتْ (٢) وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ (٣) وَأَلْقَتْ مَا فِيهَا وَتَخَلَّتْ (٤) وَأَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّهَا وَحُقَّتْ﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 1–5]. When is this? It will be on the Day of Resurrection, since the sky has not yet split.
So His words ﴿وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ﴾ (when the earth is stretched out) indicate that before this it was not stretched out but spherical. This does not contradict His words, exalted is He: ﴿أَفَلَا يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَى الْإِبِلِ كَيْفَ خُلِقَتْ (١٧) وَإِلَى السَّمَاءِ كَيْفَ رُفِعَتْ (١٨) وَإِلَى الْجِبَالِ كَيْفَ نُصِبَتْ (١٩) وَإِلَى الْأَرْضِ كَيْفَ سُطِحَتْ﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 17–20], which does not contradict it, because its being flat is in terms of what is observed: when you stand on the earth now, you find it level as far as the eye can see.

- Among the benefits of these verses, in His words ﴿رُدُّوهَا عَلَيَّ فَطَفِقَ﴾ (Bring them back to me," and he began) to its end: the permissibility of discretionary punishment (ta‘zir) by destroying property. Jurists differ on this question: may a person be disciplined by destroying his property, or not? Some scholars said it is not permissible, because destroying property is corruption of it, and we can discipline him by taking his property without destroying it, taking it and spending it in another beneficial way. Others said that it is permissible, and they cited as evidence that the thief of booty who conceals what he has taken has his baggage burned, which is destruction of it, even though the army may be in need of his property; yet we destroy it. This view is the stronger one: it is permissible to discipline by destroying property. First, because the Sunnah indicates this.
Second, because its destruction is more painful and has a greater effect; for if it were taken and spent on public interests, the punishment would be hidden. Moreover, it might open a door for oppressive rulers: if they wanted money, they would bring a case against some person and then say: "We discipline him by taking his property," and then they would take his property, claiming it would go to the public treasury, while it would actually go into the pockets of those oppressors. So when we say it is burned and destroyed before the people, that danger is removed. Accordingly, if we found with a person an instrument of amusement that could be used for something other than amusement, and we disciplined him by breaking it, that would be lawful, and we would not say: convert it into something other than an instrument of amusement, because destroying it in front of people is more painful and severe than destroying it by spending it on some purpose.
- Among the benefits of this verse: there is no harm if a person disciplines himself by destroying his own property, following the action of Solomon. So if we supposed that a person was occupied with something that distracted him from the remembrance of Allah, and he wanted to break it, that would be lawful and permissible, because this leads to his not returning to being distracted from the remembrance of Allah by some property.
- Among the benefits of this verse: the strength of Solomon's authority in his commands and prohibitions, by His words ﴿رُدُّوهَا عَلَيَّ﴾ (Bring them back to me). This indicates that he had many soldiers who carried out his command, for had he said "bring it back" (singular), the servant would have been one person. But since he said ﴿رُدُّوهَا﴾ (bring them back), this indicates that he had many servants serving him.
- Among its benefits: Solomon's swiftness and promptness in carrying out his intention to destroy this property, by His words ﴿فَطَفِقَ مَسْحًا بِالسُّوقِ وَالْأَعْنَاقِ﴾ (so he began to strike the shanks and necks).

Someone may say: Is there not in this a torment of an animal, if he began to strike its shanks with the sword?
It is answered: Yes, but the apparent meaning is that he first hamstrings it, then cuts its neck. This is not objectionable, because the pain does not last. He singled out the shanks for striking because they were swift horses; when a swift horse lifts its hoof somewhat, its shanks have a beautiful appearance, so it was the object of desire, and that is why he began to strike these shanks. As for the necks, the apparent purpose is complete destruction.

Student: Solomon knew the language of birds, and similarly matters (...). Did he take the horses, that is, give their meat in charity... (...)?
Shaykh: Yes, this is a good question. He asks: did he eat their meat, or give it in charity, or what did he do? What do you say?
Student: The author says: he gave it in charity.
Shaykh: He says: he gave it in charity. Read (...).
Student: He says: ("And the necks": that is, he slaughtered them and cut their legs, seeking nearness to Allah, the Exalted, since they had distracted him from the prayer, and he gave their meat in charity, so Allah compensated him with something better than them, and He was swifter, and that was the wind.)
Shaykh: Did you hear? This allows what the author said, that he gave them in charity, and it also allows that he did not give them in charity, because slaughtering them was a drawing near to Allah by destroying them, and what is of that kind is not eaten. A parallel: if a man committed bestiality with an animal, the animal is killed and its meat is not eaten, because it was destroyed for the sake of Allah, so it should not be eaten. In any case, it is possible that Solomon gave them in charity as the author said, or ate them, or left them. Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 26–33 (part 1 of 6):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah (successor/vicegerent) upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your] desire﴾ [Sad 26].

Allah the Exalted addresses Dawud with the vocative. Addressing someone with a vocative is intended to alert them, because there is a difference between saying "Muhammad stood up" and saying "O 'Ali, Muhammad stood up." In the second there is an alert. When speech needs an alert, this is a sign of its importance, since speech that is to be given attention is preceded by something that serves as an alert. So Allah, glorified and exalted be He, calls out to Dawud to alert him to what He is about to tell him, and says: ﴿Indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth﴾.

﴿Ja'alnaka﴾ means ṣayyarnāka (We made you). This is because ja'l (making) sometimes means taṣyīr (rendering something into a state) and sometimes means ījād (bringing into existence). In His saying ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am 1], what kind of ja'l is this? It is ījād, a ja'l of bringing into existence; that is, He brought them into being. In His saying ﴿Indeed We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3], it means ṣayyarnāh (We rendered it); it is ja'l of taṣyīr. The difference between them is that if it takes one object, it carries the meaning of bringing into existence, and if it takes two objects, it carries the meaning of rendering. Here He says ﴿We have made you khalifah﴾, and it takes two objects: the kaf (you) and "khalifah," so it carries the meaning of rendering.

His saying ﴿Indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth﴾ means: a successor to Us in conveying Our Law. It does not mean that He has a successor who comes after Him, because Allah is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward; rather, [he is] a khalifah of Allah in conveying what? In conveying His Law and His judgement among the people.

His saying ﴿so judge﴾: the fa' here is for consequence; that is, on the basis that you are a khalifah upon the earth, judge.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿a khalifah upon the earth﴾ managing the affairs of the people, as caliphs manage the affairs of those whom Allah has made shepherds over Him).

﴿So judge between the people in truth﴾: this fa' is, as I said, for consequence, on what? On His making him a khalifah.

﴿Judge between the people in truth﴾: ﴿bil-haqq﴾ means bil-'adl (with justice). This is because al-haqq, if it stands in contrast to news, means ṣidq (truthfulness), and if it stands in contrast to a ruling, it means 'adl (justice). So if one says: "Muhammad informed me of such-and-such, and it is haqq," it means truthfully. And if you say: "So-and-so ruled with such-and-such, and it is haqq," it means justly. Here He says ﴿judge between the people in truth﴾, that is, with justice, because haqq here is attributed to the judgement, so it carries the meaning of justice.

﴿So judge between the people in truth﴾, that is, with justice. This includes the judgement itself, the manner of judging, and its requirements. Judging means judging by the Sharia, and its manner (the manner of judging) is that you be just between the two litigants in everything. Scholars even say: the judge must be just between the two litigants in his words, his glance, his speech, their seating, and their entrance upon him, in everything:
In his words: he should not speak harshly to one litigant and gently to the other.
In his glance: he should not look at one litigant with an angry look and at the other with a pleased look.
In his seating: he should not seat one litigant beside him and the other far from him.
Their entrance upon him: he should not say to one of them, "Enter," before the other, even if one of them is a disbeliever. He should not give precedence to the Muslim in entering. Some scholars have said that if one of them is a disbeliever, the Muslim is given precedence in entering, but the setting is a setting of judgement, where justice is obligatory. This one's disbelief is his concern and that one's Islam is his concern. This applies if entry requires giving precedence and delay. As for when the door is open, he is not obliged to place a man at the door saying, "Enter together." He leaves the matter to whom? To the litigants: whoever comes enters, whether before or after the other. But if there is an order of entry, he should not give precedence to one over the other. This is the manner of judging.

As for the judgement itself: if he knows that the truth lies with one of them, he is obliged to rule for him, whatever he is, whether an enemy or a friend.

﴿So judge between the people in truth﴾: "al-nās" originally was (al-unās), but the hamzah was dropped for lightness, as it was dropped from (sharr) and (khayr). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 60], meaning: of what is worse than that.

Then He said: ﴿and do not follow desire﴾. ﴿Al-hawa﴾ is the desire of the self. He forbade him from following desire only to magnify this matter, and it does not follow from His prohibition of it that it is possible for him, just as Allah said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿If you should associate [others with Allah], your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar 65], and it does not follow from this that shirk is possible for him. It may also be said that Allah forbade him from following desire because of the strength of desire among human beings. Desire is something innate in mankind, for it is rare that a person whose father comes before him together with another person who is his enemy does not have a desire (inclination), or that a person whose close friend comes before him, and another of his fierce enemies, does not incline toward the first. This is rare. So, because of the strength of the motive, which is desire, Allah forbade it, even though it is not possible for him.

His saying ﴿and do not follow desire﴾, that is, the desire of the self, ﴿lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾ [Sad 26]. ﴿Fa-yudilla-ka﴾: the verb here is present tense, but it is in the subjunctive. Why is it in the subjunctive? Because it came after a prohibition with the fa', and the present verb, when preceded by fa' after a prohibition, becomes subjunctive by an obligatorily implied "an."

His saying ﴿lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾ means: it makes you stray, swerving to the right and to the left.

His saying ﴿from the way of Allah﴾: the author said: (that is, from the signs that indicate His oneness). This interpretation is very weak. Rather, what is meant by ﴿the way of Allah﴾ is His path that leads to Him, because sabīl in origin is the road, and it is attributed to Allah because Allah is the One who laid it down and legislated it, and because this path leads to whom? It leads to Allah. So it is attributed to Allah with regard both to its establishment and to its end. If we say, as you have mentioned, that what is meant by ﴿from the way of Allah﴾ is "from His way and His Sharia," it becomes more general than what the author said, more general and more closely tied to the wording, because sabīl in the language is known to mean the road, and the signs indicating monotheism are not the road itself; yet there is no doubt that reflecting upon those signs is part of the Sharia of Allah.

﴿Lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed those who stray from the way of Allah﴾ [Sad 26], to the end. Allah the Exalted did not say: "If you follow desire, or if you stray from the way of Allah, then you will have a severe punishment." Rather, He brought a separate, independent sentence. First: to avoid addressing Dawud with that, and second: so that it would be more general. There are two benefits in it: the first is avoiding addressing Dawud with that, and the second is intending generality. For this reason Allah said: ﴿He frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to him. And what would make you know?﴾ [Abasa 1–3]. He expressed it with the past tense, indicating an absent person: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, and did not say "you frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to you, and what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself." Rather He said ﴿He frowned﴾, to avoid addressing the Messenger ﷺ with such a description.

His saying ﴿Indeed those who stray from the way of Allah, for them is a severe punishment﴾: the author said: (﴿Indeed those who stray from the way of Allah﴾, that is, from faith in Allah). This too is open to question. The correct view is that the way of Allah here is the first way of Allah, and what is meant by it is His Sharia, because it is the path that leads to Him.

﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾: the sentence is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. Where is its subject?
* Student: ﴿alladhīna﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿alladhīna﴾ is the subject, and ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ is its predicate. So the sentence here is a predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and every sentence that serves as a predicate must have a link (rābiṭ) connecting it to the subject, and the link here is the pronoun in His saying ﴿for them﴾.

His saying ﴿severe (shadīd)﴾: that is, strong and great. What shows you its strength and greatness is what Allah described it with in the Noble Qur'an, of attributes that make hearts tremble and livers quake.

His saying ﴿shadīd﴾: that is, strong. ﴿For that they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Sad 26]: that is, because of their forgetting the Day of Reckoning. Here the bā' indicates cause, and "mā" is a verbal-noun particle. For this reason the author said: (because of their forgetting the Day of Reckoning, which entails their abandonment of faith; had they been certain of the Day of Reckoning, they would have believed in the world).

His saying ﴿for that they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾: the Day of Reckoning means the Day of Resurrection, and it is attributed to Reckoning because people are called to account on it for their deeds. The first thing a person is reckoned for concerning the right of Allah is the prayer, and the first thing he is reckoned for concerning the rights of the children of Adam is blood (bloodshed), as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The first matter to be judged among the people is concerning blood."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6864) from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]

* Student: (...) the prostration; he sought forgiveness from his Lord (...) the prostration, is it a prostration (...)?
* The Shaykh: As for Dawud, it is the prostration of repentance. For this reason we say that what is prescribed in our Sharia is that one pray two rakʿahs, not that one prostrate once.
As for us, the reciters of the Qur'an, the prostration is a prostration of recitation, and therefore it is recommended for a person to prostrate even if he is in prayer, contrary to those who say that the prostration of (Sad) should not be performed in prayer; this view is weak.
* Student: Is it possible (...) if one does not watch over (his duty to) Allah (...)?
* The Shaykh: Never is one safe (...) if he does not watch over Allah, but some people may be safe from desire not out of piety and watchfulness toward Allah, but out of fear of shame; for example, when the matter is clear and one judges contrary to what has become clear. Such a person may not care whether it is out of fear of Allah, but out of fear of the disgrace that will befall him among people.
* Student: The prophets (...) and their sins are forgiven before (...) to Allah?
* The Shaykh: Known. Whoever we know Allah has forgiven, he is forgiven. Here Dawud, Allah forgave him, so if Allah has forgiven him, he is not called to account for that.
* Student: Is it prescribed for a person to (...) judgeship (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, judgeship is a communal obligation (fard kifāyah), and if no one qualified exists except him, it becomes incumbent upon him. Therefore a person should take judgeship as both a responsibility and a religious duty. As for its being a responsibility, it is clear: he takes charge of people's affairs and judges between them. As for its being a religious duty, it is because this is a communal obligation; people must have judges, and because the Prophet ﷺ used to judge between people, so one follows the Messenger ﷺ in this and obtains great good.

* * *

(...) ﴿So judge between the people﴾ [Sad 26], to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of speech for Allah, the Exalted, and that it is with letters and sound. This is from His saying ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you﴾ [Sad 26], for this sentence is composed of letters, and it must be with sound because He addresses Dawud with it, and the one addressed must hear, and there is no hearing except by sound. From this is taken the refutation of the Ash'aris and others who say that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, speaks, and that His speech is the inner meaning subsisting in His essence, constantly and perpetually inseparable from Him.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the command belongs to Allah; He appoints whom He wills and removes whom He wills.
* And among them: there is no objection to a speaker saying to a sultan who holds supreme authority on earth that he is "khalifat Allah." This does not mean that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, needs to appoint someone to act on His behalf in managing creation; rather, He appointed him, that is, made him a ruler among people by what Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has legislated.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to judge between people with truth, by His saying ﴿so judge between the people in truth﴾.
From this benefit follows that the post of judgeship is a communal obligation, as the scholars have said, and if only the specific qualified person is found, it becomes an individual obligation for him.
* Among the benefits of this verse: a person should not flee from the task of judgeship when it is entrusted to him, as long as he knows in himself the competence; for if he flees from it, and the second flees, and the third and the fourth, this great post, which is the post of the messengers, would be left idle. But if this matter comes to a person without his asking, let him seek help from Allah, for Allah will help him in it.
* Among the benefits of this verse: it is obligatory to judge between people with truth, whether that concerns the manner of judging or the judgement itself:
As for the manner of judging, he must be just between people in everything; the scholars said: he must be just between the two litigants in his words, his glance, his seating, and their entrance upon him, so he gives precedence to no one over another in these.
As for the judgement, he judges between them according to what the Sharia requires, and what the Sharia requires is undoubtedly justice.
So "bil-haqq" includes both the judgement and the manner of judging. The manner of judging is treating the two litigants so that the treatment between them is on the basis of justice; and as for the judgement, it is to rule by what the Sharia requires, and what the Sharia requires is undoubtedly the truth.
* Among the benefits of this verse: it is not permissible for a judge ruling between people to show favour to anyone out of kinship, friendship, wealth, poverty, status, or otherwise; because of His saying, "with what?" ﴿with truth﴾, and His saying ﴿and do not follow desire﴾ confirms this.
* It is derived from this verse that in an important matter it is appropriate to mention the required affirmation and also to mention the required negation, in order to complete the required affirmation, as if He said: judge with truth, a judgement not entered by desire. This is a clear benefit: when the required qualities of an important matter are mentioned, it is also appropriate to mention the qualities that are not sought, so that the required qualities are free of what is not required, for perfection is affirming perfection and negating its opposite. For example: ﴿so judge between the people in truth﴾ is an affirmation of perfection, and ﴿and do not follow desire﴾ is the negation of its opposite; the opposite is negated only so that it becomes clear that what is required should be free of everything that contradicts it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: following desire is a cause of misguidance from the way of Allah, by His saying ﴿lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾.
But is the misguidance in the act of opposition itself, or is the opposition itself a going astray that becomes a cause of another misguidance?
The answer: the second. Following desire brings a person to misguidance just as it is itself misguidance. So if you follow desire in a certain matter, expect to follow desire in the matter that comes after it; for before a person falls into sin he finds himself shrinking from it and repelled by it. When he does it once, it becomes easy for him; the barrier is broken. When it has become easy the first time, the second time is easy, then the third, until the sin becomes as if it were nothing. For this reason the common people give a useful proverb: "With much touching, feeling diminishes." That is, when a person repeatedly touches a thing, his sensitivity to it decreases.
The summary: following desire is misguidance in itself and a cause of misguidance. The reason is that the self recoils from sin; once it commits it once, it becomes easy for it, then the second is easier, the third easier, the fourth easier, until the sin becomes as if it were not a sin. For this reason He said ﴿lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾. You will find, for example, a judge who could never rule with injustice and oppression, and you find him repelled by it; but when he rules unjustly once, it becomes easy for him, (...) the second time it becomes easy for him, and the third, and the fourth, and so on. For this reason He said: ﴿and do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾.

It may be said that this is not restricted to judging between people; that is, following desire is a cause of misguidance from the path of Allah in everything, even in other than judgment, even in the particular sins within yourself. If you follow your desire in them, know that this is a cause of misguidance from the path of Allah. So you must guard against sins, for they are all evil.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the religion of Allah the Exalted is one and does not branch out. This is shown by His saying ﴿from the path of Allah﴾, where He uses the singular. What supports this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And that this is My path, [being] straight, so follow it. And do not follow [other] ways, for they will separate you from His path﴾ [al-An'am 153]. So the path of Allah is one, but whatever opposes it is scattered: this one's cause is desire, that one's cause is fear of people, this one's cause is such-and-such, and that one's cause is such-and-such, so the ways diverge.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the great praise of the Shari'ah of Allah, shown by attributing it to Allah, because whatever is attributed to Allah, when the attribution is specific, that attribution indicates its nobility.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: those who stray from the path of Allah are threatened with this warning: ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾, meaning strong. From this benefit follows the call to beware of straying from the path of Allah.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: among the causes of straying from the path of Allah is forgetting the Day of Reckoning and being heedless of it, and immersion in this world until it makes a person forget what he was created for and what he is facing. For this reason He said: ﴿because they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾, meaning they were heedless of it. The forgetting intended is not the inadvertence that is excused, but rather the abandonment that is heedlessness and not caring about it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: beware of immersion in this world, which necessitates forgetting the Day of Reckoning. For this reason the Shari'ah forbade every amusement with which a person entertains himself, and said: "Every amusement a person indulges in is vain, except what is excepted," meaning: vain, with no good in it. Then it may be forbidden, or it may be a waste of time without being forbidden. But all amusement turns away from the path of Allah and makes one forget the Day of Reckoning. Therefore you will find that those least faithful in the Day of Reckoning are the most engaged in amusements. It is not possible for the remembrance of the Day of Reckoning to enter his heart except rarely, if he is granted hearing a sermon or something similar. Otherwise he is heedless and frivolous.

From this follows that a person should recognize the enmity of the enemies of Allah, who have drowned us in amusements and their varieties, until they have diverted the Islamic youth from what they should prepare themselves for. They have drowned him in amusements of every kind until a person becomes as if he were created for this idle play, and this play becomes his entire capital and the sum of all his concerns. He speaks only of it, of who has succeeded in it and who has not. Thus youth are lost because of this play they have immersed themselves in, and they have forgotten the Day of Reckoning, except whomever Allah wills.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of causes. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿because they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾, since the "bi" here denotes causation.
From this benefit follows the affirmation of the wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and that He, the Exalted, does nothing except for a cause that necessitates it. Indeed some scholars said that the fact that Allah the Mighty and Majestic created the heavens and the earth in six days, rather than creating them in an instant, is due to the ordering of this creation, one part upon another, so that the causes act by their action and produce things gradually until they are complete. This is not far-fetched, as long as we believe that Allah the Exalted is Wise and that everything occurs through a cause. It is not unlikely that the creation of the heavens and the earth extending over six days is for this very reason: so that creation is ordered, one part upon another, and built, one part upon another, until it accords with wisdom. Otherwise we know with certainty that if Allah willed, He would say "Be," and it would be in an instant. But Allah the Mighty and Majestic is Wise.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of reckoning in the Hereafter, from His saying: ﴿because they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾.
How is this reckoning?
Reckoning varies. The reckoning of the believer is that Allah will be alone with him, without anyone witnessing it, and He will make him acknowledge his sins, saying: "You did such-and-such, and you did such-and-such," until when he sees that he is ruined, Allah will say to him: "I concealed them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.] This is the reckoning of the believer, and it is an easy reckoning: ﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand, he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 7-8]. How easy it is for Allah the Mighty and Majestic to be alone with you, with no one else present, with no interpreter between you, and to say: "I concealed them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today." All praise is due to Allah, what a blessing.

As for the disbeliever, it is not so. The disbeliever is called out before all creation: ﴿These are those who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 18]. They are disgraced and exposed, ﴿who lied against their Lord.﴾ So they are humiliated and exposed by their deeds.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and that between them in vain﴾, meaning in play, ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, meaning the creation mentioned without purpose; ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ from the people of Makkah; ﴿so woe to those who disbelieved from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27], "woe" being a valley).

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and that between them in vain.﴾ ﴿Created﴾ means brought into existence. So creation means bringing into existence, but it is bringing into existence according to a measure, because bringing into existence may occur without measure or arrangement, whereas creation must be according to measure and arrangement.

He says: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth﴾. ﴿The heaven﴾ is intended as a genus, encompassing all the heavens; likewise "the earth."

His saying ﴿and that between them﴾ is conjoined to "the heaven"; that is, We did not create what is between them. What lies between the heaven and the earth consists of great creatures, some of which are known to us and some unknown to us, which we have not known until now. But it is strongly presumed that they are great creatures, because Allah the Exalted made them a counterpart to the creation of the heaven and the earth, and the counterpart of a thing must be close to it or equal to it.

His saying ﴿in vain﴾ is the locus of negation. For this reason we say: it is not permissible to pause at your recitation of ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and that between them﴾, because if you paused there, it would make the meaning vain. You must continue and say ﴿in vain﴾, because that is the locus of negation; that is, We did not create them in vain, meaning for the sake of vanity. This is like His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and that between them in play﴾ [al-Anbiya' 16]. So "vain" here means play with no benefit. Allah did not create the heaven and earth in vain. If He had created them in vain, that would be the utmost folly: that such great creatures with all that is in them would be created for nothing, but rather for play and amusement.

﴿In vain﴾: the author said, "(meaning: in play)." ﴿That﴾: meaning the belief that the creation of the heaven and earth was in vain. ﴿Is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾: meaning this is the assumption of disbelievers who think that the creation of the heavens and the earth was merely for amusement and play, and nothing follows from it. From this is their saying: ﴿It is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah 24].

Also from this is what some people suppose: that the purpose of creating the heavens and the earth is the existence of this creation followed by its annihilation without return. We say: whoever assumes that, meaning that Allah created them in vain and in play, is a disbeliever. For this reason He said: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, those who suppose that the creation of the heaven and earth was in vain.

The author's statement "from the people of Makkah" is open to scrutiny, because it restricts the evidence to some of its instances. The correct view is that it is general, covering the people of Makkah and others, for those who disbelieve only assume evil about Allah. They suppose that His actions are vain and purposeless and not for any wisdom: ﴿the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from the Fire.﴾

The author said: "(woe) is a valley." Woe is a valley, a valley in what place?

* Students: In Hell.

* The Shaykh: In Hell. But this is not correct regarding this verse. Rather the word "woe" is a word of warning, a warning of a severe matter, because He said: "Woe to them from the Fire." He threatens them with it, just as you say, "Woe to you from so-and-so." Does that mean "woe to you from so-and-so" is a valley in so-and-so? No, it is a word of warning of a severe matter. So His saying ﴿so woe﴾ means: a severe warning to those who disbelieved from the Fire; that is, how great is their woe from the Fire of Hell, may Allah protect us.

His saying ﴿to those who disbelieved﴾ is the predicate of "woe," and His saying ﴿from the Fire﴾ is an explanation of "woe"; that is, this great thing is for those who disbelieved, from the Fire.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Or shall We make those who believed and did righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad 28].

﴿Am﴾ here: is it connected or disconnected?

* A student: Disconnected.

* The Shaykh: Disconnected, because no counterpart is mentioned in it. So it means "rather" with the interrogative hamzah: that is, "rather, shall We make those who believed and did righteous deeds...?" This interrogation is intended as negation and denial; that is, it is absolutely impossible that We would make those who believed and did righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth. So "am" here means "rather" and the interrogative hamzah, and the purpose of the interrogation is negation and denial.

Now, is the transition here progressive or nullifying?

* A student: Progressive.

* The Shaykh: Progressive, yes. ﴿Shall We make﴾ means "shall We render"; it takes two objects. The first: ﴿those who believed﴾; the second: ﴿like the corrupters in the earth﴾. That is, it is impossible that We would make those who believed and did righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth.

His saying ﴿those who believed﴾: ﴿believed﴾ means they affirmed what must be affirmed, with acceptance and submission; that is, affirmation that entails acceptance and submission.

His saying ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾: that is, they did righteous deeds. Righteous deeds are those in which two things are combined:
First: sincerity to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.
Second: following the Shari'ah of Allah.

So whoever does an action that conforms to the Shari'ah in its outward form, but does it for show, his deed is not righteous. What has become defective in it?

* A student: Sincerity.

* The Shaykh: Sincerity to Allah. And whoever does an action sincerely for Allah, seeking the face of Allah, but in a way contrary to the Shari'ah, is that correct or not?

* A student: It is not correct.

* The Shaykh: Why?

* The student: Because it does not conform to the Shari'ah of Allah.

* The Shaykh: Because it does not conform to the Shari'ah of Allah. So it is necessary that one be sincere to Allah and conform to the Shari'ah of Allah.

His saying ﴿like the corrupters in the earth﴾: when Allah says "those who believed and did righteous deeds, like the corrupters," the corrupter is the opposite of those who believed and did righteous deeds. So the corrupters in the earth are intended as the disbelievers who do evil deeds.

Every disbeliever is a corrupter in the earth, in contrast to what? ﴿those who believed﴾. Every sinner is a corrupter in the earth, in contrast to ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾. Things are known by their opposites.

So when Allah says "those who believed and did righteous deeds, like the corrupters," we know that the corrupter is the one who opposes those who believed and did righteous deeds; that is, whoever is their opposite. The disbelievers are corrupters in the earth, and the people of sins are corrupters in the earth. For this reason the scholars explained His saying: ﴿And do not corrupt on the earth after its reformation﴾ [al-A'raf 56] as referring to sins; they said: "Do not corrupt on the earth" by sins. This interpretation is correct, and His saying supports it: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of that which they have done, so that they might return﴾ [al-Rum 41].

Now, demolishing houses: is it corruption in the earth?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: No, it is not corruption. Do not affirm or deny flatly. If a person demolishes them unjustly and aggressively, it is corruption in the earth, because it is sinful; it is not permissible for a person to transgress against his brother's house and demolish it. But if he demolishes it to repair it, this is not corruption in the earth.

He says: ﴿Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad 28]. This too is in the sense of "rather" and the interrogative hamzah intended as denial and negation. ﴿Shall We make the righteous﴾: that is, shall We render the righteous like the wicked; that is, it is impossible that We would make the righteous like the wicked. Yes. Who is the righteous? The righteous is one who takes a shield against the punishment of Allah by performing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is the righteous, and this is the most comprehensive of what has been said in defining the righteous.

﴿Like the wicked﴾: who are the wicked? The opposite of the righteous; that is, those who transgressed and departed from obedience to Allah into disobedience to Allah. Here He contrasted the righteous with the wicked, while in Surat al-Mutaffifin He contrasted the wicked with the pious. He said: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 7], then He said: ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the pious is in 'Illiyyin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 18]. From this we derive that piety (taqwa) and righteousness (birr), when mentioned separately, each includes the other; when they are combined, they are distinguished: righteousness is the performance of obedience and piety is avoiding disobedience. So His saying ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2] means: in performing acts of obedience and abandoning acts of disobedience.

* Student: May Allah reward you well, O Shaykh. If someone said: the salaf understood (...) the judge (...) the Messenger ﷺ said: "Two judges are in the Fire and one judge is in Paradise" [narrated by Abu Dawud (3573), al-Tirmidhi (1322), al-Hakim (7188), from the hadith of Buraydah ibn al-Husayb]. How do we, I mean, say...?

* The Shaykh: We say: this is scrupulousness in the wrong place, or perhaps they found among the people someone better than them. And the Messenger said: "Two judges are in the Fire and one judge is in Paradise." Why do you not make the decision and be among the third category? So the scrupulousness that was reported from some of the salaf is in the wrong place, unless they found among the people someone better than them, in which case it is in its proper place.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿A Book which We have revealed to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may be reminded. And We gave to David Solomon. How excellent a servant; indeed he was one who repeatedly turned back [to Allah]. When there were displayed before him in the afternoon the poised, racing (steeds). And he said, "Indeed, I preferred the love of good [i.e., horses] over the remembrance of my Lord until [the sun] was concealed by the veil"﴾ [Sad 29-32].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said... At the end of what we explained and whose benefits we took from His saying: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for their forgetting the Day of Account﴾ [Sad 26]: we have taken its benefits.

**Ibn 'Uthaymin's Commentary on the Qur'an (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim), Surah Sad 38:26–33 (Part 3 of 6)**

God the Exalted says: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and whatever is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve, from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27].

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation that God created the heavens and the earth, and that they came into being after non-existence. Nothing in the universe is eternal and everlasting. The heavens are not eternal; they had a beginning and will perish, and likewise everything will perish except what God, Mighty and Majestic, has excepted and created for permanence, such as the souls, for they were created to endure. Likewise the bliss of Paradise, the youths and the maidens of paradise, and what is similar to them. Whatever the Book and the Sunnah indicate to be enduring and everlasting, it is everlasting and perpetual. But nothing can be eternal in the sense of having no beginning, except God, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Creator of these is God, as He says: ﴿We created the heaven and the earth﴾, and this is like His saying: ﴿Or were they created by nothing, or were they the creators?﴾ [At-Tur 35–36], challenging them to say whether they created the heavens and the earth.
* Among its benefits: God the Exalted created them for a great wisdom with no folly in it, as He says: ﴿in vain﴾. For the negation that they were created in vain necessarily implies that they were created for a great and far-reaching wisdom, and this is so. This is one instance of the creatures of God, Mighty and Majestic, for God the Exalted did not create anything in vain, nor did He legislate anything in vain. Rather, everything He created, legislated and arranged is for a great wisdom, which we sometimes know and sometimes do not know.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of wisdom in God's acts, as He says: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and whatever is between them in vain﴾, for if wisdom were negated it would be possible for the heaven and the earth to have been created in vain.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: no one thinks that God created that in vain except the disbeliever, as He says: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾.
* Among its benefits: whoever thinks that is a disbeliever.

The difference between the two benefits is that in the first benefit, disbelief precedes this assumption, so disbelief is the cause of this assumption. As for the second benefit, this assumption precedes disbelief, so this assumption is the cause of disbelief. Is that clear? Good. So no one assumes that God created the heaven and the earth in vain except the disbelievers. Whoever assumes that God created that in vain becomes a disbeliever.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the threat against the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from the Fire﴾, and that they will enter the Fire and will also abide in it forever, as God has mentioned in three verses of His Book:
In Surah An-Nisa, His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and wrong, Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [An-Nisa 168–169].
And in Surah Al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever﴾ [Al-Ahzab 64–65].
And in Surah Al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [Al-Jinn 23].

After these three verses, no doubt should reach us regarding the everlastingness of the Fire, even if some people say otherwise, because this is the speech of God, it is a report, and a report in the Book of God cannot be false, nor can abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling or text by a later revelation) reach it. So no regard is given to the saying of whoever says that the Fire is not everlasting. Rather, that saying is rejected, false, and refuted by the clear indication of the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of all these noble verses: that among the wisdoms that are attributes of God, Mighty and Majestic, is that He cannot make the believer who does righteous deeds like the one who spreads corruption on the earth, because that would contradict wisdom to a great degree. The believers and the disbelievers are not equal, just as the blind and the seeing are not equal. God the Exalted said: ﴿The example of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in comparison?﴾ [Hud 24].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [Sad 28]: that faith and righteous deeds are a cause for the righteousness of the earth. This is supported by many verses, such as His saying: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth. But they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [Al-A'raf 96].
* Among its benefits also: that sins are a cause of corruption on the earth, because He contrasted this with faith and righteous deeds. This is witnessed by His saying: ﴿Corruption has appeared on the land and the sea because of what the hands of people have earned﴾ [Ar-Rum 41]. So every corruption that occurs on the earth, whether drought, poverty, sickness, spoiled fruits, or other things, is caused by sins: ﴿because of what the hands of people have earned﴾.
* Among its benefits also: that God cannot make the pious like the wicked in their final destination. The pious is in the Gardens of Bliss, and the wicked is in the torment of the Blazing Fire. ﴿Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad 28], meaning that We cannot make the pious like the wicked in their final destination, because the final destination of the pious is Paradise and the final destination of the wicked is the Fire.

* * *

Then we begin the explanation of the author, who said: (It was revealed, meaning His saying ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ to the end, when the disbelievers of Makkah said to the believers: "We will be given in the Hereafter the same as what you are given.") This may be correct or may not be correct. But if it is correct, it is like the saying of the Jews: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [Al-Baqarah 80]. Everyone claims to be upon the truth. Everyone claims that the reward is theirs and that the Hereafter is theirs. But the matter entirely depends on the one whom God testifies to in that regard.

He says: (And ﴿Am﴾ is in the sense of the interrogative hamzah of denial). ﴿Am﴾, meaning His saying: ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on the earth, or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ It has the sense of the interrogative hamzah of denial, but "bal" (rather) is to be understood before it, because this ﴿am﴾ indicates a shift of topic (idrab).

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿A Book which We have revealed to you, blessed﴾ [Sad 29]. The author said: (It is the predicate of an omitted subject; i.e., this is) a Book. The one referred to is the Noble Qur'an. ﴿Kitab﴾ means "written." The Qur'an is described as a Book for several reasons:
First: that it is written in the Preserved Tablet, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [Al-Buruj 21–22].
Second: that it is written in the scrolls held by the angels, as God the Exalted said: ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it, in honored scrolls, exalted and purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and righteous﴾ [Abasa 11–16].
Third: that it is written in the copies of the Qur'an, as is well known.
It may be claimed that it means "obligatory," since (fi'al) can mean (maf'ul), i.e., it is obligatory upon the nation to believe in it and act by it. This would be a fourth meaning of the word "written."

As for His saying: ﴿which We have revealed to you﴾, God revealed it to Muhammad (ﷺ). Its being revealed from God to Muhammad indicates that it is the speech of God. The reason is that this Book is speech, and speech necessarily has a speaker. If God is the One who revealed it, it necessarily follows that He is the One who spoke it, and this establishes that the Qur'an is the speech of God.

In His saying ﴿We have revealed to you﴾, sometimes the expression "We have revealed upon you" (anzalnahu 'alayka) is used. The reconciliation between them is that "ila" (to) indicates the end point, i.e., the ultimate goal of this revelation is Muhammad (ﷺ), and "'ala" (upon) indicates elevation, because this Qur'an came from above, i.e., from God, Mighty and Majestic. Also, "'ala" indicates bearing a thing: "He revealed it upon you" means that you are to bear it and uphold it. So the difference is in two respects:
The first respect: "ila" indicates the end point, i.e., the ultimate goal of the revelation is Muhammad (ﷺ) and does not extend beyond him to anyone else, and there is no prophet after him.
As for "'ala," it indicates elevation, i.e., it was sent down to the Messenger (ﷺ) from above, and it also indicates bearing, because "nazala 'alayhi" (it came down upon him) is as if it were above him, and what is above you must be borne. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will cast upon you a heavy word﴾ [Al-Muzzammil 5], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down to you the Qur'an in gradual revelation. So be patient for the decision of your Lord﴾ [Al-Insan 23–24], which indicates its heaviness, and it is so.

He said: ﴿We have revealed it to you, blessed﴾. ﴿Mubarak﴾ is an adjective of ﴿Kitab﴾, and the clause ﴿anzalnahu﴾ is also an adjective of ﴿Kitab﴾. This is based on the author's parsing that ﴿Kitab﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject.
It is also permissible for ﴿Kitab﴾ to be the subject, with ﴿mubarak﴾ as its predicate, and the clause ﴿anzalnahu﴾ as an adjective of ﴿Kitab﴾. The beginning with an indefinite noun is justified by describing it with the clause ﴿anzalnahu﴾.

﴿Mubarak﴾: blessed in what way?
The blessing of the Qur'an is in several respects:
The first respect: in the reward gained by reciting it. Whoever recites a letter of it has ten good deeds for each letter, and this is a great blessing.
Second: it is blessed in terms of the effect that follows from reciting it, whether general or specific. The specific effect is what a person gains by reciting the Qur'an: expansion of the chest, light of the heart, and tranquility, as is proven for one who recites the Qur'an with reflection. The general effect is that God, through this Qur'an, opened the eastern and western regions of the earth. When the Muslims adhered to this Book, they ruled the entire world, and there is no doubt that this is a blessing from this Qur'an.
Third: the blessing that comes from this Qur'an is the unity of word and the preservation of the original language of the people to whose language it was revealed. It is known that when people speak one language they tend toward unity, and when their languages differ they tend toward division, because when their languages agree they can understand one another and each knows what the other has. When languages differ, this benefit is not achieved. This is among the blessings of the Noble Qur'an.
It has other aspects that we may not be able to encompass in this place, but they are evident to whoever reflects upon them.

His saying ﴿that they may reflect upon its verses﴾ is connected to ﴿anzalnahu﴾, meaning: We revealed it so that they may reflect upon its verses. Reflection (tadabbur) means repeating the words upon the heart, again and again, until the meaning becomes clear. That is, it is an expression for contemplating the meanings of the Qur'an and repeating this contemplation until what it contains of meaning becomes clear.
The original of this word ﴿liyaddabbaru﴾ is (liyatadabbaru), where the taʼ was assimilated into the dal. When we assimilate the taʼ into the dal, we make the taʼ a dal, and it becomes ﴿liyaddabbaru ayatihi﴾.
His saying ﴿ayatihi﴾ is the plural of "ayah," and an ayah is that which ends with a pause (fasilah). Among God's preservation of this Qur'an is that its verses are preserved and numbered, or that some of them are distinguished from others until this day.
The ayat are signs. Signs of what? They are signs that this Qur'an is from God, Mighty and Majestic, through what it contains of wording and meaning. For this reason, a single verse is a miracle for humankind, indeed a miracle for all creation, because it is a verse of God's verses.
So he said: (They look into its meanings and believe). This is one of the wisdoms of revealing the Qur'an: that a person reflects upon the verses.
The second, he said: (﴿And that people of understanding may be reminded﴾, i.e., may take heed, ﴿ulu al-albab﴾, the people of intellect). This is the second benefit. But the reminding has been placed after the reflection, because a person cannot take heed of a thing unless he knows the meaning it contains. So he reflects first, then he is reminded second.

First: that a person recites the Qur'an.
The second stage: that he reflects upon it in order to understand its meanings.
The third stage: that he takes heed from it.
Taking heed from the Qur'an is being affected by it, being affected in the heart and being affected in the limbs. Being affected in the heart: the servant's sincerity to God, his turning to Him, his reliance upon Him, and similar acts of the heart. Being affected in the limbs: performing obedience to God with the outward limbs, such as purification, prayer, almsgiving, fasting, and other things.
So the benefit of revealing this blessed Qur'an is centered on two things: reflection and taking heed.

﴿And that people of understanding may be reminded﴾: ﴿Ulu﴾ means "possessors of," and it is attached to the sound masculine plural, because it has no singular from its own form, but it has a singular from its meaning. If we say its meaning is "possessors," then its singular in meaning is "possessor" (sahib). So ﴿ulu﴾ is the plural of "sahib" in meaning. For this reason we say it is attached to the sound masculine plural, because it has no singular. The sound masculine plural is that in which the form of the singular is preserved. If there is no singular, it is not a plural in the true sense, so it is attached to that category.
His saying ﴿ulu al-albab﴾ means the possessors of intellect, because the person of intellect is the one who takes heed. As for one without intellect, he does not benefit from that.

Good. The intellect here is the intellect of right guidance, not the intellect of discernment (idrak). The intellect is of two kinds: the intellect of discernment, and the intellect of right guidance. The intellect of discernment is that upon which legal responsibility depends. The intellect of right guidance is that which is shown in good conduct. For example, the disbelievers have intellects, but intellects of what?
* The students: Discernment.
* The Shaykh: Intellects of discernment, because this is what legal responsibility depends upon. But they do not have intellects of right guidance, meaning they do not have intellects of rectitude, because they did not conduct themselves well. Whoever does not conduct himself well may rightly be described as lacking intellect. God the Exalted said: ﴿Do you order the people to righteousness and forget yourselves while you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 44]. Among ourselves, if we find a person who conducts himself badly, we say: "This person has no sense." Even if he has discernment, he lacks good conduct. The intellect that is praised is the intellect of right guidance. As for the intellect of discernment, everyone has it, even disbelievers and wicked people.

His saying ﴿al-albab﴾: ﴿albab﴾ is the plural of ﴿lubb﴾, and the ﴿lubb﴾ of everything is its purpose. This is the core of a thing, its purpose. For example, the core of a seed is what is inside it, the kernel within it. What is above it is husk. The yolk inside an egg is its core, and what is above it is shell.

He said: ﴿And We gave to David, Solomon﴾ [Sad 30]. ﴿Wahabna﴾ means "We gave." God described this as a gift (hibah) because it is pure bounty from Him, not needing anything from us. God the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He grants to whom He wills females and grants to whom He wills males, or He pairs them, males and females﴾ [Ash-Shura 49–50].
So ﴿We gave to David﴾ means: We gave him as a gift, out of Our bounty and generosity, without any payment.
His saying ﴿Sulayman﴾ is not given tanwin (nunation). Why? It is diptote (mamnu' min as-sarf, not declined in the full way) because of being a proper name and the addition of the alif and nun.
* A student: Foreignness ('ujmah).
* The Shaykh: No, Sulayman is not foreign; its peace (salamah) exists in the Arabic language. Dawud is diptote because of being a proper name and foreignness. Is that right?
The author said: (﴿Sulayman﴾ his son). From where did the author know that he was his son? Is it not possible that what is meant by ﴿We gave to David Solomon﴾ is his servant?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verses 26–33 (part 4 of 6):**

The answer is: no. Allah, glorified and exalted, called children a gift (*hibah*) in His saying: ﴿He creates what He wills. He bestows females on whom He wills and bestows males on whom He wills, or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ [ash-Shura 49–50]. That is, He classifies them.

He said: (﴿An excellent servant﴾ [Sad 30], that is, Sulayman). The phrase is an expression of praise and commendation, meaning that it is used for praise and commendation. Its opposite is (*bi'sa*, "wretched"), which is an expression of blame.

As for His saying ﴿An excellent servant﴾: it is well known that (*ni'ma*, "excellent") and (*bi'sa*, "wretched") require a subject (*fa'il*) and a specified object (*mukhassas*), which is praised with *ni'ma* and blamed with *bi'sa*. Here ﴿the servant﴾ exists and is the subject, since *ni'ma* is a past-tense verb and *al-'abd* is its subject. But where is the specified object? It is either an implicit pronoun, though we do not say it is "implicit" either, since the subject is an apparent noun, ﴿the servant﴾. So we say it is omitted, and its estimated form is (*huwa*, "he"), or its estimated form is (Sulayman). In other words, we may estimate it as either an apparent noun or a pronoun.

﴿An excellent servant; indeed he is ever turning back (to Allah)﴾. ﴿Indeed he﴾ is the reason for this praise from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon Sulayman. ﴿Indeed he﴾, that is Sulayman, ﴿is ever turning back﴾, that is, returning frequently to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This may be by repeating the voice in remembrance, or by returning to obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The apparent meaning is that the verse includes both meanings: he is one who returns to the obedience of Allah, and one who returns by glorification (*tasbih*), that is, he repeats the voice in it and echoes it.

The author says here: (one who repeatedly glorifies and remembers Allah at all times). However, the correct view is that it is more general than what the author said: he returns repeatedly in glorification and remembrance, and likewise he returns to Allah in repentance and obedience.

He said: ﴿When there were displayed before him at the close of day﴾ [Sad 31]. Who is the one displaying? It is left unspecified for emphasis, because the verb here is in the passive voice, with its doer unnamed, for emphasis. It is as if it suggests that he had many soldiers who would display before him whatever they displayed.

As for His saying ﴿at the close of day﴾: (it is what follows the decline of the sun) until sunset. The *ba'* in ﴿bil-'ashiyy﴾ here is for time, meaning (*fi*, "in"). However, the usual case is that when *ba'* takes the place of *fi*, it generally covers the whole period, as if the whole evening became filled with this display, because of the large number of horses displayed before him. ﴿At the close of day, the poised, swift-footed (horses)﴾ [Sad 31]. What raised them? 

* Student: The deputy subject (*na'ib fa'il*).
* Shaykh: The deputy subject where?
* Students: ﴿was displayed﴾.
* Shaykh: The deputy subject is ﴿was displayed﴾, yes.

If someone says: ﴿al-Safinat﴾ is plural, and the verb is masculine ﴿was displayed﴾, while this is the plural of a feminine noun with a real female referent (*dhat hirr*), that is, a true feminine plural. Ibn Malik says about the *ta'* (feminine marker):

*It is only obligatory with a verb whose subject is an attached pronoun, or one that signifies a female of the kind (dhat hirr).*

What is your view? We say: the feminine marker was not required because a separator exists, which is His saying ﴿upon him﴾.

﴿al-Safinat﴾: the author said: (the horses, the plural of *safinah*, which is the one standing on three legs, with the other raised on the edge of the hoof, from *safan*, *yasfin*, *sufunan*).

﴿al-Safinat﴾ are the horses, which stand on three legs, raising the fourth slightly so that the tip of its hoof is on the ground. This shows their strength, and it is also more beautiful in appearance. If you imagine horses lined up standing in this manner, they have a majesty, and you feel something of greatness from this sight that you witness.

* * *

* Student: ﴿When there were displayed before him at the close of day the poised, swift-footed horses. He said, "Indeed I have loved the love of good (wealth) out of remembrance of my Lord" until they (the horses) disappeared behind the veil. "Bring them back to me." Then he began to pass his hand over their legs and necks﴾ [Sad 31–33]. ﴿And We had certainly tried Sulayman and placed upon his throne a body; then he returned (in repentance). He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me; indeed You are the Bestower." So We subjected to him the wind, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed, and (the) devils, every builder and diver, and others bound together in shackles. This is Our gift, so grant (favor) or withhold without account. And indeed for him is nearness to Us and a good return﴾ [Sad 31–40].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds the same as corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous the same as the wicked?﴾ [Sad 28]. We have completed its benefits.
* Student: No.
