* Among the benefits of this verse: that the whole noble Quran consists of verses indicating the One who spoke it, the Exalted. For this reason He said: ﴿that they may ponder its verses﴾, and did not say "a verse from it" or "ten verses." All the verses.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: that among the greatest purposes for which the Quran was sent down is remembrance, by His saying: ﴿and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the noble Quran was sent down as an admonition for people, as Allah, the Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ [Yunus 57]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners and when you judge between people to judge with justice. Excellent is that which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾ [an-Nisa' 58]. So the Quran was sent down to have an effect. It was not sent down merely so that a person may seek blessing by reciting it, or attain reward by reciting it. That is easy, but it must have an effect through remembrance and admonition.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that no one is reminded by the Quran except people of intellect, by His saying: ﴿and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾.
* Among its benefits: that whoever is reminded by the Quran is a person of intellect, and whoever is not reminded has no intellect. Is that right? The reason is that Allah made remembrance for those who are characterized by what? By intellects.
* Among its benefits: that the essence (*lubb*) of a person and his spirit is intellect, the intellect of right guidance, because Allah named these intellects *albab*, the plural of *lubb*, like *asbab*, the plural of *sabab*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verses 26–33 (part 5 of 6):

Then Allah, exalted is He, said concerning the story of Solomon son of David: ﴿And We bestowed upon David, Solomon, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah).﴾ He said: ﴿When there were displayed before him at evening the poised, swift horses.﴾ Up to here is the completion of his tafsir (interpretation). He said: (The plural of jawad, which means "swift." The meaning is that when they were halted, they stood still, and when they ran, they outran.) That is, these horses that were displayed before him are described by these two attributes: they are of the ṣawāfin (those who stand poised on three legs), and they are of the jiyād (the noble, swift breed). When they stand, they stand in the best posture, which is ṣufūn, and when they walk, they walk in the most perfect manner, which is judūd. They are excellent in speed and in bearing hardship, even when the journey is long. This is the utmost of what beauty in horses can be: that their posture when standing pleases the soul, and that their action and performance when moving is beneficial because they are of the noble breed.

As for the author's statement: (They were a thousand horses displayed before him after he had prayed the noon prayer, because he intended to fight jihad on them against an enemy. When the display reached nine hundred of them, the sun set, and he had not prayed the afternoon prayer, so he was distressed.)

Estimating these horses at one thousand requires evidence from an infallible source traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and there is no authentic evidence from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they were a thousand, or two thousand, or fewer or more. Therefore our responsibility is to stop where the Qur'an stopped. We should not limit them to a thousand, nor to more, nor to less. Rather, these horses were displayed to him at the end of the day, ﴿the poised, swift horses.﴾ When they were displayed to him, he forgot to pray because of the strength of his attachment in his heart to these horses, which he had prepared for jihad in the cause of Allah, or had prepared for adornment and enjoyment. This is because Solomon, peace be upon him, was among the prophet-kings, as Allah said: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me.﴾ [Sad 35] Kings are accustomed to being pleased and delighted by looking at horses. Whether he had prepared them for jihad, if he had been commanded to fight, or had prepared them to enjoy as a king, the matter is the same.

He says: ﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have loved the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord."﴾ [Sad 32] He said: (﴿I have loved﴾ means "I desired.") ﴿the love of good﴾ means its love, the love of good. "Good" is applied generally to wealth, as in Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful. And indeed, he is, to that, a witness. And indeed, he is, in love of good, intense.﴾ [al-'Adiyat 6–8], meaning, in love of wealth. The evidence that "good" means wealth is Allah's saying: ﴿It is prescribed for you that when death approaches one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, a bequest...﴾ [al-Baqarah 180]. So His saying ﴿the love of good﴾ means the love of wealth.

The author's explanation of this "good" as horses is more specific than the wording's general meaning. It has already passed with us that it is not permissible to interpret a more general term by a more specific meaning, because this is a deficiency in tafsir. However, the author may be excused, since the context is about horses, and so he restricted this general term to the specific meaning by the indication of the context. Here, however, there is a difficulty: His saying ﴿I have loved the love of good﴾. Does love love? That is, if someone says: why is the verse not "Indeed, I have loved good," as Allah said: ﴿And indeed, he is, in love of good, intense﴾?

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, interpreted the love that came in verbal form as intention, saying: (﴿I have loved﴾ means "I intended the love of good"). But although he, may Allah have mercy on him, escaped the contradiction in the wording, he did not escape the corruption of the meaning. Because if he says, "I intended the love of good," then what is intended may or may not be attained, whereas his love is certainly present. However, the answer to this is that we say: the first ﴿I have loved﴾ is in its own sense, and the second ﴿I have loved﴾ is also in its own sense, as emphasis (ta'kid), as if he loved the love of good, not merely good. Whoever loves the love of a thing necessarily loves the thing. It is like if you say: "I love to love so-and-so," or "I love to love reading such-and-such a book." This is emphasis, as if he repeated the love twice. By this we escape the objection that is raised against the author's explanation, may Allah have mercy on him.

As for His saying ﴿over the remembrance of my Lord﴾, the author said: (That is, the afternoon prayer). This too is an explanation of the general by what is more specific, which is a deficiency in tafsir, because remembrance (dhikr) is more general than prayer. Every prayer is a remembrance, but not every remembrance is a prayer. Is this correct? Every prayer is remembrance, but not every remembrance is prayer. Is this correct? Yes indeed. So if we explain remembrance as prayer, then we have explained the more general by the more specific, and this is a deficiency. Perhaps the author may be excused by the context, but this excuse is not accepted, because who says that Solomon intended by the remembrance of his Lord the afternoon prayer? He may have meant the remembrance of Allah in the evening, since the evening has specific adhkar (remembrances), and the afternoon prayer would be included in this remembrance. This is the correct view: the correct view is that what is meant by the remembrance in His saying ﴿over the remembrance of my Lord﴾ is the general remembrance, which includes the afternoon prayer.

His saying ﴿over the remembrance of my Lord﴾ includes remembrance of the heart, which is mental remembrance, includes speech, which is remembrance of the tongue, and includes action, which is the actions of the limbs, if we include the afternoon prayer in this, because the prayer comprises all three kinds of remembrance. The prayer includes remembrance of the heart, remembrance of the tongue, and remembrance of the limbs.

His saying ﴿over the remembrance of my Lord﴾, in attributing lordship (rububiyyah) to Allah, is a supplication (isti'tf) by Solomon to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since he acknowledged Him as Lord, which requires that he be occupied with remembering Him, glorified and exalted is He.

His saying ﴿Indeed, I have loved the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord﴾: some scholars found it problematic that the verb is transitive with ʿan (عن), "I loved it over the remembrance of my Lord." How? It was said: ʿan here means min (مِنْ), i.e., in exchange for, meaning in place of the remembrance of my Lord. Some scholars said: ﴿I have loved﴾ is implicitly containing the meaning of "I preferred," so that the sense is "I preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord." It has already passed with us that when a complement is brought which does not apparently suit the verb, the grammarians have two views on that:

The first view: the verb is implicitly given a meaning that suits the complement (tadmin, implicit inclusion of the meaning of one verb in another).

The second: the preposition that does not suit the complement is given the meaning of a preposition that suits it.

We have mentioned that the better course is to make the figurative usage in the verb.

His saying ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾: ﴿until they were hidden﴾. The author said: (That is, the sun, ﴿behind the veil﴾, meaning it concealed itself by that which hides it from the eyes.) ﴿they were hidden behind the veil﴾, ﴿they were hidden﴾.

If someone says: the pronoun is concealed, and the sun has not been mentioned before, so why is it not said: ﴿until they were hidden﴾ (meaning the horses) behind the veil? That is, they went far away until they were out of sight, as if he was occupied with looking at them while they chased and raced each other, until they reached a distance where they were out of his sight?

We say: there is no doubt that this meaning is possible in the verse. His saying ﴿Indeed, I have loved the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord until they were hidden﴾, i.e., these horses, so they went away and were concealed. However, there are narrations that support what the author went to, that what was hidden was the sun, ﴿behind the veil﴾, meaning by that which hides it from the eyes. So what is this veil? The veil is the earth. The veil that hides the sun when it sets is the earth, as Allah said about Dhul-Qarnayn: ﴿until, when he reached the setting place of the sun, he found it setting in a murky spring﴾ [al-Kahf 86], meaning in the sea. Thus what conceals it when it sets is the earth. This is because the earth is spherical in shape. When the sun revolves around it and reaches the curved side, it must set. In this way it sets for each people, little by little, until it rises upon those from whom it had set first.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿"Return them to me."﴾ The pronoun in ﴿return them﴾ refers to the horses that were displayed to him. He commanded that they be returned to him and brought back to him a second time, so that he could strike them out of anger for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and as a punishment to his own self, which had become attached to these horses and had turned away by them from the remembrance of Allah.

He said: (﴿Return them to me﴾, that is, the displayed horses, so they returned them. ﴿So he began passing his hand﴾ with the sword ﴿over the legs﴾, the plural of sāq, ﴿and the necks﴾.) The plural of ʿunuq (neck). He said: ﴿Return them to me,﴾ so they returned them to him.

﴿So he began﴾: ṭafiqa is a past verb of beginning (af'al al-shurū'), and its predicate is a verb. Accordingly, His saying ﴿passing his hand﴾ (mashan) is not its predicate. Rather it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) for the omitted verb which is the predicate, and the estimate is: ﴿so he began passing his hand, passing.﴾

His saying ﴿passing his hand over the legs﴾ means that he struck them along with their legs, the plural of sāq, and the necks along with the neck. This is because the soul is attached to horses in terms of their walking, their poised standing, and in terms of the neck, what is upon it of hair, and the beauty of the neck. For this reason, peace be upon him, he struck the places of beauty in horses, which are their legs and their necks, and Allah knows best.

Student: (...) the general remembrance.

Shaykh: More general than prayer.

Student: So is it the afternoon prayer, or (...)?

Shaykh: No, because the evening remembrances continue to after sunset.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: General. The remembrance is general, it includes prayer and other things.

Student: (...) the remembrances that are not restricted to the evening.

Shaykh: Yes, if they are not restricted to the evening, then there is no difference whether one mentions them after sunset or before it.

Student: I am saying: I mean that sunset (...) the afternoon prayer.

Shaykh: And are there no remembrances after the afternoon?

Student: No, there are remembrances.

Shaykh: Then why do we not make it general, including prayer?

Student: (...) sunset?

Shaykh: Yes, because the evening remembrances take place after the afternoon, so he remembers Allah after the afternoon, and he was occupied from that.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: How?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, it is written with an alif as long as it is not joined to a pronoun. If it is joined to a pronoun, there is no need for the alif.

Student: What need, when the waw is in the position of this...

Shaykh: That is, if he said ruddū alone, he would not say hā.

Student: In ruddū, the pronoun refers to whom?

Shaykh: No, my point is: you are saying, why was no alif written after the waw? Is that what you mean or not? I am saying: the alif is not written after the waw with a pronoun. If you say ruddūhu, you do not write an alif. Ruddūhā, you do not write an alif. But ruddū Zaydan, you write an alif.

Student: And in ruddū, the pronoun refers to whom?

Shaykh: The waw refers to the addressee.

Student: To the addressee; it is for the plural.

Shaykh: Yes, and it is for the plural, addressing a group. And hā refers to the horses; that is, return the horses to me.

Student: Yes, and the waw is for the absent party.

Shaykh: No, it is for the addressee. An imperative directed to a group is not for the absent. If it were a past verb, it would be for the absent, but this is an imperative verb, and the waw attached to an imperative verb is for the addressee.

Student: I thought it was past.

Shaykh: No, if it were past he would say ruddūhā. The past is said ruddūhā.

Student: I said it could be passive.

Shaykh: No, passive would be with the object: ruddūhā.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: In any case, it is an imperative verb; he orders them to return them to him.

Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Someone asked a mufti, saying: I was a disobedient person, and I have cassettes of songs and so on. What should I do with them? Should I record religious lectures on them, or what should I do with them, or burn them? He said to him: burn them, and he cited this verse as evidence, saying: Solomon, peace be upon him, slaughtered the horses.

Shaykh: This question is ahead of its time, because it will be among the benefits, God willing.

Student: Why was it better to make the verb implicitly carry a meaning rather than the imperative verb?

Shaykh: Yes indeed, because when you make the verb implicitly carry a meaning, you gain a new meaning in addition to the original meaning of the verb. For example, if we say, regarding His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan 6], that the intended meaning is "they are quenched by it," this includes two meanings: drinking and quenching. If you say that the bāʾ in ﴿from which they drink﴾ means min (مِنْ), "they drink from it," we gain only one meaning, which is drinking.

Student: If we make the verb implicitly carry a meaning, O Shaykh, it is as if we have brought something additional.

Shaykh: No, it is not additional, because when we say yarwā (is quenched), we have brought the original meaning of "drink," since there is no quenching except after drinking. What made us bring the additional meaning, which is quenching, is that, true, quenching is additional to mere drinking. What made us bring it is that the bāʾ does not take yashrabu (drink) as its complement.

Student: Shaykh, may Allah pardon you, (...) some scholars (...)?

Shaykh: Yes, this is the amulet (tamimah). If we permit amulets with the Qur'an, some people came and included shirkī (polytheistic) things in them. What do you say? We say: the ruling revolves around its cause. If they write polytheistic things, it becomes forbidden because of shirk. But if they write something of the Qur'an, there is no shirk in it. That is, the one who writes the amulet must be trustworthy.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: He brought what?

Student: I am saying: they are common in some places in the Hijaz (...), the northern and southern land.

Shaykh: What is common?

Student: These hangings that contain shirk.

Shaykh: No, that is prohibited, this.

* * *

Student: ﴿And We had certainly tried Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he returned (in repentance). He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom not appropriate for anyone after me; indeed, You are the Bestower." So We subjected to him the wind, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed. And the devils, every builder and diver, and others bound together in chains. This is Our gift, so grant or withhold without account. And indeed, he has with Us closeness and a good return.﴾ [Sad 34–40]

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We bestowed upon David, Solomon, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah). When there were displayed before him at evening the poised, swift horses.﴾ [Sad 30–31], and so on to the end. Where is the complement of ﴿idh﴾ (when) in His saying: ﴿when there were displayed﴾?

Student: Yes, ﴿when there were displayed﴾.

Shaykh: That is, idh is a temporal adverb and needs a complement.

Student: It is omitted; its estimate is: "remember when there were displayed."

Shaykh: "Remember when there were displayed." His saying: ﴿the poised﴾, what are ﴿the poised﴾ (...)?

I loved the love of good intensely.

What is meant by "good" here?

Student: The author explained it as horses, and this is a deficiency.

Shaykh: What led him to explain it as horses?

Student: It is excused by the context, the context of the verse.

Shaykh: Where He said: ﴿the poised, swift horses﴾. And the second view, or the second possibility?

Student: That it is general, including horses and other wealth and so on, since "good" is applied to wealth.

Shaykh: What is the proof or evidence that "good" means wealth?

Student: ﴿And indeed, he is, in love of good, intense.﴾

Shaykh: ﴿And indeed, he is, in love of good, intense﴾ [al-'Adiyat 8]. And what is meant by "good" here?

Student: Wealth.

Shaykh: Wealth. What is the evidence that it means wealth? ﴿And you love wealth with immense love﴾ [al-Fajr 20].

His saying: ﴿over the remembrance of my Lord﴾. What is meant by the remembrance of his Lord?

Student: According to the author's view, he said it is the afternoon prayer, but the remembrance includes more than prayer, and includes the evening remembrances as well as prayer.

Shaykh: Well done. His saying: ﴿I have loved the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord﴾. What is the position of ʿan (over/from) here?

Student: In meaning, you mean?

Shaykh: Yes, what is the meaning of "I loved it over the remembrance of my Lord"?

Student: That is: "apart from the remembrance of my Lord."

Shaykh: That means what?

Student: That is: I loved the love of good apart from the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted.

Shaykh: What does it mean according to this?

Student: In the sense of "other than."

Shaykh: ʿan in the sense of "other than"?

Student: In the sense of "other than Allah, exalted is He"; that is, other than the remembrance of Allah.

Another student: "In exchange for his worship."

Shaykh: That is, what?

Student: Instead of mentioning his Lord.
Shaykh: "Instead of mentioning his Lord" is one interpretation. Is there another?
Student: Or that it is implied (muḍammana).
Shaykh: Implied; that is, he preferred love of good over remembering Him.

Regarding His words ﴿حَتَّى تَوَارَتْ بِالْحِجَابِ﴾ (until it was hidden behind the veil): to what does the pronoun refer?
Student: There are two opinions. The first is that the pronoun refers to the horses: he saw them moving away from him, far off.
Shaykh: He kept watching them going and coming.
Student: The second opinion is that it was hidden by the veil from the sun.
Shaykh: The sun. And what is meant by "the veil" on this view?
Student: The veil means the earth.
Shaykh: The earth, correct? He says: ﴿فَطَفِقَ مَسْحًا﴾ (so he began to strike). Is "ṭafiqa" one of the verbs of beginning?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: And where is its predicate?
Student: (...).
Shaykh: Its predicate is omitted: "so he began to strike, striking." ﴿بِالسُّوقِ﴾ (with the shanks): what does it mean?
Student: It is the plural of (sāq, shank).
Shaykh: The plural of "sāq." That is, he strikes their shanks until he hamstrings them. And "al-a'nāq" (the necks)?
Student: It is the plural of (‘unuq, neck), and he strokes their necks.
Shaykh: With his hand? He strokes with his hand like this. So the meaning of your words is that he strokes their shanks with his hand, and likewise strokes their necks.
Student: That is, striking with the sword.
Shaykh: Even on the shanks?
Student: Yes.
Shaykh: And the necks are for slaughter. Let us take the benefits.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿وَوَهَبْنَا لِدَاوُودَ سُلَيْمَانَ نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ﴾ (And We gave to David, Solomon; an excellent servant).
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: children are a gift from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the servant, and it follows from this that the servant must thank Allah, exalted is He, for this blessing.
- Among the benefits of this noble verse: the praise of Solomon in His words ﴿نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ﴾ (an excellent servant). Here "servanthood" is the special servanthood.
- Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of causes and means, by His words ﴿إِنَّهُ أَوَّابٌ﴾ (indeed, he was one who often turned back), for this is the cause of his being praised.
- Among its benefits: the virtue of returning to Allah and turning back to Him with the heart and with action, because Allah praised Solomon for this.
- Among the benefits of the noble verse in His words ﴿إِذْ عُرِضَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ (when there were displayed before him) to its end: the demonstration of the greatness of Solomon's kingdom, since people would present these horses to him for enjoyment, and to view and inspect them. The evidence for this is that He said ﴿إِذْ عُرِضَ عَلَيْهِ﴾, which indicates that there were people who would present these horses to him.
- Among the benefits of this verse: this custom, namely the displaying of horses and enjoying their running at the end of the day, is an ancient custom that people still practise to this day. You hardly find anyone holding a horse race at the beginning of the day; it takes place at the end of the day, and this is one of the ancient customs of people that continues to this day.
- Among the benefits of this verse: it is appropriate to select good, beautiful horses that delight the soul in seeing them and in their running, by His words ﴿الصَّافِنَاتُ الْجِيَادُ﴾ (the swift, well-bred horses standing on three legs).
- Among its benefits: it is appropriate to keep horses, since this was the practice of the messengers, peace be upon them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Good is tied to the foreheads of horses until the Day of Resurrection" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2850) and Muslim (1873/98), from the hadith of ‘Urwah ibn al-Ja‘d]. So whenever horses are instruments of war, the good is in their foreheads until the Day of Resurrection.
- Among the benefits of this verse: the mention of an example of describing Solomon as "awwāb" (one who often turns back), where He said ﴿إِنِّي أَحْبَبْتُ حُبَّ الْخَيْرِ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّي﴾ (Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord) to its end.
- Among its benefits: wealth is good, and it is so, because when a person is granted wealth he is able to enjoy fully what pertains to wealth, unlike when wealth is restricted for him, for then he cannot enjoy it.
- Among the benefits of the noble verse: turning away from the remembrance of Allah for the sake of worldly matters is blameworthy, because Solomon reproached himself for loving good and giving it precedence over the remembrance of Allah.
- Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation that the sun moves continuously and does not set; that is, it is hidden from sight in the sky, by His words ﴿حَتَّى تَوَارَتْ بِالْحِجَابِ﴾.
- Among its benefits: the affirmation that the sun is what revolves around the earth in its rising and setting, because He attributed the action to it, saying ﴿حَتَّى تَوَارَتْ﴾. If the matter were as the geographers of today say, that the earth is what revolves and the sun is hidden because of its rotation, He would have said "until you (fem.) were hidden behind the veil," or "until it was hidden," meaning [the earth] — because if you are the one who revolves while your counterpart is stationary, which one is hidden? The stationary or the revolving one? The revolving one. So when Allah affirmed that the hiding belongs to the sun, this indicates that it is the one that revolves. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَتَرَى الشَّمْسَ إِذَا طَلَعَتْ تَزَاوَرُ عَنْ كَهْفِهِمْ ذَاتَ الْيَمِينِ وَإِذَا غَرَبَتْ تَقْرِضُهُمْ ذَاتَ الشِّمَالِ﴾ [al-Kahf 17], where these are four verbs, all attributed to the sun.

In the authentic collection, it is related from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was with the Prophet (ﷺ) when the sun set, and he said to him: "Do you know where it goes?" I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Indeed, it prostrates beneath the Throne and seeks permission; permission is granted to it, and it is said to it: 'Return from where you came,' so it rises from its place of setting" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3199) and Muslim (159/250), from the hadith of Abu Dharr].

This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and it is obligatory upon the believer to follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, for this is the method in all matters. As you know, regarding the Names and Attributes of Allah we follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and as you know, regarding the legal rulings we follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Therefore, in cosmic matters too we follow the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, for the apparent meaning of the Qur'an comes from the All-Knowing Creator, so He is more knowing of His creation than they are. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿مَا أَشْهَدْتُهُمْ خَلْقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَلَا خَلْقَ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation) [al-Kahf 51]. If this comes from the most knowing, it is obligatory upon us to affirm it.

It is therefore obligatory for us to let the apparent meanings of the Book and the Sunnah stand as they are, until there is a clear, sensory proof showing that the wording is not to be taken in its apparent sense. Even if it were made clear, as clear as the sun, that the earth is what revolves, we would say: these verbs whose apparent meaning is that the sun revolves were expressed in terms of what we observe, so the setting is in terms of our observation, for what is observed by the senses, according to the apparent view of common people, is that the earth is stationary and the sun revolves around it. So the expression follows what people apparently observe. But when do we need to interpret verses? When something has been established by a certain sensory proof with no difficulty, because the apparent meaning is only probable in its indication, and this indication cannot be displaced except by a definitive proof stronger than it.

- Among the benefits of this verse: the earth is spherical. For when it was established that the sun is hidden by the veil, this indicates that the earth is what casts the veil over it, and as we observe, the sun descends from the high point of the sky, then descends little by little until it is at the lowest point, in the earth. This indicates that the earth is spherical. This is also a definite matter with no difficulty; it is apparent from the Qur'an and apparent also from reality. In the Qur'an Allah says: ﴿إِذَا السَّمَاءُ انْشَقَّتْ (١) وَأَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّهَا وَحُقَّتْ (٢) وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ (٣) وَأَلْقَتْ مَا فِيهَا وَتَخَلَّتْ (٤) وَأَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّهَا وَحُقَّتْ﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 1–5]. When is this? It will be on the Day of Resurrection, since the sky has not yet split.
So His words ﴿وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ﴾ (when the earth is stretched out) indicate that before this it was not stretched out but spherical. This does not contradict His words, exalted is He: ﴿أَفَلَا يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَى الْإِبِلِ كَيْفَ خُلِقَتْ (١٧) وَإِلَى السَّمَاءِ كَيْفَ رُفِعَتْ (١٨) وَإِلَى الْجِبَالِ كَيْفَ نُصِبَتْ (١٩) وَإِلَى الْأَرْضِ كَيْفَ سُطِحَتْ﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 17–20], which does not contradict it, because its being flat is in terms of what is observed: when you stand on the earth now, you find it level as far as the eye can see.

- Among the benefits of these verses, in His words ﴿رُدُّوهَا عَلَيَّ فَطَفِقَ﴾ (Bring them back to me," and he began) to its end: the permissibility of discretionary punishment (ta‘zir) by destroying property. Jurists differ on this question: may a person be disciplined by destroying his property, or not? Some scholars said it is not permissible, because destroying property is corruption of it, and we can discipline him by taking his property without destroying it, taking it and spending it in another beneficial way. Others said that it is permissible, and they cited as evidence that the thief of booty who conceals what he has taken has his baggage burned, which is destruction of it, even though the army may be in need of his property; yet we destroy it. This view is the stronger one: it is permissible to discipline by destroying property. First, because the Sunnah indicates this.
Second, because its destruction is more painful and has a greater effect; for if it were taken and spent on public interests, the punishment would be hidden. Moreover, it might open a door for oppressive rulers: if they wanted money, they would bring a case against some person and then say: "We discipline him by taking his property," and then they would take his property, claiming it would go to the public treasury, while it would actually go into the pockets of those oppressors. So when we say it is burned and destroyed before the people, that danger is removed. Accordingly, if we found with a person an instrument of amusement that could be used for something other than amusement, and we disciplined him by breaking it, that would be lawful, and we would not say: convert it into something other than an instrument of amusement, because destroying it in front of people is more painful and severe than destroying it by spending it on some purpose.
- Among the benefits of this verse: there is no harm if a person disciplines himself by destroying his own property, following the action of Solomon. So if we supposed that a person was occupied with something that distracted him from the remembrance of Allah, and he wanted to break it, that would be lawful and permissible, because this leads to his not returning to being distracted from the remembrance of Allah by some property.
- Among the benefits of this verse: the strength of Solomon's authority in his commands and prohibitions, by His words ﴿رُدُّوهَا عَلَيَّ﴾ (Bring them back to me). This indicates that he had many soldiers who carried out his command, for had he said "bring it back" (singular), the servant would have been one person. But since he said ﴿رُدُّوهَا﴾ (bring them back), this indicates that he had many servants serving him.
- Among its benefits: Solomon's swiftness and promptness in carrying out his intention to destroy this property, by His words ﴿فَطَفِقَ مَسْحًا بِالسُّوقِ وَالْأَعْنَاقِ﴾ (so he began to strike the shanks and necks).

Someone may say: Is there not in this a torment of an animal, if he began to strike its shanks with the sword?
It is answered: Yes, but the apparent meaning is that he first hamstrings it, then cuts its neck. This is not objectionable, because the pain does not last. He singled out the shanks for striking because they were swift horses; when a swift horse lifts its hoof somewhat, its shanks have a beautiful appearance, so it was the object of desire, and that is why he began to strike these shanks. As for the necks, the apparent purpose is complete destruction.

Student: Solomon knew the language of birds, and similarly matters (...). Did he take the horses, that is, give their meat in charity... (...)?
Shaykh: Yes, this is a good question. He asks: did he eat their meat, or give it in charity, or what did he do? What do you say?
Student: The author says: he gave it in charity.
Shaykh: He says: he gave it in charity. Read (...).
Student: He says: ("And the necks": that is, he slaughtered them and cut their legs, seeking nearness to Allah, the Exalted, since they had distracted him from the prayer, and he gave their meat in charity, so Allah compensated him with something better than them, and He was swifter, and that was the wind.)
Shaykh: Did you hear? This allows what the author said, that he gave them in charity, and it also allows that he did not give them in charity, because slaughtering them was a drawing near to Allah by destroying them, and what is of that kind is not eaten. A parallel: if a man committed bestiality with an animal, the animal is killed and its meat is not eaten, because it was destroyed for the sake of Allah, so it should not be eaten. In any case, it is possible that Solomon gave them in charity as the author said, or ate them, or left them. Allah knows best.

Student: "And We certainly tried Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (in repentance). (34) He said, 'My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me; indeed You are the Bestower.' (35) So We subjected to him the wind, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed, (36) and [subjected to him] the devils, every builder and diver, (37) and others bound together in shackles. (38) This is Our gift, so grant [favors] or withhold without account. (39) And indeed for him is nearness to Us and a good return." [Sad 34–40].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted says: "And We certainly tried Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back." This sentence, as is well known, is emphasized with three emphatics: the implied oath, the lam of emphasis which accompanies the oath (called the lam al-muwatta’ah lil-qasam, the preparatory lam for the oath), and the third, qad.

"And We certainly tried Solomon": that is, We tested him. The pronoun in "fatannā" refers to the Lord, Exalted is He, and He used the plural form out of magnification, not enumeration, since Allah the Almighty is One, yet He sometimes refers to Himself in the singular and sometimes in the plural.

He says: Solomon was the son of David. Allah the Almighty did not specify this trial, neither its identity nor its type. For this reason we should leave unspecified what Allah left unspecified, and keep general what He kept general, and know that if there were any benefit for us in specifying what He left unspecified, He would have mentioned it, because Allah the Exalted says: "And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things" [al-Nahl 89]. So everything in which there is a benefit, Allah the Mighty and Majestic will certainly make clear. Therefore we say: if someone asks us, "What is the type of this trial? What is its identity?", we say: "Allah knows best," because Allah the Exalted has not made it clear to us, and it has not been reported in an infallible report. So it is obligatory upon us to remain silent. As for what is mentioned at this point of Israelite narrations (isra'iliyyat), these are false Israelite narrations, unworthy of the station of prophethood. But the Israelites brought them, because they do not believe that David and Solomon were messengers; they believe they were kings, and anything may be attributed to a king.

He says: ("'And We certainly tried Solomon' [Sad 34]: We afflicted him by stripping him of his kingdom"). Here the author begins with the Israelite story ("by stripping him of his kingdom; this was because he married a woman he loved, who was worshipping an idol"). We ask Allah for well-being. That is, they made both David and Solomon lovers who had no concern but women. As we have already noted, David wanted to marry a man's wife, and David had ninety-nine wives, so he wanted to complete the hundred. As for Solomon, they say he fell in love with a woman. This false story says: he fell in love with her and became infatuated with her ("and she was worshipping an idol in his house without his knowledge"). So the house became a house of disbelief and polytheism without his knowledge. We are certain this is a lie, because if she had been an unbeliever, Allah would have clarified that, as He clarified it regarding the wives of Noah and Lot.

He says: ("His kingdom was in his ring. When he wished to enter the privy, he would take it off and place it with his wife named Amina, as was his custom. A jinn came to her in the form of Solomon and took it from her"). This is the story: "his kingdom was in his ring." When he wanted to enter the privy he removed it, and I do not know what the reason was for removing it. Why would he remove it? The name of Solomon contains no divine name, nor any of Allah's names, so one could say he was guarding against entering with something bearing the remembrance of Allah. Also, he placed it with his wife named Amina as his custom.

This too shows the story is false. First: how can the kingdom be only in a ring?! Second: if his kingdom was in his ring, could he be so careless as to leave it with a woman? Someone may say: she was trustworthy. We say: what is the evidence for this? "A jinn came to her in the form of Solomon and took it from her." Took what? The ring. When he took the ring, he became Solomon, because the kingdom follows this ring.

Allah the Exalted says: "and We placed upon his throne a body" (it was that jinn, and he is Sakhr or someone else). That is, his name was (Sakhr or someone else), who sat on Solomon's throne, and the birds and others gathered around him. Solomon came out in a different form, saw him on his throne, and said to the people: "I am Solomon." They denied him. Poor man! When he came, he found this jinn named Sakhr or another on the throne, so he began saying to the people, "I am Solomon." They said, "No, you are not Solomon; go back." Why? Because Solomon is the one sitting on the throne of kingship, while you are not Solomon. So what would his distress be? It would be severe. "Then he turned back."

In truth, regarding "and We placed upon his throne a body," some scholars say it was a devil. But setting aside the matter of the kingdom being in the ring, and his giving it to his wife, and the jinn coming to her and taking it from her, the verse says that Allah placed upon his throne a body; that is, during Solomon's absence, because Solomon was not always on the throne. But Allah the Almighty empowered a devil who sat on the throne and began to manage the state. When Solomon came to his seat, he found it occupied by this ifrit, and he was unable to remove him from the throne or to resume managing the affairs of the realm. So he knew he was being tested, and that Allah had empowered this devil to test him, Exalted is He. This is the view of some scholars, and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was a devil. But Ibn 'Abbas, as is well known, took much from the Children of Israel, and perhaps this is among what he took.

In any case, this is a view other than what the author stated. The author holds that this occurred because the kingdom was in the ring, and this jinn took it from the trusted woman, sat on the throne, and said, "I am Solomon." That is the first view.

The second: that Allah empowered a devil without the ring being taken, without the jinn taking a form. He empowered a devil who sat on the throne and began to manage the affairs of the realm, and seized the authority from Solomon, because Solomon was not always on the throne.

The third view: that the body is the half-child, the one by which Allah tested Solomon when he said: "Tonight I shall go in unto ninety women, each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2819) and Muslim (1654/25) from Abu Hurayrah.] He swore that he would have intercourse with ninety women, and that each would bear a boy who would fight in the cause of Allah. The king said to him: "Say: if Allah wills." He did not say "if Allah wills," relying on the resolve in his heart to carry out what he wished. He carried it out and had intercourse with ninety women, but what Allah willed did not come to pass for him, namely that each woman would bear a boy who would fight in the way of Allah. One woman bore a half-person, half a human, so that Solomon and others would know that the matter is in Allah's hand, and that no one may presume upon his Lord, Exalted is He. Some exegetes say this child was the body, because this child was not fully capable of managing affairs, being half a person. How could he manage? This is the one placed upon the throne, through whom Solomon was tested.

The fourth view: that His saying "and We placed upon his throne a body" refers to Solomon himself. "We tried Solomon": We tested him. "And We placed upon his throne a body": that is, We placed him, himself, upon his throne as a body, and the body is one that does not manage and has no thought. That is, Allah stripped Solomon of the thinking by which he managed his kingdom, so he became unable to manage well, and one who cannot manage well is like a body without a soul. So what is meant by "body"? Solomon himself. The sense would be: "and We placed him as a body upon his throne, unable to manage well." This is also plausible: Allah the Exalted may strip a person of his reason and thought until he becomes a body without a spirit. It is well known that a great kingdom like Solomon's, if it lacks a manager, will become disordered and shaken. So these are four views on the meaning of His saying: "and We placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back."

As for what the author mentioned, it is undoubtedly false. As for what was mentioned about the half-child, it appears weak. There remain two views:

The first: that it was a devil empowered over Solomon's throne, who remained there and began to manage the affairs of the kingdom.

The second: that Solomon himself was stripped by Allah of thought and of managing the affairs of the kingdom, so he became unable to manage well.

Both views are possible, and the closer of them by wording is the first, namely that it was a devil placed upon the throne, because "jasadan" is indefinite, which suggests that what was placed is other than the one placed upon his throne. But the second is closer in meaning: that when Allah the Exalted strips a person of his reason, thought, and authority, he becomes like a body.

In any case, this trial that befell Solomon through placing a body upon his throne, whether it was himself or a devil who sat on the throne, is undoubtedly a great trial, and no one can imagine it who has not been touched by such a trial, because the trials and calamities we hear of pass through our minds merely as thoughts, and this is not like one who directly experiences the calamity or the matter itself. When Solomon's situation reached this point, he turned back to Allah, because it is in human nature that when a person is struck by calamity, he examines himself. Before being struck he may be heedless, but once struck he begins to examine himself and returns to Allah. Even the polytheists, when they board ships and are struck by waves that crash upon one another, turn to whom? To Allah, Exalted is He, calling upon Him, sincere in religion, that He may save them. So it is in human nature to return to the power that can ward off the calamity that has befallen him. Whoever departs from this nature, some people may depart from this natural disposition, as Allah the Exalted said: "And We had seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate" [al-Mu'minun 76]. Some people may depart from this innate nature, so that calamities, disasters and punishment strike them, yet their hearts remain hard and unaffected. We ask Allah for well-being.

He says: ("'Then he turned back' [Sad 34]: Solomon returned to his kingdom after some days, when he reached the ring, put it on, and sat upon his throne"). This is among the furthest things from the truth, a distortion of the words of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. "Then he turned back": that is, he returned to his kingdom?! What is clearly meant is that he turned back to Allah. That is, he recognized that what had befallen him was because of something that had happened from him, so he returned to Allah, turned to Him in repentance, made his repentance sincere, and corrected his conduct.

He said: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me." This. "My Lord, forgive me": he began with seeking forgiveness before seeking the great kingdom that would not belong to anyone after him. This is because the removal of the effects of sins is what achieves the purpose, for sins in reality accumulate upon the heart and prevent it from many of its interests, so a person asks to be freed from the effects of these sins before asking for what he desires.

"My Lord, forgive me": forgiveness (maghfirah) is derived from (al-mighfar), which is what is placed upon the head to protect it from arrows during battle, a piece of iron called the helmet, which protects the head and at the same time covers it. For this reason we say that the forgiveness of sins is their concealment from creation, together with overlooking their punishment. That is, it combines two meanings: concealment and overlooking the sin, meaning that Allah does not punish for it.

"And grant me a kingdom": that is, give me a kingdom. "That will not belong to anyone after me": "will not belong" means it is not fitting that it should be for anyone after me, that is, a great kingdom that no one after me could conceive of. So Allah forgave him and answered him.

Allah the Exalted says: "after me" (that is, other than me, as in: "Who then can guide him after Allah?" [al-Jathiyah 23], meaning other than Him). That is, the author says that the meaning of "after me" is "other than me," and that it does not mean after me in time. Rather, it means no one in my time or after my time shall have it; the meaning of "after" here is "other than." He cited as evidence the Exalted's saying: "Who then can guide him after Allah?", and it is known that there is no one after Allah, for Allah is the Last, after whom there is nothing; but the meaning of "after Allah" is "other than Allah."

He said: "and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me; indeed You are the Bestower." Its connection to what precedes it is that it is a form of seeking nearness (tawassul): when he asked Allah to grant him a kingdom, he sought nearness to Allah by a name suited to what he asked for: "indeed You are the Bestower." The "anta" in "innaka anta al-wahhab" is what the scholars call the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and it conveys three things: emphasis, restriction, and distinguishing between the attribute and the predicate.

"Al-Wahhab" is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah), due to the abundance of Allah's gifts and the multitude of those to whom Allah gives. Every blessing in creation is a gift from Allah, and how numerous are the blessings upon man himself, and how many people Allah has favored. For this reason the intensive form came: "indeed You are the Bestower."

Allah the Exalted says: "So We subjected to him the wind." The "fa" here indicates causation in one respect and sequence in another; that is, because of his supplication, and because of its immediacy: why do we say "because"? Because "fa" indicates causation. "Immediacy" is because "fa" also indicates sequence: when he supplicated, Allah answered him. "So We subjected to him the wind": that is, We made it subservient to him. We made the wind subservient to him, and the wind is the air.

He says: "blowing gently by his command wherever he directed." "Blowing" means it moves. "By his command" means in accordance with his order. "Gently" means soft. "Wherever he directed" means wherever he intended. "Wherever" is an adverbial complement of "blowing," meaning it moves toward the direction he wanted, "gently," soft in its movement and its blowing, soft in its obedience, not disobedient. If the wind were blowing from the south now, for example, and he wanted to go south, he would command it to blow north, and it would blow north, and he would travel upon it. "Blowing by his command," even if the prevailing direction of the wind were south, and he commanded it to be east, it would go east; if north, it would go north. It would move wherever he wished.

As for the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "blowing gently by his command," someone may ask: how is "gently" reconciled with another verse: "And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, violent, blowing by his command toward the land which We had blessed, and We are ever Knowing of all things" [al-Anbiya' 81]?

The answer: the reconciliation is easy. It is gentle, meaning it has no violent shaking; and it is violent, meaning it is swift. The "violence" in "'asifah" means it is swift, not slow, for its morning journey was a month's distance and its evening journey was a month's distance. It moves in the morning, and by the time the sun passes its zenith it has covered a month's distance, and after noon it moves on, and by the time of sunset it has covered another month's distance. How was this? Did he fly by himself? No. The scholars said: he would place something like a carpet on the ground, and he and his retinue would sit on this carpet, then he would command the wind, and it would carry it, flying between heaven and earth. Yet it was gentle. One would expect such flight to disturb those riding on the carpet, but Allah made it gentle and soft, as if it were not moving, as if they were not flying, so there was no disturbance. This is among the signs of Allah. He said: "wherever he directed," that is, wherever he wished.

As for the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "blowing gently by his command" [Sad 36], someone may ask: how is "gently" reconciled with His saying in another verse: "And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, violent, blowing by his command toward the land which We had blessed, and We are ever Knowing of all things" [al-Anbiya' 81]?

The answer is that reconciling the two verses is easy. The wind was gentle (*rukhā'*), meaning it did not shake or jolt, yet it was also swift (*'āṣifah*). The meaning of "*'aṣf*" in His words ﴿*'āṣifatan*﴾ ("a strong wind") is that it was swift, not slow, because its morning journey was a month's distance and its evening journey was a month's distance. That is, it would travel in the morning, and by the time the sun reached its zenith it would have covered a month's distance, and after the zenith it would travel until sunset, having covered another month's distance.

How was that? Did he himself fly with it? No. The scholars said: he would place something like a carpet on the ground, and he and his courtiers would sit on this carpet, and then he would command the wind, and it would carry them, flying between the heaven and the earth. Yet it was gentle. One would expect that such flying would unsettle those riding on this carpet, but God made it gentle, so gentle that it seemed as if it were not moving, as if they were not flying, and there was no discomfort in it. This is one of the signs of God.

He said: ﴿*ḥaythu aṣāba*﴾ [38:36], meaning: wherever he wished, that is, to whatever direction he desired. This is one point, and to our knowledge no one other than him has been granted this. No king among the kings has had what the Messenger had, namely that he commands the wind and it travels wherever he wishes.

Secondly, He said: ﴿*wa-sh-shayāṭīn*﴾ [38:37], meaning: We subjected the devils to him. *Shayāṭīn* is the plural of *shayṭān*, and they are the powerful jinn (*'afārīt*).

He subjected to him ﴿*kulla bannā'in*﴾ ("every builder") who builds wondrous structures, ﴿*wa-ghawwāṣin*﴾ [38:37] ("and diver") who dives in the sea to extract pearls, ﴿*wa-ākharīna muqarranīna*﴾ [38:38] ("and others bound together"), those bound in ﴿*al-aṣfād*﴾ [38:38] ("chains"), the shackles that bind their hands to their necks. And so on to the end.

God subjected the devils to him, making them submissive, obeying his command. He classified and ranked them according to their abilities and specialisations. Among them are those who build for him towering, wondrous buildings: ﴿*yaʿmalūna lahu mā yashā'u min maḥārība wa-tamāthīla wa-jifānin ka-l-jawābi wa-qudūrin rāsiyāt*﴾ [34:13] ("They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, statues, bowls like water troughs, and fixed cauldrons"). This is one category. Another category are divers, who dive into the seas and bring him all kinds of pearls, coral, gems and other things. Whatever he wants, they dive and bring him what he wants. Among them are rebellious devils who harm people and sometimes rebel against him and disobey him. He binds these in chains, tying their hands to their necks and imprisoning them in shackles.

Someone may say: is this part of the subjugation? We say: yes, this is part of the subjugation. God gave him authority over them. God made them disobey him and rebel against him, or harm those in his kingdom, so that he would punish them in this way, and thereby the completeness of his dominion over these devils would become evident. For the completeness of authority is recognised only through such things, that is, only through imposing punishments on rebels. As for a ruler who is lenient and compromises with rebels, this indicates what? It indicates weakness of authority and that he does not have the ability to manage his kingdom. So God made these devils rebel against Solomon, or harm those in his kingdom, so that he would inflict his might upon them, and it would be known that he is strong and possesses authority and control over these jinn: ﴿*wa-ākharīna muqarranīna fī l-aṣfād*﴾.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿*hādhā ʿaṭāʾunā*﴾ [38:39] ("This is Our gift"). ﴿*Hādhā*﴾ ("This") refers to what God subjected to him of the wind and authority over the devils.

﴿*ʿaṭāʾunā*﴾ ("Our gift") means what We have given you, because he had said: ﴿*wa-hab lī mulkan lā yanbaghī li-aḥadin min baʿdī*﴾ [38:35] ("Grant me a kingdom which none after me shall have"). So God granted him this gift, and what we understand from what He gave him is the subjugation of the wind and the subjugation of the devils.

(﴿*hādhā ʿaṭāʾunā fa-mnun*﴾: give from it to whomever you wish, ﴿*aw amsik*﴾: or withhold from giving, ﴿*bi-ghayri ḥisāb*﴾: without account, meaning there is no accountability for you in that.)

God granted him this kingdom and said to him: you have the choice. Bestow favour upon whom you wish, and withhold favour from whom you wish, and there is no account for you in that. This is absolute discretion in disposal. It will come to us, God willing, in the explanation of the benefits that a choice may be absolute and may be restricted in some matters. For example, in the expiations for oaths (*kaffārāt*), there is a choice; but is it absolute or restricted? It is restricted, among specific things. And there is an absolute choice, which says: do what you wish and leave what you wish. This absolute choice is what was granted to Solomon, peace be upon him.

Then He said: ﴿*wa-inna lahu ʿindanā la-zulfā wa-ḥusna maʾāb*﴾ [38:40] ("Indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good final return"). When God mentioned what He had bestowed upon him in this world, He mentioned what He had bestowed upon him in the Hereafter, namely that he has with God an elevated rank, a nearness to God.

﴿*Ḥusna maʾāb*﴾ means: a good place of return, because his return is to Paradise, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

Here, ﴿*wa-inna lahu ʿindanā la-zulfā*﴾: we mentioned previously that the "with-ness" (*ʿindiyyah*) attributed to God is divided into what? 

* Students: Two parts.

* The Shaykh: What are they? The "with-ness" of attribute (*ʿindiyyat al-ṣifah*) and the "with-ness" of nearness (*ʿindiyyat al-qurb*). The "with-ness" of nearness is like this verse. The "with-ness" of attribute is like His saying: ﴿*wa-ʿindahu mafātiḥu l-ghaybi lā yaʿlamuhā illā huwa*﴾ [6:59] ("With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He"). This is "with-ness" of attribute. As for "with-ness" of nearness, it is separate from God: a thing is "with God," meaning near to Him.

As for His saying: ﴿*la-zulfā wa-ḥusna maʾāb*﴾, *zulfā* means nearness, because the highest ranks of creation are the prophets: ﴿*wa-man yuṭiʿi llāha wa-r-rasūla fa-ulāʾika maʿa lladhīna anʿama llāhu ʿalayhim mina n-nabiyyīna wa-ṣ-ṣiddīqīna wa-sh-shuhadāʾi wa-ṣ-ṣāliḥīn*﴾ [4:69].

* Student: ﴿*wa-sh-shayāṭīna kulla bannā'in wa-ghawwāṣ*﴾ [38:37], and "all" (...) all of them, and "others" some of it, this indicates (...).

* The Shaykh: No. ﴿*kulla bannā'in wa-ghawwāṣ*﴾ refers to the builders and divers, and "others" refers to those other than these.

* Student: Meaning "all" (...).

* The Shaykh: By compulsion of some. God divided the devils into two groups: a group of builders and divers, and another group other than them, ﴿*wa-ākharīna*﴾. Because *ākhar* (with a fatḥah) means "different," i.e., different.

* Student: Meaning all from the first group.

* The Shaykh: From the first group.

* Student: Meaning (...) all from the first group.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the first group is all builders.

* Student: The second group.

* The Shaykh: Yes (...).

* * *

* Student: (...) ﴿*wa-dhkur ʿabdanā Ayyūba idh nādā rabbahu annī massaniya sh-shayṭānu bi-nuṣbin wa-ʿadhāb. Irkuḍ bi-rijlika hādhā mughtasalun bāridun wa-sharāb. Wa-wahabnā lahu ahlahu wa-mithlahum maʿahum raḥmatan minnā wa-dhikrā li-ūlī l-albāb. Wa-khudh bi-yadika ḍighthan fa-ḍrib bihi wa-lā taḥnath innā wajadnāhu ṣābiran niʿma l-ʿabdu innahu awwāb*﴾ [38:41–44].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿*wa-laqad fatannā Sulaymāna wa-alqaynā ʿalā kursiyyihi jasadan thumma anāb*﴾ [38:34]. What is meant by this trial (*fitnah*)?

* Student: This trial has four opinions. Some scholars said that when Solomon, peace be upon him, wanted to (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: The trial is a test.

* Another student: What is meant by the trial is something God, blessed and exalted, has concealed, and it is incumbent upon us to remain silent about it.

* The Shaykh: Excellent, well done (...). ﴿*fatannā Sulaymān*﴾: if it is asked, "What is this trial?" – God knows best – we do not know.

His words: ﴿*wa-alqaynā ʿalā kursiyyihi*﴾, what is meant by this phrase?

* Student: There are four opinions regarding this phrase. The first opinion, according to the author's statement, is that Solomon had a wife (...) who worshipped an idol in his house, and he had a ring, and when he entered the privy he placed the ring with her, and then the devil came (...).

The second opinion: he, peace be upon him, swore that he would go round to ninety or a hundred wives, and each would bear him a boy who would fight in the cause of God, or a man who would fight in the cause of God.

* The Shaykh: How? He swore that he would go round to ninety women, each of whom would bear a boy who would fight in the cause of God.

* Student: But he had no child except a half-body of a man. They said: that is what is meant (...).

The third opinion: a devil was cast onto Solomon's throne, setting aside the story the author mentioned.

The fourth opinion: Solomon was cast onto his throne, but he had taken from it the management of the kingdom...

* The Shaykh: And the authority.

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Excellent. His words: ﴿*thumma anāb*﴾: what is the meaning of *anāb*?

* Student: ﴿*anāb*﴾ means: returned.

* The Shaykh: Returned to what?

* Student: The author said: he returned to his kingdom (...). The correct view is that he returned to God, glorified and exalted is He (...).

* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿*wa-hab lī mulkan lā yanbaghī li-aḥadin min baʿdī*﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿*lā yanbaghī*﴾?

* Student: ﴿*lā yanbaghī*﴾ means: it should not be.

* The Shaykh: That is: it should not be. And what is meant by His words ﴿*min baʿdī*﴾: is it the temporal *baʿda* (after) or the personal *baʿda*?

* Student: No, besides me; the personal one.

* The Shaykh: Besides me. Do you have evidence that *baʿda* comes with the meaning of *siwā* (besides)?

* Student: ﴿*fa-man yahdīhi min baʿdi llāh*﴾ [45:23].

* The Shaykh: The saying of God: ﴿*fa-man yahdīhi min baʿdi llāh*﴾ [45:23] is not the temporal *baʿda*, because God is the one after whom there is nothing, i.e., besides God.

What is the position of His words ﴿*innaka anta l-Wahhāb*﴾ in relation to what precedes them?

* Student: A causal clause.

* The Shaykh: Causal; meaning: I asked You, O Lord, to grant me, because You are the Bestower.

﴿*Al-Wahhāb*﴾ here: is it an intensive form (*ṣīghat mubālagha*) or a relational form (*nisbah*)?

* Student: An intensive form?

* The Shaykh: Why?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: And the recipient too.

* Student: Many.

* The Shaykh: Many. His words: ﴿*tajrī bi-amrihi rukhāʾan*﴾?

* Student: ﴿*rukhāʾan*﴾ means soft.

* The Shaykh: Soft.

* Student: It has no violent shaking.

* The Shaykh: May God bless you. How do you reconcile this with His words: ﴿*wa-li-Sulaymāna r-rīḥa ʿāṣifatan*﴾ [21:81]?

* Student: There, it means swift.

* The Shaykh: In the sense of swift.

* Student: And here it means soft, not (...), meaning it is not swift and not violently shaking, nor...

* The Shaykh: So it is gentle and yet swift.

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: May God bless you. His words: ﴿*wa-sh-shayāṭīn*﴾: what governs it in the accusative?

* Student: He subjected the devils.

* The Shaykh: Meaning: what is it governed by?

* Student: It is conjoined.

* The Shaykh: Conjoined to what?

* Student: To the wind.

* The Shaykh: To the wind. ﴿*kulla bannā'in wa-ghawwāṣ*﴾ [38:37, 38] How many categories did God divide the devils into, in relation to him?

* Student: Three categories: builders, divers, and others bound in chains.

* The Shaykh: Why were these bound ones bound?

* Student: Because they were rebellious.

* The Shaykh: They rebelled against him.

* Student: Yes indeed.

* The Shaykh: What is the benefit of mentioning this? Because their rebellion against him might be said to indicate weakness of his authority?

* Student: We say: this is among (...) his authority is strength.

* The Shaykh: This is among what indicates the strength of his authority, and that the rebel among them has no reward except this.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: His words: ﴿*fa-mnun aw amsik*﴾, what is their meaning?

* Student: ﴿*fa-mnun*﴾ its meaning is (...), and ﴿*amsik*﴾ means: restrain or withhold.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, meaning that God gave him the choice between?

* Student: Between giving and giving abundantly, or withholding and refraining (...).

* The Shaykh: And this is a metaphor that God gave him an absolute kingdom, in which he does whatever he wishes.

What is the benefit of His words: ﴿*wa-inna lahu ʿindanā la-zulfā wa-ḥusna maʾāb*﴾?

* Student: When God, mighty and majestic, mentioned his status in this world (...) and the favour bestowed upon him, He mentioned his status in the Hereafter.

* The Shaykh: Correct, lest it be thought that this kingdom in this world contradicts the reward of the Hereafter.

* * *

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿*wa-laqad fatannā Sulaymāna wa-alqaynā ʿalā kursiyyihi jasadan thumma anāb*﴾ [38:34].

* Among the benefits of this verse: God, glorified and exalted, may test His chosen servants with whatever test He wills, and it is appropriate, as we said in the exegesis, that we leave vague what God left vague, and not search for it with the excessive effort that some people undertake.

* Among its benefits: Solomon had a throne on which he sat as kings sit, because God combined for him prophethood and kingship.

* Among its benefits: a person may be deprived of some blessings, either as a consequence of a deed he committed for which he deserved to be deprived of some blessings, or so that he may ascend to the rank of the patient, because patience is a high station that is attained only through the means of patience. For example, patience is of three kinds: patience in obedience to God, patience in refraining from disobedience, and patience in God's decrees. As for patience in obedience and in refraining from disobedience, these are by a person's choice. As for God's decrees, they are beyond one's choice, and God may test a servant with decrees that require patience and perseverance, so that he may complete the ranks of patience, and among these is the casting of the body onto Solomon's throne.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the prophets, peace be upon them, must return to God and become attentive; this is from His words: ﴿*thumma anāb*﴾, unlike others, for they may be tried with sins and not return from them. This is the difference between the prophets and others: the prophets are protected from persisting in sins, whereas others are not. This is the difference. What difference did you just mention?

* Student: The prophets are protected from sins.

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: From persisting in sins.

* The Shaykh: From persisting in sins; unlike others, for a person is tested with sin and is not granted success in repenting from it.

* Among the benefits of this verse: one who has been stripped of authority and power is like a body without a soul; this is from His words: ﴿*wa-alqaynā ʿalā kursiyyihi jasadan*﴾, and this is according to one of the four opinions we mentioned.

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿*qāla rabbi ghfir lī wa-hab lī*﴾ [38:35], and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the prophets, peace be upon them, are more concerned with the matters of the Hereafter; for this reason he asked God for forgiveness before he asked for kingship.

* Among its benefits: the prophets, peace be upon them, are in need of God's forgiveness; this is from His words: ﴿*qāla rabbi ghfir lī*﴾.

* Among its benefits: they are servants who are nurtured, not lords; this is from His words: ﴿*rabbi ghfir*﴾.

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of sins being committed by the prophets. From where is this derived?

* Student: From His words: ﴿*thumma anāb*﴾.

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: ﴿*qāla rabbi ghfir lī*﴾.

* The Shaykh: From His words: ﴿*qāla rabbi ghfir lī*﴾. What is the basis of this?

* Student: That he had sought forgiveness for a sin he had committed.

* The Shaykh: Because if there had been no sin, he would not have sought forgiveness.

* Among the benefits of this verse: it is permissible for a person to ask for kingship; that you ask God to grant you something to rule; this is from His words: ﴿*wa-hab lī mulkan*﴾. But this is conditional upon the person having the readiness to carry out what he asks for. As for saying, "O Lord, grant me a kingdom," while intending to squander it, this is not permissible.

The scholars have differed regarding the permissibility of asking for leadership: is it permissible for a person to ask for leadership, or judgeship, or similar positions of authority?

Some scholars said that this is permissible, some said it is forbidden, and some made a distinction. As for those who said it is permissible, they cited the story of Yusuf, when he said to the king of Egypt: ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land; indeed I am a knowing guardian﴾ [Yusuf 55]. So he asked for authority. The law of those before us is law for us as long as our law does not contradict it. They also cited the hadith of 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, when he said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Make me the imam of my people." He said: "You are their imam." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (531) and al-Nasa'i (672) from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan.]

As for those who forbade it, they cited the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah, that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Do not ask for leadership. For if you are given it because you asked for it, you will be left to it (to handle it alone); and if you are given it without asking, you will be helped with it." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6622) and Muslim (1652/19) from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah.] So the Prophet ﷺ forbade him to ask for leadership and explained the reason: whoever is given it because he asked for it is left to it and Allah does not help him, while whoever is given it without asking is helped by Allah in it. They also cited the report that a man asked the Messenger of Allah to appoint him as an official, and he said: "We do not appoint to this matter anyone who asks for it." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2261) and Muslim (1733/14) from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.] This indicates that one should not ask, and that whoever asks is not fit to be appointed.

Others made a distinction and said: if he asks for it in order to correct what has become corrupt in it, then it is permissible when he knows in himself that he is capable; otherwise it is not permissible, because safety for a person is safer. This distinguished view is the correct one, because it brings the evidences together. For example, if a person sees an authority held by someone who is not fit for it, either in his religion or his trustworthiness and conduct, or in his religion or his conduct, while he knows in himself the ability to carry it out in the best manner, or at least in a better manner than it is currently being done, then there is no harm in his asking for it, because his purpose in that is a personal purpose or a practical and reformist purpose. What matters is the intention of the person. But if there is no such reason, or if the person knows that he is weak and cannot carry it out, then he should not ask, and it is not permissible for him to ask.

* Among the benefits of this verse: Solomon, peace be upon him, asked Allah for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, meaning a kingdom that no one could overpower him in. It does not mean that no one could attain it after his death. This is according to one of the two opinions, and it is the one the author (Ibn Kathir) followed. Based on this, the objection is answered, which is that his saying ﴿that should not belong to anyone after me﴾ indicates that Solomon was envious and stingy. Otherwise, why would he restrict something vast and want to confine the kingdom to himself?

The second opinion is that what is meant by ﴿that should not belong to anyone after me﴾ is: after me in time, later, as we mentioned in the tafsir. We said that this is supported by his saying ﷺ when an 'Ifrit escaped from him while he was praying, and he wanted to seize it and tie it to a pillar of the mosque so that the children of the people of Madinah could play with it. He said: "Had I not remembered the words of my brother Solomon, ﴿Grant me a kingdom that should not belong to anyone after me﴾, I would have done it." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (461) and Muslim (541/39) from Abu Hurayrah.] This indicates that what is meant by "after me" is, in time. So it is preferred that Solomon, peace be upon him, asked for a great kingdom that would not belong to anyone after him. Based on this opinion, the difficulty arises: why did this kingdom become restricted? How is this answered?

We may say that the first opinion is more correct, and that the Prophet ﷺ left that out out of scrupulousness, because he feared that Solomon's meaning was "should not belong to anyone after me in time." So leaving it was a matter of caution. But this answer also has some weakness, because when the Prophet ﷺ explains a verse in a particular way, or relates something that points to one interpretation of it, there is no doubt that it takes precedence over the other possibility, which is that what is meant by ﴿after me﴾ is "other than me." And Allah knows best.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praising Allah, the Exalted, as the Bestower who gives abundantly.

* Among its benefits: seeking a means to Allah in supplication by means of the name that suits what one asks for, because his saying ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ fits his saying ﴿Grant me﴾. This is one of the meanings of the Exalted's saying: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf 180], because one of their meanings is that you make them a means for what you call upon Him for. So when you want to ask for forgiveness, you say: "O Most Forgiving," or for mercy: "O Most Merciful," and so on.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, running gently by his command wherever he intended﴾, to the end [Sad 36].

* Among its benefits: the demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the completeness of His dominion, in that He subjected the wind and made it submissive.

* Among its benefits: the generality of Allah's dominion over inanimate things, living beings, and others, because He commanded the wind, and the wind is inanimate, yet it complied.

* Among its benefits: that Allah may subject a part of creation to one of His servants, as He subjected the wind to Solomon. It is permissible for Him to subject it to others when He is called upon.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that winds have awareness and will, from His saying ﴿running by his command﴾. Because if it is commanded and it perceives the command and then complies, this is evidence that it has awareness and will. Likewise, everything in creation has awareness and will according to what is fitting for it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him﴾ [al-Isra' 44]. There is no glorification except with will, and no glorification except with awareness of the greatness of the One being glorified.

From this we respond to those who said that the meaning of Allah's saying ﴿a wall that wanted to collapse﴾ [al-Kahf 77] is figurative. We say to them: What prevents the wall from having will? The wall has will, but it is not like the will of humans or of moving animals that move by will. Rather, it has will while it is still and does not move.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that this subjected wind moves with ease and gentleness, not with a violent storm that unsettles, as is the usual habit of winds. The usual habit of stormy winds, as you know, is that they are unsettling, but this one was not unsettling; it was gentle, soft, and easy, as if they were on a surface.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that whoever leaves something for the sake of Allah, Allah compensates him with something better. Because many exegetes made the subjecting of the wind to Solomon, carrying him wherever he wished, a substitute for the horses he destroyed out of anger for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when they had distracted him from the remembrance of Allah. It may be that this is literally so: that what Allah gave him from (...) was a reward for his action with the horses. There is no doubt that whoever leaves something for Allah, Allah gives him something better in return. This happens often in many matters. If you want to test this on yourself, then try it.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that this wind goes in the direction Solomon intended. Even if it was originally blowing in another direction, meaning: if the wind was blowing from the south and he wanted to go south, he would command it to become...?

* Students: northern.

* Shaykh: The wind is southern, and he wants to go south, so he commands it to become northern to carry him to the south. If he commanded it to be southern, it would take him back north.

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver﴾, to the end [Sad 37].

* In this also: a demonstration of the authority that Allah granted Solomon, in that the harmful devils of the children of Adam were subjected to him in this great manner and this division.

* And among its benefits, that is, the benefits of the verse: the excellent management of Solomon, in that he distributed this host of devils according to what suits them. Among them are builders and among them are divers.

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of making buildings grand and numerous..

* Student: Because ﴿builder﴾ is an intensive form.

* Shaykh: Because ﴿builder﴾ is an intensive form. A building that the devils build must be grand and sturdy. But can it be said that this was in the law of Solomon, because he was a king who needs majesty, greatness, displaying strength, displaying wealth, and displaying authority, whereas the general population does not? For this reason our law condemns those who put their wealth into building. It may be said that a distinction is made between a king who possesses authority and others, because a ruler presenting himself with an air of greatness before his enemies is certainly something desirable.

It is mentioned that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, was governor of Syria during the leadership of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and when a person came to Mu'awiyah, he would find a gatekeeper, guards, and some grandeur. But when he went to the caliph above him, he would find the opposite: a patched garment and a patched wrap, and a man sleeping in the mosque, piling up a heap of pebbles and using them as a pillow, with no chamberlain before him and no soldiers around him. So he would be amazed: how is it that this governor is in such grandeur while the caliph above him is in such weakness and humility?!

The scholars answered this by saying that Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, was in the lands of Syria, and they would not submit to their governors and rulers unless they saw them in a manner full of grandeur and majesty. So Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, saw that it was appropriate for his situation to honor himself to the utmost, and his intention was not to show arrogance. The evidence for this is that when 'Umar's letter reached him, I think it was regarding the matter of the Jew whose house had been taken into the public treasury after he had been given a large compensation for it.
