It is like His saying about the jinn: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10]. The jinn said: ﴿Evil is intended for those on the earth﴾ [al-Jinn 10], and it is known that the one who intends evil is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for a wisdom; ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10]. They omitted the agent out of courtesy toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because evil is not attributed to Him.

In any case, it was Shaytan who touched Ayyub, and you know that his touch was either a harm to the self or a sensory harm.

Allah the Exalted said, after his heart had been emptied of all besides Allah and he had turned to his Lord: (﴿Strike﴾: hit ﴿with your foot﴾) strike the earth with it. He struck it with it, and water sprang forth from it by the permission of Allah. He needed no digger and no one to help, one strike, and water gushed forth, and Allah is powerful over all things. This is one of the strikes by which water gushed forth as a sign from the signs of Allah. The second was Musa striking the rock, whereupon twelve springs gushed forth. The third: Jibril struck with his heel or his wing at the place of Zamzam, and water sprang forth; and Allah, glorified and exalted, is powerful over all things.

So he struck the earth with his foot, (and a spring of water gushed forth, and it was said to him: ﴿This is a cool washing place﴾: water with which you wash, ﴿and a drink﴾: you drink from it). Allahu akbar; meaning he was permitted to bathe and to drink. This water also, although it sprang from the earth, and what springs from the earth is usually hot, became cool. (So he bathed in it and drank from it, and every ailment that was in his inside and outside departed from him) by the power and will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then He said: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾ [Sad 43]. The author said: (i.e., Allah revived for him those of his children who had died and gave him the like of them.) The author made the giving (hibah) mean reviving (ihyaʾ), but there is a concern with this, because reviving requires that death had occurred beforehand, and there is nothing in the verse indicating this. Rather, Allah gave him his family when they came back to him after they had fled from him; because the man, due to the psychological illness, and perhaps we say: the psychological and the bodily sensory illness, his family fled from him, they were unable to live with him, so they fled. When Allah healed him, his family returned to him. This giving is then a restoration of what had been previously given, just as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab named the performance of the night prayer of Ramadan in congregation an innovation,[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2010) from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.]] although in reality it is not an innovation; and likewise this is not a gift in the strict sense but the restoration of a gift that had fled.

As for the view that He revived them after they had died, this requires that death had occurred beforehand. But the correct view is that neither death nor revival is established; rather this giving is: what? It is the restoration of a previously given gift, because they had recoiled from him and fled from him.

As for His saying ﴿and the like of them with them﴾, this is what we say: Allah granted him new children, because his wife returned, his condition improved, and he began to have children, and Allah blessed him in his offspring.

(﴿And the like of them with them as a mercy﴾: a blessing ﴿from Us and a reminder﴾: an admonition ﴿for those of understanding﴾.)

As for His saying ﴿as a mercy﴾: if it refers to the family and to those given to him anew, then it is a created mercy, and mercy may be applied to the created, as Allah the Exalted said about Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. On this basis, is the author's explanation of mercy as blessing: correct or incorrect?
* Students: Correct.
* Shaykh: Correct. If we take the mercy here as referring to the children, the family and their like with them, then his explanation is correct, because the mercy here is created. But if by mercy is meant an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning that this comes from Our mercy, i.e., arises from the mercy of Allah, then the mercy here is what? It is uncreated; the mercy here is uncreated, because the attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted, are uncreated.

Therefore the author's words cannot be judged wrong absolutely in that he explained mercy as blessing. It is known that the Ash'aris interpret the mercy of Allah as what? As blessing or as kindness, and they do not hold that Allah has a mercy which is His attribute. So the author's words are not criticized in every respect, since it is possible that by mercy is meant what Allah granted him of family and their like with them, meaning that the thing meant is the granted gift, and the granted gift is undoubtedly created.

But if we intend ﴿a mercy from Us﴾ as the mercy which is an attribute of Allah, i.e., that this arises from Our mercy with which We are described, and He is the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, then the author's explanation is not correct, because the mercy then becomes what? An attribute of the attributes of Allah, not a blessing, a created entity separate from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying ﴿mercy﴾, how do we parse it?
* Students: Object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi).
* Shaykh: Yes, an object of purpose, and this is the cause of the preceding. Causes are of two kinds: a final cause that is anticipated, and a preceding cause that is motivating. For example, if a person becomes angry and beats his child, the beating here is from the anger; the cause is preceding, is it not?
* Students: Preceding.
* Shaykh: Preceding. So it is a motivating cause. If a person travels to trade, here the cause is final and subsequent, not preceding. The first is a motivating, driving cause; no, the impulsion is in both causes, but the first is a motivating cause carrying the person, and the second is a subsequent final cause.

﴿A mercy from Us﴾ means Himself, blessed and exalted; and He used the plural form to magnify Allah. Strangely, this plural is among the ambiguous expressions which the Christian has cited as evidence for a plurality of gods, because the Christian says: God is the third of three, not one God, and says: I have proof: ﴿We created﴾ [al-Araf 181], ﴿We sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah 99], ﴿from Us﴾, ﴿from Our presence﴾ [Maryam 13], ﴿with Us﴾, all of these indicate plurality. So we say to him: there is deviation in your heart, because you followed the ambiguous: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ [Al Imran 7]. What blinded your insight regarding the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 163]?! This is clear (muhkam). Using the plural form for magnification is a common feature of the Arabic language; even people themselves, who are human and do not deserve the greatness that the Creator deserves, refer to themselves in the plural form to magnify themselves.

(﴿A mercy from Us and a reminder﴾: admonition ﴿for those of understanding﴾: for people of intellect.) ﴿A mercy from Us﴾ is specific to Ayyub and his family; ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾ is general, by which people of intellect are reminded. By what do they get reminded in this story? They are reminded in this story that calamities befall prophets and others, and that Shaytan may be empowered over a messenger.

They are reminded by it, because when a person turns to his Lord and calls upon his Lord, Allah answers him.

They are reminded by it, because whenever distress intensifies, one should await relief. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Know that victory comes with patience, relief comes with distress, and with hardship comes ease."[[Narrated by Ahmad (2803) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]] Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them and they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?" Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ [al-Baqarah 214]. This means: near to this condition which reached the messengers to the point that they said: "When is the help of Allah?", meaning they were asking for it out of longing, not out of disbelief in it; they were saying, as it were: "O Lord, hasten victory for us." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ [al-Baqarah 214].

So, ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾ in what respects? In that calamity encompasses the prophets.

Second: that Shaytan may be empowered over the prophets.

Third: that Allah the Exalted answers the supplication of those who are distressed and turn to Him, if the person is sincere in his supplication. Allah, glorified and exalted, answers the supplication; we ask Allah to grant us sincerity with Him.

Fourth: that whenever affairs become severe, one should await relief; this is why Ayyub, when his situation became severe and he turned to Allah, Allah answered his supplication.

Fifth: that the removal of the distress of the Prophet Ayyub, upon him be prayers and peace, came through his own hand; because Allah did not send down healing without an apparent means, but with a means that he himself carries out. How? He was told: "Strike with your foot," and a remedy came forth; and it was said: "Bathe," and he treated himself. So it was he who brought forth the remedy and undertook the treatment, and his cure came through his hand: by extracting the remedy, by the treatment, and by the manner of using the remedy.

(﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it﴾: it is a bundle of grass or rods ﴿and do not break your oath﴾ [Sad 44]: by not striking her. He had sworn to strike his wife a hundred blows because she had been slow to him one day; so he took a hundred stalks of idhkhir or other, and struck her one blow with them.) This was a ruling (fatwa) from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to Ayyub, by which He gave him and his family ease. We pointed out a little earlier that he was afflicted with this calamity from Shaytan, a psychological calamity and an apparent bodily calamity. Where did his family go? They fled, and among them his wife, who should have remained with him in ease and hardship. So he swore to strike her a hundred times, to flog her a hundred lashes, because she had angered him and left him. When Allah healed him from the illness, it remained for him to fulfil his oath, to be faithful to his oath: to strike his wife a hundred blows. A hundred blows may involve some repugnance on her part and embarrassment on his. So Allah gave him this ruling: He said: take in your hand a bundle with a hundred twigs and strike her with it once, and that suffices in place of a hundred blows. He did so; he took in his hand a bundle and struck her once, and that became fulfilment of his oath. Therefore He said: ﴿strike with it and do not break your oath﴾.

Where is the object of ﴿strike﴾? It is omitted, and it was omitted, and Allah knows best, for concealment; because the Qur'an does not state that he was commanded to strike his wife, but this came in the well-known narratives among the Children of Israel. The purpose is not to know the identity of the one struck; the purpose is to know that the striking he had sworn to do is fulfilled by taking this bundle and striking with it.

As for Allah's saying ﴿and do not break your oath﴾: the root of ḥanth is sin, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they used to persist in the great sin (al-ḥinth al-ʿaẓīm)﴾ [al-Waqiʿah 46], meaning in great sin. The meaning of ḥanth here is not fulfilling one's oath: not fulfilling an oath means either leaving what one swore to do, or doing what one swore to leave. This is ḥanth. If he swore to buy a book and said: "By Allah, I will buy a book," and did not buy it, what do you say?
* Students: He broke it (ḥanth).
* Shaykh: He broke it by what? By leaving what he swore to do.
If he swore not to sell this book and said: "By Allah, I will not sell this book," then sold it, he broke it by what? By doing what he swore to leave.
If he swore to buy this book and bought it, what do we say? He fulfilled his oath.
If he swore not to sell this book and did not sell it either, he fulfilled his oath. So agreement with the oath is fulfilment (birr), and opposition to it is breaking (ḥanth).

The people of knowledge said: it is derived from this that not fulfilling an oath is disliked by Allah, because it is called ḥanth. But by Allah's grace He permitted His servants to do it, yet when they do it, they make expiation for what? For the oath or for the breaking?
* Students: For the breaking.
* Shaykh: For the breaking; because if it were for the oath, then whoever swears would have to expiate. But it is for the breaking, because the sin lies in violating the oath. But by the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He permitted us to break it and to expiate for it; this is why He said: ﴿strike with it and do not break your oath﴾.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [Sad 44]: that is, We found Ayyub, meaning: We found him ﴿patient﴾. What governs the accusative of ﴿patient﴾? ("Found" takes how many objects?)
* Students: Two objects.
* Shaykh: Two objects: the first is the pronoun in ﴿We found him﴾, and the second is ﴿patient﴾.

The patience of Ayyub, upon him be prayers and peace, was patience with the decree of Allah, and it was patience in refraining from the disobedience of Allah; he did not complain or express anger, and it was patience in obedience to Allah. In what way? It was patience with the decrees of Allah, clearly, because he endured what Shaytan had touched him with; and it was patience in refraining from disobedience to Allah, because he did not show displeasure; and it was patience in obedience to Allah, because he turned to Allah and called upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He answered him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verses 41–44 (part 2 of 3):

Sometimes the cure through supplication is far more effective than material medicine. In the past, when a delivery became difficult, a person would be brought in and asked to recite over the woman in labor. He would recite over water, and then they would take it and wipe the area around the abdomen with it, and the woman would drink from it and give birth without pain. This is something tested and witnessed, and it is much easier than treatment with physical, material medicines. He (ﷺ) turned to Allah and asked Him for healing, and this is patience in what? In obedience to Allah. So he attained all kinds of patience.

He says: (﴿What an excellent servant﴾ Ayyub) (...) ﴿What an excellent servant﴾. He was patient with this great patience: with illness, with the loss of his children, and with the loss of his family. Yet he never forgot Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and he turned to Him in times of hardship.

﴿What an excellent servant﴾, grammatical analysis (i'rab): we say ﴿ni'ma﴾ (what an excellent) is a past-tense verb that does not inflect, correct? ﴿al-'abd﴾ (the servant) is the subject (fa'il). This verb and those like it need two things: a subject and a specified object (makhsus, the thing praised). If something preceding indicates the specified object, one relies on what came before; otherwise it is supplied (muqaddar). If it is apparent, then it is apparent.

So here, for example, ﴿What an excellent servant﴾: we say the context indicates the specified object, and therefore there is no need to supply it. It is well known who ﴿the excellent servant﴾ is: Ayyub. So there is no need for supplying it. However, some grammarians supply it even when it is known, because they hold that the subject and the specified object must both be mentioned.

The author says: (﴿What an excellent servant﴾ Ayyub). Ayyub is the specified object, and ﴿al-'abd﴾ is the subject.

﴿Indeed he was ever-returning﴾: this sentence is a resumptive (istiʾnafiyya) sentence giving the reason (ta'liliyya), an explanation of the praise of Ayyub as an excellent servant, because he was awwab, that is, one who constantly returns to Allah, the Exalted.

* Student: Shaykh, regarding His saying: ﴿So strike with it and do not break your oath﴾. He swore to strike her one hundred times, but he struck her with a single strike (...) is one strike with a hundred rods or not?

* Shaykh: They are rods, a hundred rods that struck her all at once.

* Student: (...) one hundred strikes.

* Shaykh: One hundred strikes.

* Student: (...) a repetition.

* Shaykh: That happened, because this was only sequential, and now it has become gathered together.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding the quality of patience in Ayyub. Do we say that every prophet has a prominent quality, or do we say (...) he combined absolute perfection of human qualities (...)? The Prophet (ﷺ) is the most patient of people. Is he more patient than Ayyub, or do we say that Ayyub, in terms of patience, is more patient than the Prophet (ﷺ)?

* Shaykh: Excellence is of two kinds: specific excellence and general excellence. General excellence may exist in the lesser one (al-mafdul) with a specific quality that distinguishes him.

* Student: Over the Prophet.

* Shaykh: Even among the prophets. One of the prophets may have a specific quality that distinguishes him.

* Student: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾. This is a statement of speech (maqūlat al-qawl) (...). Before the supplication of Ayyub, the Blessed and Most High said to him: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾, and ﴿this is a bath﴾, this is also a statement of speech.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Apparently it follows the first.

* Student: The mughtasal (the place of bathing) is the water (...). The mughtasal is water that is bathed in.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: The water is what bathes in it, meaning (...).

* Shaykh: No. The one who bathes (mughtasil) is the person. You say: "I bathed with the water," so the water is mughtasal bihi (that with which one bathes). Look: we have the water and the place of the water. The water is mughtasal bihi (that with which one bathes), and the place of the water is mughtasal (the place of bathing). As for the agent, mughtasil, that is the person.

* Student: And the intended meaning here is the place of the water.

* Shaykh: The place.

* Student: (...) We said that he took one hundred rods (...) one rod and repeated it one hundred times, because even if he struck with a hundred, not all the rods would strike (...) except the opposite side (...).

* Shaykh: What is the benefit of the bundle (ḍigth)? One stick is enough.

* Student: (...) The ḍigth is the single one.

* Shaykh: No, not (...). He takes one rod and strikes one hundred times.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, with this bundle (...).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The benefits have not come out.

* Student: (...) The patience of Ayyub (...). Muhammad (ﷺ) had the patience of a messenger (...).

* Shaykh: That is another patience, a second type. But the Messenger was not afflicted with an illness like the illness of Ayyub. This is a second type of patience.

* Student: The saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and [We gave him] their like along with them﴾ [38:43] (...). It could be a second wife. Is that possible?

* Shaykh: It is possible, but we do not know this. What is known is that he had one wife. It is not impossible that Allah gave him two wives. Allah knows best.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, owners of strength and vision. Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Home. And indeed they are, with Us, among the chosen and the excellent. And remember Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhul-Kifl, and each of them is among the excellent. This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is a good return: gardens of perpetual residence, whose doors are opened for them. Reclining therein, they call for abundant fruit and drink. And with them are women restraining their glances, of equal age.﴾ [38:45–52].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, Satan has touched me with distress and torment."﴾ [38:41]. What is the (distress and torment) that touched him?

* Student: (Distress) is a torment, physical or psychological, from Satan, and torment...

* Shaykh: Distress is harm.

* Student: Harm, physical or psychological.

* Shaykh: That is, bodily or psychological.

* Student: (And torment) is pain.

* Shaykh: Why did he attribute it to Satan?

* Student: Because it was caused by Satan.

* Shaykh: And who empowered him?

* Student: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, empowered him for a wisdom He intended.

* Shaykh: For a wisdom He intended.

His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [38:42]. What is the meaning of ﴿strike﴾?

* Student: It means: strike.

* Shaykh: Strike what?

* Student: He strikes the earth with his foot, and water came out.

* Shaykh: His saying: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ [38:43]. What is the meaning?

* Student: It has been said: they were brought back to life after their death. This view is open to scrutiny. Rather, the correct view is that when he was afflicted with this harm, they abandoned him (...). Then Allah, the Exalted, returned them to him.

* Shaykh: ﴿We gave him﴾ means: We restored.

* Student: We restored to him his family.

* Shaykh: We restored to him his family.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it﴾ [38:44]. What is the ḍigth (bundle)?

* Student: It is a collection of grass, or a bundle of grass, sticks with which he strikes his wife one hundred times. That means one strike suffices in place of the hundred.

* Shaykh: The reason. Why one hundred?

* Student: Because he swore to strike his wife (...) with his family, one hundred lashes.

* Shaykh: One hundred lashes, so Allah gave him a ruling accordingly.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was ever-returning﴾. What is the position of this sentence relative to what precedes it?

* Student: Causal (ta'liliyya).

* Shaykh: Giving the reason for what? Because a cause must have an effect?

* Student: Yes; because it is a returning to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Another student: (...).

* Another student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿What an excellent servant﴾, is a reason for His saying: ﴿What an excellent servant﴾.

* In these verses: praise of Ayyub, peace be upon him, for the qualities mentioned.

* Also in it: the proclaiming of his virtues, as Allah commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to mention His servant Ayyub.

* Among its benefits: the clarification that the prophets, peace be upon them, do not possess for themselves any benefit or harm, as in His saying: ﴿when he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, Satan has touched me"﴾ [38:41]. And the clarification of the sincerity of their turning to Allah, in that they seek refuge in Him in times of hardship, as in His saying: ﴿"Indeed, Satan has touched me with distress and torment"﴾ [38:41].

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of attributing things to their causes, since Ayyub attributed this harm to Satan because Satan was its cause.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the permissibility of seeking a means (tawassul) to Allah through the condition of the servant, since Ayyub sought a means to Allah through his condition, namely that Satan had touched him with distress and torment. A parallel to this is Moses's saying: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾ [28:24]. He sought a means to Allah by mentioning his condition, that he was in need of Allah, the Exalted. This is one of the permissible types of tawassul. It is good here to mention, or to recall, these types. They are:

First: seeking a means to Allah through His names.

Second: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through His attributes.

Third: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through His actions.

Fourth: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, by mentioning the condition of the one supplicating.

Fifth: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through the supplication of one whose answer is hoped for.

Sixth: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through faith.

Seventh: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through righteous deeds.

All of these are permissible types of tawassul. Seeking a means to Allah through His names is like your saying: "O Allah, O Forgiving, forgive me."

Through His attributes: like your saying: "O Allah, by Your mercy I seek help. O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, give me life if You know life to be good for me."

Through His actions: "O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent prayers upon Abraham and the family of Abraham."

Through mentioning the condition of the supplicant, as in the verse.

Through the supplication of one whose answer is hoped for, like the Companions seeking a means through the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Through faith, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ [3:16], and ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed﴾ [3:193].

Seventh: seeking a means to Allah through righteous deeds, like the story of the three who took refuge in a cave, and the rock closed over them, so each of them sought a means through his righteous deed.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2272) and Muslim (2743/99), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]] These are the permissible types of tawassul.

As for what is forbidden, it is seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree. Seeking a means to Allah through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree, is prohibited, and it is a kind of mockery of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

That is, seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree. Seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree, is prohibited, and it is a kind of mockery of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is as if a person presents something he makes a means while it is not a means, as if he considers Allah ignorant, seeking a means to Him through something that is not a means and making it a means. So Allah is, by this action or on the basis of this seeking, ignorant.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the clarification that Allah answers supplication, and it is evidence of His favor upon His servants, as in His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [38:42].

* Among its benefits: the clarification of Allah's power, in that He caused water to gush forth from the striking of a foot.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of causes, as in His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾. Had Allah willed, He could have caused water to gush forth for him without striking with the foot, but Allah, the Exalted, made that a cause.

* Among its benefits: that Allah, the Exalted, may make a weak cause, one that does not by itself produce the effect, into an effective cause, just as He is able to prevent an effective cause from being effective. Striking with the foot is not customarily what causes water to gush forth, and throwing someone into fire is customarily what burns. Abraham was thrown into the fire but was not burned, and Ayyub struck with his foot and water gushed forth. So this is evidence that Allah may make a weak cause strong and effective, and make a strong, effective cause ineffective.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the clarification of divine power in that this water gushing from the depths of the earth is cool and fit for drinking.

* Among its benefits: an indication of the purifier of the inner body, which is known among people now as (...). That is, they use substances that soften the belly and cleanse it, as in His saying: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾.

* Among its benefits: that Allah, the Exalted, bestows upon the servant more than what he has lost when he is patient and seeks reward. Because Ayyub, Allah gave him back his family and their like along with them. So be patient, and you will be victorious.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whatever blessing a person receives is by the requirement of Allah's mercy, as in His saying: ﴿as a mercy from Us﴾ [38:43].

* Among its benefits: that in this great story there is ﴿a reminder for people of understanding﴾. We have already explained the aspect of this reminder. Do we recall how many aspects we mentioned? Four aspects or five.

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of using a lawful stratagem, as in His saying: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it﴾ [38:44]. This ruling is established even in Islamic law.

If a man swears that he will strike a person one hundred times, and that person cannot bear being struck one hundred times, the scholars say: he may take a bundle containing one hundred twigs and strike with it. On this they built the case where a sick man committed fornication with an illness whose cure is not hoped for and who cannot bear one hundred lashes separately. They said: a bundle containing one hundred twigs is gathered for him and he is struck with it in one blow, taking as evidence what Allah gave a fatwa on, to whom? To Ayyub.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that breaking an oath is, in principle, or that violating an oath is, in principle, forbidden, as in His saying: ﴿and do not break your oath﴾. However, Allah made things easy for His servants and permitted them to break an oath with expiation, and for this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But He will hold you accountable for oaths you have intentionally sworn﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and guard your oaths﴾ [5:89].

The scholars said: "guard your oaths" means: do not multiply oaths. Some of them said: guard them from breaking, so do not break them. Both views are not contradictory. The essential point is that a person should guard his oath and not break it, but nevertheless, sometimes breaking it is better.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, divided breaking an oath into the five legal categories. They said: breaking an oath may be obligatory, it may be forbidden, it may be disliked, it may be recommended, and it may be permissible.

If one swears not to pray in congregation, then breaking the oath is obligatory: he must pray and make expiation. If one swears to drink wine, then breaking the oath is obligatory: he must abandon it and make expiation. If one swears not to drink wine, breaking the oath is forbidden, because if he drank, he would commit something forbidden and fall into what is prohibited. If one swears not to pray the regular sunnah prayer before noon, then breaking the oath here is recommended. If one swears to eat onions or garlic while he is one who attends the mosque, breaking the oath is recommended. If one swears not to eat them, it is disliked. The essential point is that the disliked and the recommended are opposites, and the obligatory and the forbidden are opposites. As for the permissible, it is when the benefit and the harm are equal.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the praise of Ayyub for his patience, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [38:44]. This extends to others, for whoever is patient is worthy of praise.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the praise of Ayyub with this description: ﴿What an excellent servant﴾. Servitude to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is undoubtedly the completion of freedom. Whoever is more devoted in servitude to Allah is more truly free than one who is the opposite. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said a verse in the Nuniyya:

They fled from the bondage for which they were created,
and were afflicted with the bondage of the self and Satan.

May Allah have mercy on him. That is, a person must submit to something. So these people

They fled from the bondage for which they were created
.............................

which is the worship of Allah.

................................
and were afflicted with the bondage of the self and Satan.

They became slaves to their souls and their devils. The noblest attribute of a human being is to be a servant of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. I ask Allah to make me and you among the righteous servants of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the praise of Ayyub for being one who constantly returns to Allah, the Exalted, through performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was ever-returning﴾. On this basis, this attribute is praise for everyone who is characterized by it, for whoever constantly returns to Allah is praised.

Among the benefits of the verses: affirming causes, and the permissibility of attributing a thing to its known cause, whether known through the senses or through the Sharia. That is, it is permissible to attribute a thing to a cause that is known through the senses or through the Sharia, without attributing it to Allah. So if you say, for example: "I fell into the sea, and if it were not for so-and-so, I would have drowned," this is correct. Why? Because you attributed it to a known cause: so-and-so is the one who pulled you out of the water. But if you said: "I fell into the sea, and if it were not for so-and-so the dead saint, I would have perished," this would be shirk, and in this case it is major shirk.

The point is that attributing a thing to its known cause, without attributing it to Allah, is permissible. Among the examples of this is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about his uncle Abu Talib: "Had it not been for me, he would have been in the lowest level of the Fire"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883) and Muslim (209 / 357), from the hadith of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib.]], "Had it not been for me," so he attributed the thing to its known cause. As for attributing it to an unknown cause, this is a kind of shirk; it may be major, and it may be minor, depending on the circumstances.

* A student: The benefit is what we mentioned. From where did we derive it?
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Indeed, harm has touched me from Shaytan﴾ [Sad 41], He attributed it to the cause.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub﴾ [Sad 41]. ﴿Remember﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is permissible that it be directed to everyone among mankind to whom address can be made.

As for His saying ﴿And remember Our servant﴾, He repeated the verb ﴿remember﴾, whereas in the story of Sulayman He did not repeat it but said: ﴿And We gave to Dawud, Sulayman﴾ [Sad 30], and did not mention ﴿remember﴾. Some scholars said: because Sulayman son of Dawud, their stories are close, as if they were the story of one Prophet, whereas Ayyub is separate from them: ﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub﴾. The meaning of "servant" here is one who humbles himself in obedience to Allah, and this servitude is of the kind that is most special, for it is the servitude of messengerhood.

As for His saying ﴿Ayyub﴾: is this an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) or a substitution (badal)?
* Student: Explicative apposition.
* Shaykh: From where?
* Student: From ﴿Our servant﴾.
* Shaykh: From ﴿Our servant﴾.

﴿When he called out to his Lord﴾: ﴿when﴾ is connected to ﴿remember﴾, and it is permissible that it be connected to an implied element as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "servant", meaning: in the state of his calling out to his Lord.

﴿When he called out to his Lord﴾ means: he called upon Him with a raised voice, because nidāʾ (calling out) is with a raised voice, while najāʾ (secret conversation) is with a lowered voice. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount and brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam 52].

(﴿When he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, I﴾ i.e., that ﴿affliction has touched me, Shaytan﴾) The author estimated the preposition "bi" here, because the hamza of "anna" is open (fatḥa). The rule is that the hamza of "inna" is kasra when it comes after a verb of saying, as in Allah's saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah"﴾ [Maryam 30]. But here it is open, so the author estimated the bāʾ; because if we estimate the bāʾ, it and what follows it become a verbal noun (maṣdar), and when "anna" and what follows it stand in place of a verbal noun, its hamza is open, as Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the Alfiyya:
"Open the hamza of 'inna' to fill the place of a verbal noun, and otherwise kasra it."

(﴿When he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, I" i.e., that﴾) ﴿has touched me, Shaytan, with fatigue and torment﴾ [Sad 41]. ﴿Has touched me﴾ means: has afflicted me. And ﴿Shaytan﴾ is the devil of the jinn.

(﴿With fatigue﴾: harm, ﴿and torment﴾: pain.) The Shaytan had harmed him. But is this a harm to the self, by casting into his heart whisperings which wore out his body, or a sensory harm, as some said: that Shaytan blew into his body until his whole body became covered with boils, meaning harmful sores? Allah knows best; both possibilities are admitted.

Nuṣb means harm, and ʿadhāb means pain. When he called upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and humbled himself to Him, and knew that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him, then relief came to him, and it was said to him: (﴿Strike﴾: hit ﴿with your foot﴾) and this is a command from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Before this the author said: (He attributed that to Shaytan, although all things are from Allah, out of courtesy toward Him, exalted is He.) He attributed that to Shaytan because he was the cause; otherwise the whole matter is by the decree of Allah, for Allah in His wisdom gave Shaytan power over him. The Shaytan was the direct agent of the affliction, but his power was by the decree and destiny of Allah. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, took a path other than the one I have just stated. I say: he attributed it to Shaytan because he is it?
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: No, he is the direct agent of the affliction and is without doubt a cause, but a direct cause. In reality, Shaytan was only empowered by the decree and destiny of Allah. The author holds that it was attributed to Shaytan out of courtesy, whereas the original attribution is to Allah. It is like His saying about the jinn: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10]. The jinn said: ﴿Evil is intended for those on the earth﴾ [al-Jinn 10], and it is known that the one who intends evil is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for a wisdom; ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10]. They omitted the agent out of courtesy toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because evil is not attributed to Him.

In any case, it was Shaytan who touched Ayyub, and you know that his touch was either a harm to the self or a sensory harm.

Allah the Exalted said, after his heart had been emptied of all besides Allah and he had turned to his Lord: (﴿Strike﴾: hit ﴿with your foot﴾) strike the earth with it. He struck it with it, and water sprang forth from it by the permission of Allah. He needed no digger and no one to help, one strike, and water gushed forth, and Allah is powerful over all things. This is one of the strikes by which water gushed forth as a sign from the signs of Allah. The second was Musa striking the rock, whereupon twelve springs gushed forth. The third: Jibril struck with his heel or his wing at the place of Zamzam, and water sprang forth; and Allah, glorified and exalted, is powerful over all things.

So he struck the earth with his foot, (and a spring of water gushed forth, and it was said to him: ﴿This is a cool washing place﴾: water with which you wash, ﴿and a drink﴾: you drink from it). Allahu akbar; meaning he was permitted to bathe and to drink. This water also, although it sprang from the earth, and what springs from the earth is usually hot, became cool. (So he bathed in it and drank from it, and every ailment that was in his inside and outside departed from him) by the power and will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then He said: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾ [Sad 43]. The author said: (i.e., Allah revived for him those of his children who had died and gave him the like of them.) The author made the giving (hibah) mean reviving (ihyaʾ), but there is a concern with this, because reviving requires that death had occurred beforehand, and there is nothing in the verse indicating this. Rather, Allah gave him his family when they came back to him after they had fled from him; because the man, due to the psychological illness, and perhaps we say: the psychological and the bodily sensory illness, his family fled from him, they were unable to live with him, so they fled. When Allah healed him, his family returned to him. This giving is then a restoration of what had been previously given, just as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab named the performance of the night prayer of Ramadan in congregation an innovation,[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2010) from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.]] although in reality it is not an innovation; and likewise this is not a gift in the strict sense but the restoration of a gift that had fled.

As for the view that He revived them after they had died, this requires that death had occurred beforehand. But the correct view is that neither death nor revival is established; rather this giving is: what? It is the restoration of a previously given gift, because they had recoiled from him and fled from him.

As for His saying ﴿and the like of them with them﴾, this is what we say: Allah granted him new children, because his wife returned, his condition improved, and he began to have children, and Allah blessed him in his offspring.

(﴿And the like of them with them as a mercy﴾: a blessing ﴿from Us and a reminder﴾: an admonition ﴿for those of understanding﴾.)

As for His saying ﴿as a mercy﴾: if it refers to the family and to those given to him anew, then it is a created mercy, and mercy may be applied to the created, as Allah the Exalted said about Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. On this basis, is the author's explanation of mercy as blessing: correct or incorrect?
* Students: Correct.
* Shaykh: Correct. If we take the mercy here as referring to the children, the family and their like with them, then his explanation is correct, because the mercy here is created. But if by mercy is meant an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning that this comes from Our mercy, i.e., arises from the mercy of Allah, then the mercy here is what? It is uncreated; the mercy here is uncreated, because the attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted, are uncreated.

Therefore the author's words cannot be judged wrong absolutely in that he explained mercy as blessing. It is known that the Ash'aris interpret the mercy of Allah as what? As blessing or as kindness, and they do not hold that Allah has a mercy which is His attribute. So the author's words are not criticized in every respect, since it is possible that by mercy is meant what Allah granted him of family and their like with them, meaning that the thing meant is the granted gift, and the granted gift is undoubtedly created.

But if we intend ﴿a mercy from Us﴾ as the mercy which is an attribute of Allah, i.e., that this arises from Our mercy with which We are described, and He is the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, then the author's explanation is not correct, because the mercy then becomes what? An attribute of the attributes of Allah, not a blessing, a created entity separate from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying ﴿mercy﴾, how do we parse it?
* Students: Object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi).
* Shaykh: Yes, an object of purpose, and this is the cause of the preceding. Causes are of two kinds: a final cause that is anticipated, and a preceding cause that is motivating. For example, if a person becomes angry and beats his child, the beating here is from the anger; the cause is preceding, is it not?
* Students: Preceding.
* Shaykh: Preceding. So it is a motivating cause. If a person travels to trade, here the cause is final and subsequent, not preceding. The first is a motivating, driving cause; no, the impulsion is in both causes, but the first is a motivating cause carrying the person, and the second is a subsequent final cause.

﴿A mercy from Us﴾ means Himself, blessed and exalted; and He used the plural form to magnify Allah. Strangely, this plural is among the ambiguous expressions which the Christian has cited as evidence for a plurality of gods, because the Christian says: God is the third of three, not one God, and says: I have proof: ﴿We created﴾ [al-Araf 181], ﴿We sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah 99], ﴿from Us﴾, ﴿from Our presence﴾ [Maryam 13], ﴿with Us﴾, all of these indicate plurality. So we say to him: there is deviation in your heart, because you followed the ambiguous: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ [Al Imran 7]. What blinded your insight regarding the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 163]?! This is clear (muhkam). Using the plural form for magnification is a common feature of the Arabic language; even people themselves, who are human and do not deserve the greatness that the Creator deserves, refer to themselves in the plural form to magnify themselves.

(﴿A mercy from Us and a reminder﴾: admonition ﴿for those of understanding﴾: for people of intellect.) ﴿A mercy from Us﴾ is specific to Ayyub and his family; ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾ is general, by which people of intellect are reminded. By what do they get reminded in this story? They are reminded in this story that calamities befall prophets and others, and that Shaytan may be empowered over a messenger.

They are reminded by it, because when a person turns to his Lord and calls upon his Lord, Allah answers him.

They are reminded by it, because whenever distress intensifies, one should await relief. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Know that victory comes with patience, relief comes with distress, and with hardship comes ease."[[Narrated by Ahmad (2803) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]] Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them and they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?" Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ [al-Baqarah 214]. This means: near to this condition which reached the messengers to the point that they said: "When is the help of Allah?", meaning they were asking for it out of longing, not out of disbelief in it; they were saying, as it were: "O Lord, hasten victory for us." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ [al-Baqarah 214].

So, ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾ in what respects? In that calamity encompasses the prophets.

Second: that Shaytan may be empowered over the prophets.

Third: that Allah the Exalted answers the supplication of those who are distressed and turn to Him, if the person is sincere in his supplication. Allah, glorified and exalted, answers the supplication; we ask Allah to grant us sincerity with Him.

Fourth: that whenever affairs become severe, one should await relief; this is why Ayyub, when his situation became severe and he turned to Allah, Allah answered his supplication.

Fifth: that the removal of the distress of the Prophet Ayyub, upon him be prayers and peace, came through his own hand; because Allah did not send down healing without an apparent means, but with a means that he himself carries out. How? He was told: "Strike with your foot," and a remedy came forth; and it was said: "Bathe," and he treated himself. So it was he who brought forth the remedy and undertook the treatment, and his cure came through his hand: by extracting the remedy, by the treatment, and by the manner of using the remedy.

(﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it﴾: it is a bundle of grass or rods ﴿and do not break your oath﴾ [Sad 44]: by not striking her. He had sworn to strike his wife a hundred blows because she had been slow to him one day; so he took a hundred stalks of idhkhir or other, and struck her one blow with them.) This was a ruling (fatwa) from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to Ayyub, by which He gave him and his family ease. We pointed out a little earlier that he was afflicted with this calamity from Shaytan, a psychological calamity and an apparent bodily calamity. Where did his family go? They fled, and among them his wife, who should have remained with him in ease and hardship. So he swore to strike her a hundred times, to flog her a hundred lashes, because she had angered him and left him. When Allah healed him from the illness, it remained for him to fulfil his oath, to be faithful to his oath: to strike his wife a hundred blows. A hundred blows may involve some repugnance on her part and embarrassment on his. So Allah gave him this ruling: He said: take in your hand a bundle with a hundred twigs and strike her with it once, and that suffices in place of a hundred blows. He did so; he took in his hand a bundle and struck her once, and that became fulfilment of his oath. Therefore He said: ﴿strike with it and do not break your oath﴾.

Where is the object of ﴿strike﴾? It is omitted, and it was omitted, and Allah knows best, for concealment; because the Qur'an does not state that he was commanded to strike his wife, but this came in the well-known narratives among the Children of Israel. The purpose is not to know the identity of the one struck; the purpose is to know that the striking he had sworn to do is fulfilled by taking this bundle and striking with it.

As for Allah's saying ﴿and do not break your oath﴾: the root of ḥanth is sin, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they used to persist in the great sin (al-ḥinth al-ʿaẓīm)﴾ [al-Waqiʿah 46], meaning in great sin. The meaning of ḥanth here is not fulfilling one's oath: not fulfilling an oath means either leaving what one swore to do, or doing what one swore to leave. This is ḥanth. If he swore to buy a book and said: "By Allah, I will buy a book," and did not buy it, what do you say?
* Students: He broke it (ḥanth).
* Shaykh: He broke it by what? By leaving what he swore to do.
If he swore not to sell this book and said: "By Allah, I will not sell this book," then sold it, he broke it by what? By doing what he swore to leave.
If he swore to buy this book and bought it, what do we say? He fulfilled his oath.
If he swore not to sell this book and did not sell it either, he fulfilled his oath. So agreement with the oath is fulfilment (birr), and opposition to it is breaking (ḥanth).

The people of knowledge said: it is derived from this that not fulfilling an oath is disliked by Allah, because it is called ḥanth. But by Allah's grace He permitted His servants to do it, yet when they do it, they make expiation for what? For the oath or for the breaking?
* Students: For the breaking.
* Shaykh: For the breaking; because if it were for the oath, then whoever swears would have to expiate. But it is for the breaking, because the sin lies in violating the oath. But by the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He permitted us to break it and to expiate for it; this is why He said: ﴿strike with it and do not break your oath﴾.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [Sad 44]: that is, We found Ayyub, meaning: We found him ﴿patient﴾. What governs the accusative of ﴿patient﴾? ("Found" takes how many objects?)
* Students: Two objects.
* Shaykh: Two objects: the first is the pronoun in ﴿We found him﴾, and the second is ﴿patient﴾.

The patience of Ayyub, upon him be prayers and peace, was patience with the decree of Allah, and it was patience in refraining from the disobedience of Allah; he did not complain or express anger, and it was patience in obedience to Allah. In what way? It was patience with the decrees of Allah, clearly, because he endured what Shaytan had touched him with; and it was patience in refraining from disobedience to Allah, because he did not show displeasure; and it was patience in obedience to Allah, because he turned to Allah and called upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He answered him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verses 41–44 (part 2 of 3):

Sometimes the cure through supplication is far more effective than material medicine. In the past, when a delivery became difficult, a person would be brought in and asked to recite over the woman in labor. He would recite over water, and then they would take it and wipe the area around the abdomen with it, and the woman would drink from it and give birth without pain. This is something tested and witnessed, and it is much easier than treatment with physical, material medicines. He (ﷺ) turned to Allah and asked Him for healing, and this is patience in what? In obedience to Allah. So he attained all kinds of patience.

He says: (﴿What an excellent servant﴾ Ayyub) (...) ﴿What an excellent servant﴾. He was patient with this great patience: with illness, with the loss of his children, and with the loss of his family. Yet he never forgot Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and he turned to Him in times of hardship.

﴿What an excellent servant﴾, grammatical analysis (i'rab): we say ﴿ni'ma﴾ (what an excellent) is a past-tense verb that does not inflect, correct? ﴿al-'abd﴾ (the servant) is the subject (fa'il). This verb and those like it need two things: a subject and a specified object (makhsus, the thing praised). If something preceding indicates the specified object, one relies on what came before; otherwise it is supplied (muqaddar). If it is apparent, then it is apparent.

So here, for example, ﴿What an excellent servant﴾: we say the context indicates the specified object, and therefore there is no need to supply it. It is well known who ﴿the excellent servant﴾ is: Ayyub. So there is no need for supplying it. However, some grammarians supply it even when it is known, because they hold that the subject and the specified object must both be mentioned.

The author says: (﴿What an excellent servant﴾ Ayyub). Ayyub is the specified object, and ﴿al-'abd﴾ is the subject.

﴿Indeed he was ever-returning﴾: this sentence is a resumptive (istiʾnafiyya) sentence giving the reason (ta'liliyya), an explanation of the praise of Ayyub as an excellent servant, because he was awwab, that is, one who constantly returns to Allah, the Exalted.

* Student: Shaykh, regarding His saying: ﴿So strike with it and do not break your oath﴾. He swore to strike her one hundred times, but he struck her with a single strike (...) is one strike with a hundred rods or not?

* Shaykh: They are rods, a hundred rods that struck her all at once.

* Student: (...) one hundred strikes.

* Shaykh: One hundred strikes.

* Student: (...) a repetition.

* Shaykh: That happened, because this was only sequential, and now it has become gathered together.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding the quality of patience in Ayyub. Do we say that every prophet has a prominent quality, or do we say (...) he combined absolute perfection of human qualities (...)? The Prophet (ﷺ) is the most patient of people. Is he more patient than Ayyub, or do we say that Ayyub, in terms of patience, is more patient than the Prophet (ﷺ)?

* Shaykh: Excellence is of two kinds: specific excellence and general excellence. General excellence may exist in the lesser one (al-mafdul) with a specific quality that distinguishes him.

* Student: Over the Prophet.

* Shaykh: Even among the prophets. One of the prophets may have a specific quality that distinguishes him.

* Student: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾. This is a statement of speech (maqūlat al-qawl) (...). Before the supplication of Ayyub, the Blessed and Most High said to him: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾, and ﴿this is a bath﴾, this is also a statement of speech.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Apparently it follows the first.

* Student: The mughtasal (the place of bathing) is the water (...). The mughtasal is water that is bathed in.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: The water is what bathes in it, meaning (...).

* Shaykh: No. The one who bathes (mughtasil) is the person. You say: "I bathed with the water," so the water is mughtasal bihi (that with which one bathes). Look: we have the water and the place of the water. The water is mughtasal bihi (that with which one bathes), and the place of the water is mughtasal (the place of bathing). As for the agent, mughtasil, that is the person.

* Student: And the intended meaning here is the place of the water.

* Shaykh: The place.

* Student: (...) We said that he took one hundred rods (...) one rod and repeated it one hundred times, because even if he struck with a hundred, not all the rods would strike (...) except the opposite side (...).

* Shaykh: What is the benefit of the bundle (ḍigth)? One stick is enough.

* Student: (...) The ḍigth is the single one.

* Shaykh: No, not (...). He takes one rod and strikes one hundred times.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, with this bundle (...).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The benefits have not come out.

* Student: (...) The patience of Ayyub (...). Muhammad (ﷺ) had the patience of a messenger (...).

* Shaykh: That is another patience, a second type. But the Messenger was not afflicted with an illness like the illness of Ayyub. This is a second type of patience.

* Student: The saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and [We gave him] their like along with them﴾ [38:43] (...). It could be a second wife. Is that possible?

* Shaykh: It is possible, but we do not know this. What is known is that he had one wife. It is not impossible that Allah gave him two wives. Allah knows best.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, owners of strength and vision. Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Home. And indeed they are, with Us, among the chosen and the excellent. And remember Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhul-Kifl, and each of them is among the excellent. This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is a good return: gardens of perpetual residence, whose doors are opened for them. Reclining therein, they call for abundant fruit and drink. And with them are women restraining their glances, of equal age.﴾ [38:45–52].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, Satan has touched me with distress and torment."﴾ [38:41]. What is the (distress and torment) that touched him?

* Student: (Distress) is a torment, physical or psychological, from Satan, and torment...

* Shaykh: Distress is harm.

* Student: Harm, physical or psychological.

* Shaykh: That is, bodily or psychological.

* Student: (And torment) is pain.

* Shaykh: Why did he attribute it to Satan?

* Student: Because it was caused by Satan.

* Shaykh: And who empowered him?

* Student: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, empowered him for a wisdom He intended.

* Shaykh: For a wisdom He intended.

His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [38:42]. What is the meaning of ﴿strike﴾?

* Student: It means: strike.

* Shaykh: Strike what?

* Student: He strikes the earth with his foot, and water came out.

* Shaykh: His saying: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ [38:43]. What is the meaning?

* Student: It has been said: they were brought back to life after their death. This view is open to scrutiny. Rather, the correct view is that when he was afflicted with this harm, they abandoned him (...). Then Allah, the Exalted, returned them to him.

* Shaykh: ﴿We gave him﴾ means: We restored.

* Student: We restored to him his family.

* Shaykh: We restored to him his family.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it﴾ [38:44]. What is the ḍigth (bundle)?

* Student: It is a collection of grass, or a bundle of grass, sticks with which he strikes his wife one hundred times. That means one strike suffices in place of the hundred.

* Shaykh: The reason. Why one hundred?

* Student: Because he swore to strike his wife (...) with his family, one hundred lashes.

* Shaykh: One hundred lashes, so Allah gave him a ruling accordingly.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was ever-returning﴾. What is the position of this sentence relative to what precedes it?

* Student: Causal (ta'liliyya).

* Shaykh: Giving the reason for what? Because a cause must have an effect?

* Student: Yes; because it is a returning to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Another student: (...).

* Another student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿What an excellent servant﴾, is a reason for His saying: ﴿What an excellent servant﴾.

* In these verses: praise of Ayyub, peace be upon him, for the qualities mentioned.

* Also in it: the proclaiming of his virtues, as Allah commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to mention His servant Ayyub.

* Among its benefits: the clarification that the prophets, peace be upon them, do not possess for themselves any benefit or harm, as in His saying: ﴿when he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, Satan has touched me"﴾ [38:41]. And the clarification of the sincerity of their turning to Allah, in that they seek refuge in Him in times of hardship, as in His saying: ﴿"Indeed, Satan has touched me with distress and torment"﴾ [38:41].

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of attributing things to their causes, since Ayyub attributed this harm to Satan because Satan was its cause.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the permissibility of seeking a means (tawassul) to Allah through the condition of the servant, since Ayyub sought a means to Allah through his condition, namely that Satan had touched him with distress and torment. A parallel to this is Moses's saying: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾ [28:24]. He sought a means to Allah by mentioning his condition, that he was in need of Allah, the Exalted. This is one of the permissible types of tawassul. It is good here to mention, or to recall, these types. They are:

First: seeking a means to Allah through His names.

Second: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through His attributes.

Third: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through His actions.

Fourth: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, by mentioning the condition of the one supplicating.

Fifth: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through the supplication of one whose answer is hoped for.

Sixth: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through faith.

Seventh: seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through righteous deeds.

All of these are permissible types of tawassul. Seeking a means to Allah through His names is like your saying: "O Allah, O Forgiving, forgive me."

Through His attributes: like your saying: "O Allah, by Your mercy I seek help. O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, give me life if You know life to be good for me."

Through His actions: "O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent prayers upon Abraham and the family of Abraham."

Through mentioning the condition of the supplicant, as in the verse.

Through the supplication of one whose answer is hoped for, like the Companions seeking a means through the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Through faith, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ [3:16], and ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed﴾ [3:193].

Seventh: seeking a means to Allah through righteous deeds, like the story of the three who took refuge in a cave, and the rock closed over them, so each of them sought a means through his righteous deed.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2272) and Muslim (2743/99), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]] These are the permissible types of tawassul.

As for what is forbidden, it is seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree. Seeking a means to Allah through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree, is prohibited, and it is a kind of mockery of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

That is, seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree. Seeking a means to Allah, the Exalted, through something He has not made a means, neither by legislation nor by decree, is prohibited, and it is a kind of mockery of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is as if a person presents something he makes a means while it is not a means, as if he considers Allah ignorant, seeking a means to Him through something that is not a means and making it a means. So Allah is, by this action or on the basis of this seeking, ignorant.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the clarification that Allah answers supplication, and it is evidence of His favor upon His servants, as in His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [38:42].

* Among its benefits: the clarification of Allah's power, in that He caused water to gush forth from the striking of a foot.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of causes, as in His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾. Had Allah willed, He could have caused water to gush forth for him without striking with the foot, but Allah, the Exalted, made that a cause.

* Among its benefits: that Allah, the Exalted, may make a weak cause, one that does not by itself produce the effect, into an effective cause, just as He is able to prevent an effective cause from being effective. Striking with the foot is not customarily what causes water to gush forth, and throwing someone into fire is customarily what burns. Abraham was thrown into the fire but was not burned, and Ayyub struck with his foot and water gushed forth. So this is evidence that Allah may make a weak cause strong and effective, and make a strong, effective cause ineffective.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the clarification of divine power in that this water gushing from the depths of the earth is cool and fit for drinking.

* Among its benefits: an indication of the purifier of the inner body, which is known among people now as (...). That is, they use substances that soften the belly and cleanse it, as in His saying: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾.

* Among its benefits: that Allah, the Exalted, bestows upon the servant more than what he has lost when he is patient and seeks reward. Because Ayyub, Allah gave him back his family and their like along with them. So be patient, and you will be victorious.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whatever blessing a person receives is by the requirement of Allah's mercy, as in His saying: ﴿as a mercy from Us﴾ [38:43].

* Among its benefits: that in this great story there is ﴿a reminder for people of understanding﴾. We have already explained the aspect of this reminder. Do we recall how many aspects we mentioned? Four aspects or five.

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of using a lawful stratagem, as in His saying: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it﴾ [38:44]. This ruling is established even in Islamic law.

If a man swears that he will strike a person one hundred times, and that person cannot bear being struck one hundred times, the scholars say: he may take a bundle containing one hundred twigs and strike with it. On this they built the case where a sick man committed fornication with an illness whose cure is not hoped for and who cannot bear one hundred lashes separately. They said: a bundle containing one hundred twigs is gathered for him and he is struck with it in one blow, taking as evidence what Allah gave a fatwa on, to whom? To Ayyub.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that breaking an oath is, in principle, or that violating an oath is, in principle, forbidden, as in His saying: ﴿and do not break your oath﴾. However, Allah made things easy for His servants and permitted them to break an oath with expiation, and for this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But He will hold you accountable for oaths you have intentionally sworn﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and guard your oaths﴾ [5:89].

The scholars said: "guard your oaths" means: do not multiply oaths. Some of them said: guard them from breaking, so do not break them. Both views are not contradictory. The essential point is that a person should guard his oath and not break it, but nevertheless, sometimes breaking it is better.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, divided breaking an oath into the five legal categories. They said: breaking an oath may be obligatory, it may be forbidden, it may be disliked, it may be recommended, and it may be permissible.

If one swears not to pray in congregation, then breaking the oath is obligatory: he must pray and make expiation. If one swears to drink wine, then breaking the oath is obligatory: he must abandon it and make expiation. If one swears not to drink wine, breaking the oath is forbidden, because if he drank, he would commit something forbidden and fall into what is prohibited. If one swears not to pray the regular sunnah prayer before noon, then breaking the oath here is recommended. If one swears to eat onions or garlic while he is one who attends the mosque, breaking the oath is recommended. If one swears not to eat them, it is disliked. The essential point is that the disliked and the recommended are opposites, and the obligatory and the forbidden are opposites. As for the permissible, it is when the benefit and the harm are equal.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the praise of Ayyub for his patience, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ [38:44]. This extends to others, for whoever is patient is worthy of praise.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the praise of Ayyub with this description: ﴿What an excellent servant﴾. Servitude to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is undoubtedly the completion of freedom. Whoever is more devoted in servitude to Allah is more truly free than one who is the opposite. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said a verse in the Nuniyya:

They fled from the bondage for which they were created,
and were afflicted with the bondage of the self and Satan.

May Allah have mercy on him. That is, a person must submit to something. So these people

They fled from the bondage for which they were created
.............................

which is the worship of Allah.

................................
and were afflicted with the bondage of the self and Satan.

They became slaves to their souls and their devils. The noblest attribute of a human being is to be a servant of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. I ask Allah to make me and you among the righteous servants of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the praise of Ayyub for being one who constantly returns to Allah, the Exalted, through performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was ever-returning﴾. On this basis, this attribute is praise for everyone who is characterized by it, for whoever constantly returns to Allah is praised.

Among the benefits of the verses: affirming causes, and the permissibility of attributing a thing to its known cause, whether known through the senses or through the Sharia. That is, it is permissible to attribute a thing to a cause that is known through the senses or through the Sharia, without attributing it to Allah. So if you say, for example: "I fell into the sea, and if it were not for so-and-so, I would have drowned," this is correct. Why? Because you attributed it to a known cause: so-and-so is the one who pulled you out of the water. But if you said: "I fell into the sea, and if it were not for so-and-so the dead saint, I would have perished," this would be shirk, and in this case it is major shirk.

The point is that attributing a thing to its known cause, without attributing it to Allah, is permissible. Among the examples of this is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about his uncle Abu Talib: "Had it not been for me, he would have been in the lowest level of the Fire"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883) and Muslim (209 / 357), from the hadith of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib.]], "Had it not been for me," so he attributed the thing to its known cause. As for attributing it to an unknown cause, this is a kind of shirk; it may be major, and it may be minor, depending on the circumstances.

* A student: The benefit is what we mentioned. From where did we derive it?
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Indeed, harm has touched me from Shaytan﴾ [Sad 41], He attributed it to the cause.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 45–64 (part 1 of 4):

He says: "And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, possessors of strength and of insight" [38:45]. Remember, O Muhammad, and let the one addressed also remember these noble masters. "Remember Our servants Abraham": "Abraham" is a substitute (badal) for "Our servants," a substitute of part from whole, and what is conjoined to it completes the whole.

"Remember Our servants": the word "servants" here refers to the most special of the special, because it is the servanthood of messengership and prophethood. "Abraham" is the imam of the ḥanīfs, whose creed (millah) we have been commanded to follow: "Then We revealed to you, [Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham" [16:123]. "And Isaac," his son, "and Jacob," his grandson, the son of his son.

("Possessors of strength" means people of strength in worship, "and of insight" means insight in religion.) That is, mention them while indicating their strength in religion, because "aydī" is the plural of "yad" (hand), and what is meant by "yad" here is strength. Likewise "al-abṣār" means insight in the religion of God, because they were messengers, and the people most perceptive (abṣar) in the worship of God are the messengers.

(In one reading, "ʿabdanā Ibrāhīm" is an explanation of it, and what follows is conjoined to "ʿabdanā.") That is, it is read in the plural and in the singular. Is this reading canonical (sabʿiyyah) or irregular (shādhdhah)? It is canonical (sabʿiyyah), because the rule is that when the author (may God have mercy on him) says "and in one reading," it is canonical, and when he says "it was read," it is irregular.

Then He says: "Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality" [38:46]. "Akhlaṣnāhum" means: We cleansed them and chose them, because the purification (ikhlāṣ) of a thing is to remove its impurities until it remains pure, and from it comes the purification of religion for God, which is to remove from it the impurities of polytheism.

His statement "with a pure quality" is clarified by His words: it is "the remembrance of the Abode" (dhikrā al-dār). The author has informed us that "dhikrā" is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "it is remembrance." It is permissible for "dhikrā" to be a substitute for "khāliṣah," or an explanatory apposition to it. What is meant by "al-dār" here is the Hereafter.

("The remembrance of the Abode" is the Hereafter; that is, remembering it and working for it. In another reading it is in the genitive construction: "bi-khāliṣati dhikrā al-dār"), and it is explanatory (lil-bayān), meaning the construction here is explanatory, estimated as "min" (of), because the explanatory genitive is estimated as "min," as you say: "a ring of silver" (khātamu fiḍḍah), i.e., of silver; "a garment of silk" (thawbu khazz), i.e., of silk; "a door of wood" (bābu khashab), i.e., of wood, and so on. He says: "the remembrance of the Abode," meaning the Hereafter; that is, remembering it and working for it.

("And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones" [38:47], the chosen, the good ones; "akhyār" is the plural of "khayyir" with shadda.) "And indeed they" — the pronoun refers to the three: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. "With Us" means with God, and the "withness" here is a withness of rank, not of place, because their rank with God is that they are among these.

"Al-muṣṭafā" is a passive participle meaning "the chosen." Here "al-muṣṭafayn" is a masculine sound plural, but there is a difficulty: it is known that the masculine sound plural has the letter before the yā' kasra, as you say: "al-muslimīn," "al-mu'minīn," "al-qānitīn," "al-ṣābirīn," "al-ṣādiqīn." Here the letter before the yā' is fatḥa, and what is known to have fatḥa before the yā' is the dual, as you say: "al-rajulayn," "al-muslimayn," "al-mu'minayn," and so on. So why was the letter before the yā' given fatḥa here?

The grammarians said: because its original form is "al-muṣṭafā" with an alif, and the alif was deleted because the yā' is sākin and the alif is sākin, so it is deleted, as Ibn Mālik said:

"If two sākin letters meet, make what precedes kasra; and if it is a soft letter, its deletion is deserved."

So now an alif and a yā' have met, and the first of them is deleted, which here is the alif, and the fatḥa remains as evidence of it.

"Al-muṣṭafayn" means: in worship, knowledge and messengership. "Al-akhyār" is the plural of "khayr," and "khayyir" is on the pattern "fayʿil," meaning abundant in good. There is no doubt that these three messengers possessed much good, and from their lineage came noble messengers and some of the best nations; from the lineage of Abraham came the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the best of nations and the most honored of them with God.

"And remember Ismāʿīl and al-Yasaʿ" [38:48]. Ismāʿīl, son of Abraham, is mentioned singly because his lineage differs from the lineage of Isaac and Jacob. The lineage of Isaac and Jacob is the Children of Israel, while the lineage of Ismāʿīl is the Arabs, and for this reason he is singled out.

"Al-Yasaʿ," who is a prophet, and the lām is extra (zāʾidah). If the lām is extra, the original form is "Yasaʿ," and he is a prophet, but a prophet and messenger, because every prophet mentioned in the Qur'an is a messenger.

"Dhā al-Kifl": his prophethood is disputed. It was said that he is a prophet, and "al-kifl" means deed and portion, that is, the one of abundant deed and portion. This is according to the view that he is a messenger. As for the view that he is not a messenger, the author said: "It was said: he took responsibility (kafala) for a hundred prophets who fled to him from killing," and the word "it was said" indicates that it is weak. The apparent meaning of "dhā al-kifl" is: the one of deed, the one of great diligence and vigor.
