("The remembrance of the Abode" is the Hereafter; that is, remembering it and working for it. In another reading it is in the genitive construction: "bi-khāliṣati dhikrā al-dār"), and it is explanatory (lil-bayān), meaning the construction here is explanatory, estimated as "min" (of), because the explanatory genitive is estimated as "min," as you say: "a ring of silver" (khātamu fiḍḍah), i.e., of silver; "a garment of silk" (thawbu khazz), i.e., of silk; "a door of wood" (bābu khashab), i.e., of wood, and so on. He says: "the remembrance of the Abode," meaning the Hereafter; that is, remembering it and working for it.

("And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones" [38:47], the chosen, the good ones; "akhyār" is the plural of "khayyir" with shadda.) "And indeed they" — the pronoun refers to the three: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. "With Us" means with God, and the "withness" here is a withness of rank, not of place, because their rank with God is that they are among these.

"Al-muṣṭafā" is a passive participle meaning "the chosen." Here "al-muṣṭafayn" is a masculine sound plural, but there is a difficulty: it is known that the masculine sound plural has the letter before the yā' kasra, as you say: "al-muslimīn," "al-mu'minīn," "al-qānitīn," "al-ṣābirīn," "al-ṣādiqīn." Here the letter before the yā' is fatḥa, and what is known to have fatḥa before the yā' is the dual, as you say: "al-rajulayn," "al-muslimayn," "al-mu'minayn," and so on. So why was the letter before the yā' given fatḥa here?

The grammarians said: because its original form is "al-muṣṭafā" with an alif, and the alif was deleted because the yā' is sākin and the alif is sākin, so it is deleted, as Ibn Mālik said:

"If two sākin letters meet, make what precedes kasra; and if it is a soft letter, its deletion is deserved."

So now an alif and a yā' have met, and the first of them is deleted, which here is the alif, and the fatḥa remains as evidence of it.

"Al-muṣṭafayn" means: in worship, knowledge and messengership. "Al-akhyār" is the plural of "khayr," and "khayyir" is on the pattern "fayʿil," meaning abundant in good. There is no doubt that these three messengers possessed much good, and from their lineage came noble messengers and some of the best nations; from the lineage of Abraham came the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the best of nations and the most honored of them with God.

"And remember Ismāʿīl and al-Yasaʿ" [38:48]. Ismāʿīl, son of Abraham, is mentioned singly because his lineage differs from the lineage of Isaac and Jacob. The lineage of Isaac and Jacob is the Children of Israel, while the lineage of Ismāʿīl is the Arabs, and for this reason he is singled out.

"Al-Yasaʿ," who is a prophet, and the lām is extra (zāʾidah). If the lām is extra, the original form is "Yasaʿ," and he is a prophet, but a prophet and messenger, because every prophet mentioned in the Qur'an is a messenger.

"Dhā al-Kifl": his prophethood is disputed. It was said that he is a prophet, and "al-kifl" means deed and portion, that is, the one of abundant deed and portion. This is according to the view that he is a messenger. As for the view that he is not a messenger, the author said: "It was said: he took responsibility (kafala) for a hundred prophets who fled to him from killing," and the word "it was said" indicates that it is weak. The apparent meaning of "dhā al-kifl" is: the one of deed, the one of great diligence and vigor.

("And all" means all of them), and on this basis the tanwīn in "kull" is a substitute for a noun (all of them are "from the good ones," "akhyār," the plural of "khayyir" with tathqīl). His statement here, "the plural of khayyir with tathqīl," is the same as his earlier statement "the plural of khayyir with tashdīd."

("This is a remembrance" [38:49] for them, with fine praise here, "and indeed for the righteous is a good return," meaning an abode in the Hereafter.) His statement "This is a remembrance" may bear what the author said, namely that "this is a remembrance" for these masters with fine praise; and it may mean that "this is a remembrance" for the people, that is, a reminder for them, as God said at the beginning of the surah: "Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder" [38:1]. This latter is more preponderant. That is, what is mentioned in this surah is a remembrance for whom? For all people.

Then people are divided into the God-fearing and the non-God-fearing: "and indeed for the righteous," and among them are the messengers, indeed they are the masters of the righteous and at their head, "a good return," that is, an abode. Here He said "la-ḥusna" (a good), and there is a difficulty in it, since it is in the accusative with the lām entering upon it.

* Student: What is the grammatical reason for the emphasis of the subject of "inna"?
* The Shaykh: This is the delayed subject of "inna," and "lil-muttaqīn" is the fronted predicate.

("Gardens of Eden" [38:50] is a substitute or explanatory apposition, "a good return.") For this reason it was put in the accusative, though it is in the accusative by kasra standing in for fatḥa. The "gardens" originally means an orchard with many trees, named so because it conceals (yajunnu) whoever is in it, that is, it covers him. What is meant is the abode of bliss that God has prepared for the righteous in the Hereafter. "'Adn" means residence, that is, the gardens in which their inhabitants reside, from which they do not move, and which they do not desire to leave; and each one of the people of Paradise sees that no one has merit over him, and this is the completeness of bliss, because when a person sees that another is better than him, he belittles what God has given him. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Look at those who are below you, and do not look at those who are above you." [Reported by Muslim (2963) from Abū Hurayrah.]

He says: ("Gardens of Eden, whose doors are opened for them" [38:50]), "mufattaḥah" (opened, in the feminine intensive form) rather than "maftūḥah" (opened), because of the multitude of those who open, or the multitude of doors, or both. According to the first, the multitude of openers means they have many servants whose task is to open the doors for them; according to the second, it indicates that its doors are many because of the multitude of those who enter it. It is known that the principal great doors of Paradise are how many? Eight. But there are chambers in the middle of Paradise with rivers flowing beneath them, which have doors, and so the doors are opened for them.

"Reclining therein" [38:51]; that is, in these gardens. Reclining indicates calm, tranquility and freedom from anxiety, and indicates that the person is one of authority who is served and does not serve. His words "therein" mean in the gardens.

The author explained what they recline upon, saying: "on couches," as stated in another verse: "Therein they call for abundant fruit and drink" [38:51]. "Yadʿūna" means they ask for, that is, they say: bring fruit, "abundant," abundant in kind or in individual items, or both? Abundant in kind and in individual items; that is, many kinds and likewise many items, so that whatever you ask for, you obtain it.

"And drink": God has explained that its kinds or types are four: "Therein are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey" [47:15]. These are four kinds of the drink of Paradise.

But notice that these names differ from what is in this world with a great difference. That is, do not think that the water is like the water of this world, or the honey like the honey of this world, or the milk like the milk of this world, or the wine like the wine of this world. No, they differ greatly, because of God's words: "No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes" [32:17]. If it did not differ, we would know this. God said in the sacred hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (3244) and Muslim (2824) from Abū Hurayrah.] O God, make us among its people.

"And with them are those restraining their glances" [38:52]. "Qāṣirāt al-ṭarf": the author said: "withholding the eyes." "Al-ṭarf" means the gaze; that is, they restrict their gaze to their husbands. This is one meaning. The second meaning: restraining the glances of their husbands, so that the husbands do not look at others. The difference between them is clear, but the wording is suitable for both: they restrain their own glances, looking at no one other than their husbands, and they restrain the glances of their husbands, so that the husbands do not look at other women.

Are the women of this world like this? Not at all. When a woman goes out to the market, she begins looking at the men and comparing this man with her husband. Likewise when a man goes out to the market, some people look at women and compare the woman with his wife, and you find that if he sees a woman more beautiful than his wife, his heart becomes occupied with her and he turns away from his wife and loses interest in her. This is from the great wisdom behind the obligation of covering the face. But fools are ignorant. From the great wisdom is that when a man does not see a woman, his gaze does not change regarding his wife; but if he sees a woman like the sun while his wife is like the Suhā star, his heart becomes attached to this woman who is like the sun, and he loses interest in this woman who is like the Suhā, and hardly sees her. Thus it is from the wisdom of God Mighty and Majestic that women were obligated to cover their faces.

("Restraining the glances, of equal age" [38:52], of the same age, and they are young women, daughters of thirty-three years.) "Atrāb" means that they are of one age, young women, daughters of thirty-three years. Likewise the people of Paradise enter Paradise as sons of thirty-three years, and none of them changes; each remains as he is.

As for their being "atrāb," it may be said that they are of equal age, equal in beauty, and equal in everything, so that a person does not incline toward one who surpasses the others, and his gaze upon them is on equal terms.

God said: ("This" which is mentioned, "is what you are promised," in the third person and the second person by iltifāt [shift], "for the Day of Reckoning") — "This is what you are promised" — the author said: "in the third person and the second person"; the second person is "mā tūʿadūn," the third person is "mā yūʿadūn," and both readings are canonical. The author said: "by iltifāt" (shift). Which of them is the shift: the third person or the second person?

* Student: The second person.
* Another student: The third person.
* The Shaykh: The second person, the third person; not the second person nor the third person, the second and the third person, what do we say?
* Students: The second person.
* The Shaykh: "This is a remembrance, and indeed for the righteous is a good return. Gardens of Eden, whose doors are opened for them" [38:49–50]: "them" is third person. "Reclining therein, they call for" [38:51]: "they call" is third person. "And with them" [38:52] is third person. So where is the iltifāt? In the second person: "This is what you are promised" [38:53]; that is, it is said to them: "This is what you are promised," with the pronoun of address; and with the pronoun of the third person it becomes a report from God Mighty and Majestic that what is mentioned is what they are promised on the Day of Resurrection.

("For the Day of Reckoning," that is, because of it.) This is what the author followed: that the lām is causal. But the correct view is that the lām is temporal, as in His words: "So divorce them for their waiting period" [65:1]. So the lām here means "in" (fī), because it is temporal: that is, this is what you are promised on that day, the Day of Reckoning, which is the Day of Resurrection, and it is called "the Day of Reckoning" because people are reckoned on their deeds in it.

He says: "Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end" [38:54]. "Indeed this" refers to what has been mentioned of the bliss of Paradise. "Is Our provision": Our gift. The lām in "la-rizqunā" is for emphasis. "Mā lahu min nafād": "min nafād" is a delayed subject, and the extra "min," extra in wording and extra in meaning, entered upon it; that is, "it has no end," meaning it has no cessation. Is "mā" here Ḥijāzī or do the Tamīmīs and Ḥijāzīs agree on it?

* Student: They agree.
* The Shaykh: They agree. Why? Because the predicate is fronted, and "mā" is not Ḥijāzī except with the order, according to Ibn Mālik's saying:

"... with the persistence of negation and order is established."

So we say: "nafād" is the subject in both dialects. The author said: ("mā lahu min nafād," that is, cessation, and the sentence is a circumstantial clause from "rizqunā," or a second predicate of "inna"; that is, permanently or permanent.) A very concise statement.

("The sentence is a circumstantial clause from 'rizqunā'"), and on this basis the meaning is: "mā lahu min nafād," that is, according to the author's explanation, permanently or permanent? Permanently. Or we say: a second predicate: "Indeed this is Our provision, indeed this has no end," and the estimate is: permanent or permanently? Permanent. So in the sentence there is a chiasmus (laff wa-nashr); is it ordered or unordered? The circumstantial clause from "rizqunā" puts the circumstance first, or another second predicate, namely "permanently," the predicate is delayed, so the order is ordered.

He said: ("This" which is mentioned, "is for the believers," "and indeed for the tyrants") — "This" is a subject which must have a predicate, whose predicate is omitted, as the author estimated, for whom? For the believers. The author says "for the believers," but the correct view is that we estimate "for the God-fearing," because God said: "This is a remembrance, and indeed for the righteous is a good return." So it is better to say: this is for the God-fearing.

As for others, he said: ("And indeed for the tyrants" is a resumed statement.) "And indeed for the tyrants": "tāghīn" is the plural of "ṭāghiyah," and the tyrant (ṭāghī) is one who exceeds the limit. The human limit is to be a servant of God, obeying His command and avoiding His prohibition; whoever does not obey the command is a tyrant, and whoever commits the prohibition is a tyrant. "Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed" [20:43]. So tyranny is exceeding the limit, and the limit for a human is the worship of God; whoever exceeds this limit, by opposing the command or committing the prohibition, is a tyrant.

If someone says: What is the evidence that tughyān means exceeding the limit?
We say: His words: "Indeed, when the water overflowed [tagha al-mā'], We carried you in the sailing ship" [69:11]; that is, it exceeded its limit.

("This, and indeed for the tyrants," is a resumed statement.) "Evil return" [38:55]: that is, the worst return. "Sharra" is in the accusative as the delayed subject of "inna," which is what? "Evil return." He said: "Hell, they will burn therein" [38:56]; this is an explanatory apposition for "evil return," and it is the Fire: Jahannam. The Fire was named by this name because it includes gloom (jahmah) due to its blackness, since there is no light in it, and the depth of its bottom, and we seek refuge with God.

The Prophet ﷺ once heard, while he and his Companions were in Madinah, a thud, meaning the fall of something. He said: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "This is a stone that was thrown into the Fire seventy years ago, and it has been falling into it until now, and has only now reached its bottom." [Narrated by Muslim (2844/31) from Abu Hurayrah.] Seventy years, and it is a large stone with a great sound, falling into the Fire. So its depth is very great, and for this reason it has become dark and black, and Allah forbid. It has also been said that "Jahannam" is not Arabic, and that its origin in Persian is "kahnam," but it was Arabized and became "Jahannam."
* Student: "Kahnam" in Persian?
* The Shaykh: In Persian, yes. And on this view, what we said, that it is derived from "jahama" (darkness and remoteness), does not apply to us; it is then said to be a proper name for the Fire, not derived. Whatever the case, it is one of the names of the Fire; we seek refuge in Allah from it.

﴿يَصْلَوْنَهَا﴾ is a description of "Jahannam," or rather a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because "Jahannam" is definite, and a clause following a definite noun is a circumstantial clause. ﴿يَصْلَوْنَهَا﴾ means: they enter it. But it is not enough to say "they enter it"; rather ﴿يَصْلَوْنَهَا﴾ means they are tormented by its heat (ṣalā), which is its intense heat.

(﴿فَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾ the bed.) As Allah the Exalted says: ﴿أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ الْأَرْضَ مِهَادًا﴾ [An-Naba' 6], and in another verse: ﴿الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ فِرَاشًا﴾ [Al-Baqarah 22]. So "al-mihad" means the bed. ﴿فَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾ means: this is it, ﴿فَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾, because its spreading beneath them is harsh, and its covering is harsh, ﴿لَهُمْ مِنْ فَوْقِهِمْ ظُلَلٌ مِنَ النَّارِ وَمِنْ تَحْتِهِمْ ظُلَلٌ﴾ [Az-Zumar 16]; we seek refuge in Allah.

(﴿هَذَا﴾ [Sad 57], i.e., the punishment implied by what follows, ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾.) It is also permissible for ﴿هَذَا﴾ to be the subject, with the predicate omitted, i.e., "this is what is theirs," ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾. The lām in His saying ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ is the lām of command, and the evidence that it is the lām of command and not the lām of purpose is that it is vowelled with sukūn after the fā', and the lām of command is vowelled with sukūn after fā', wāw and thumma.

﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ means: let them be burned by its heat. Being burned by its heat is "tasting." And the tasting of each thing is according to its nature: in food and drink a person tastes it with the palate of the mouth, while the Fire is tasted by what? By its heat, at whatever part of the body; and cold likewise is tasted by its sting at whatever part of the body.

(﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ حَمِيمٌ﴾ i.e., scalding, burning water, ﴿وَغَسَّاقٌ﴾ with light and emphatic pronunciation.) That is, ﴿غَسَاقٌ﴾ is the light pronunciation, ﴿غَسَّاقٌ﴾ the emphatic pronunciation, (what flows from the pus of the people of the Fire); we seek refuge in Allah.

Now we say: ﴿هَذَا﴾ is the subject, and ﴿حَمِيمٌ وَغَسَّاقٌ﴾ is the predicate and its conjoined element. We have thus departed from what we mentioned before, namely: this is what is theirs of punishment, where we placed the predicate first: "what is theirs of punishment." We have found it better to make ﴿حَمِيمٌ﴾ the predicate and ﴿وَغَسَّاقٌ﴾ conjoined to it, and the clause ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ becomes a parenthetical clause between the subject and the predicate, to hasten their humiliation, since the saying "let them taste the punishment" is undoubtedly a humiliation. Because of this haste, "this" (﴿هَذَا﴾) was placed before the predicate; i.e., the phrase ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ was placed first, while the original order of the speech is: this is scalding water and pus, so let them taste it.

Consider the drink: ﴿حَمِيمٌ﴾ is water that is hot, and its heat is not gentle or light. ﴿وَإِنْ يَسْتَغِيثُوا يُغَاثُوا بِمَاءٍ كَالْمُهْلِ﴾ (...) oil, ﴿يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ﴾ [Al-Kahf 29]. First: this drink does not come to them easily. When does it come to them? After they become intensely thirsty, then they call for help, asking Allah to relieve them of this thirst. And when they are given this water, ﴿كَالْمُهْلِ يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ﴾ [Al-Kahf 29], when it approaches their faces to drink it, it roasts them. The scholars said: the flesh of the face falls off. Then when they drink it into their bellies, ﴿وَسُقُوا مَاءً حَمِيمًا فَقَطَّعَ أَمْعَاءَهُمْ﴾ [Muhammad 15], it cuts their insides and their outsides, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Compare this drink with the drink of the people of Paradise: ﴿أَنْهَارٌ مِنْ مَاءٍ غَيْرِ آسِنٍ وَأَنْهَارٌ مِنْ لَبَنٍ لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ طَعْمُهُ وَأَنْهَارٌ مِنْ خَمْرٍ لَذَّةٍ لِلشَّارِبِينَ وَأَنْهَارٌ مِنْ عَسَلٍ مُصَفًّى﴾ [Muhammad 15], and yet they drink whenever they wish. They direct these rivers as they please, without digging channels and without effort; that is, they do not build a wall to stop the water so that it does not flow to right and left, nor do they dig. Ibn al-Qayyim said in the Nuniyyah:

Its rivers flow without a trench, glory be to Him who holds them back from overflowing.

Al-Ghassaq, and we seek refuge in Allah, as soon as you hear its meaning you recoil: the pus of the people of the Fire, the pus that flows from their bodies from their burning. This is a kind of their drink, so their drink is either scalding water that roasts the faces and cuts the bowels, or the pus of the people of the Fire: ﴿يَتَجَرَّعُهُ وَلَا يَكَادُ يُسِيغُهُ وَيَأْتِيهِ الْمَوْتُ مِنْ كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَمَا هُوَ بِمَيِّتٍ وَمِنْ وَرَائِهِ عَذَابٌ غَلِيظٌ﴾ [Ibrahim 17].

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: (﴿وَآخَرُ﴾ [Sad 58], in the plural and singular forms.) ﴿آخَرُ﴾ is singular, ﴿أُخَرُ﴾ is plural; there are therefore two readings, both from the seven canonical readings.

﴿مِنْ شَكْلِهِ﴾ [Sad 58], i.e., of its kind: (i.e., like what was mentioned of scalding water and pus, ﴿أَزْوَاجٌ﴾ i.e., kinds; i.e., their punishment is of various types.)

﴿آخَرُ مِنْ شَكْلِهِ﴾: of its kind, or ﴿أُخَرُ﴾ of its kind, ﴿أَزْوَاجٌ﴾: kinds of punishment by which they are tormented as Allah the Mighty and Majestic willed, and they are humiliated to the utmost degree; they are rebuked and reproached, then they are given hope of coming out. The Fire rises with them until, when they approach its gates, ﴿كُلَّمَا أَرَادُوا أَنْ يَخْرُجُوا مِنْهَا أُعِيدُوا فِيهَا﴾ [As-Sajdah 20]. And this is from the severity of the torment, my brothers. If a prisoner who is imprisoned approaches the door thinking he will leave, and then is sent back, this is more painful for him than if he remained in his place. They are subjected to great varieties of punishment that do not occur to the mind nor come to the imagination. O Allah, save us from the Fire.

(﴿وَآخَرُ مِنْ شَكْلِهِ أَزْوَاجٌ﴾ i.e., kinds; i.e., their punishment is of various types. And it will be said to them when they enter the Fire, along with their followers: ﴿هَذَا فَوْجٌ﴾ [Sad 59], a company, ﴿مُقْتَحِمٌ﴾ rushing in, ﴿مَعَكُمْ﴾ into the Fire with force. The leaders will say: ﴿لَا مَرْحَبًا بِهِمْ﴾, i.e., there is no welcome for them, ﴿إِنَّهُمْ صَالُو النَّارِ﴾. ﴿قَالُوا﴾ i.e., the followers: ﴿بَلْ أَنْتُمْ لَا مَرْحَبًا بِكُمْ أَنْتُمْ قَدَّمْتُمُوهُ﴾ i.e., disbelief, ﴿لَنَا فَبِئْسَ الْقَرَارُ﴾.)

Look: ﴿الْأَخِلَّاءُ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَعْضُهُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ إِلَّا الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 67]. See how the enmity among the people of the Fire is: ﴿كُلَّمَا دَخَلَتْ أُمَّةٌ لَعَنَتْ أُخْتَهَا﴾ [Al-A'raf 38]. Likewise, criminals in this world who support one another will on the Day of Resurrection become enemies. No one has any loyalty in the Hereafter except the one who was God-fearing; these are the ones whose loyalty remains. As for those who were not God-fearing, although they were allies in this world, their loyalty in the Hereafter will completely cease.

Look at the verse ﴿هَذَا فَوْجٌ مُقْتَحِمٌ مَعَكُمْ﴾. ﴿هَذَا فَوْجٌ﴾: al-fawj is a group, and it usually refers to a large group. ﴿مُقْتَحِمٌ مَعَكُمْ﴾ means: entering with difficulty, since iqtiḥām requires great crowding, as in ﴿فَلَا اقْتَحَمَ الْعَقَبَةَ﴾ [Al-Balad 11], i.e., he climbed it with difficulty.

These enter the Fire with severe crowding; so it is ﴿فَوْجٌ مُقْتَحِمٌ مَعَكُمْ﴾, meaning it will be said to them, and they will say: ﴿لَا مَرْحَبًا بِهِمْ﴾, meaning: we do not want them; we disown them, and our hearts and our places have no room for them. The word "marḥaban" derives from "raḥbah," which means spaciousness. So he says: ﴿لَا مَرْحَبًا بِهِمْ﴾, meaning: we do not welcome them and do not want them; rather we reject them utterly, ﴿إِنَّهُمْ صَالُو النَّارِ﴾. ﴿إِنَّهُمْ﴾ i.e., these who rushed in with us, ﴿صَالُو النَّارِ﴾. (﴿قَالُوا﴾ i.e., the followers) say to whom? To the leaders: ﴿بَلْ أَنْتُمْ لَا مَرْحَبًا بِكُمْ﴾ [Sad 60]. Note that ﴿بَلْ﴾ here is a rebuttal: they refute their words ﴿لَا مَرْحَبًا بِكُمْ﴾ and say: we reject this speech and do not accept it; rather, it is you to whom there is no welcome. ﴿أَنْتُمْ قَدَّمْتُمُوهُ لَنَا﴾: meaning, you brought disbelief to us, made its path easy for us, and made it attractive in our souls until we followed you, ﴿فَبِئْسَ الْقَرَارُ﴾ (for us and for you, the Fire). We seek refuge in Allah. Each of them now disowns the other.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: (﴿قَالُوا رَبَّنَا مَنْ قَدَّمَ لَنَا هَذَا فَزِدْهُ عَذَابًا ضِعْفًا﴾ [Sad 61], i.e., double the punishment for his disbelief, ﴿فِي النَّارِ﴾.) ﴿مَنْ قَدَّمَ لَنَا هَذَا﴾: what is the referent?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. The referent of ﴿مَنْ قَدَّمَ لَنَا هَذَا﴾ is disbelief; i.e., whoever brought disbelief to us, namely the leaders.

﴿فَزِدْهُ عَذَابًا ضِعْفًا فِي النَّارِ﴾. ﴿ضِعْفًا﴾: i.e., an increase over the punishment of the original offense; that is, punish them for their disbelief, and punish them for having brought disbelief to us. But is this in their hands? No, it is not in their hands; for each person is repaid for what he did. Did these leaders force the followers to follow them? Never, they did not force them. ﴿وَإِذْ يَتَحَاجُّونَ فِي النَّارِ فَيَقُولُ الضُّعَفَاءُ لِلَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا إِنَّا كُنَّا لَكُمْ تَبَعًا فَهَلْ أَنْتُمْ مُغْنُونَ عَنَّا نَصِيبًا مِنَ النَّارِ﴾ [Ghafir 47]. What did they say? ﴿قَالَ الَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا إِنَّا كُلٌّ فِيهَا إِنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ حَكَمَ بَيْنَ الْعِبَادِ﴾ [Ghafir 48], He judged among the servants with His justice, recompensing each one of them according to what he deserves.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿وَقَالُوا مَا لَنَا لَا نَرَى رِجَالًا كُنَّا نَعُدُّهُمْ مِنَ الْأَشْرَارِ﴾ [Sad 62]. ﴿قَالُوا﴾: the author says: (i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah, who are in the Fire). The correct view is that what is meant is all disbelievers. The disbelievers see the believers as misguided: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أَجْرَمُوا كَانُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَضْحَكُونَ (29) وَإِذَا مَرُّوا بِهِمْ يَتَغَامَزُونَ (30) وَإِذَا انْقَلَبُوا إِلَى أَهْلِهِمُ انْقَلَبُوا فَكِهِينَ (31) وَإِذَا رَأَوْهُمْ قَالُوا إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ لَضَالُّونَ﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29-32]. This is not specific to the disbelievers of Makkah; all disbelievers until today see the believers as wicked and misguided, and describe them as tyrants who spread corruption on earth. The reality is the reverse: the tyrants who spread corruption on earth, the misguided, the oppressors and transgressors, are the disbelievers, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَالْكَافِرُونَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 254]. No one is more corrupt, more oppressive, or more tyrannical than the disbeliever, because he enjoys the blessings of Allah and wars against Allah by disbelieving in Him. They, the disbelievers, say: ﴿مَا لَنَا لَا نَرَى رِجَالًا كُنَّا نَعُدُّهُمْ مِنَ الْأَشْرَارِ﴾. ﴿نَعُدُّهُمْ﴾: in this world; ﴿مِنَ الْأَشْرَارِ﴾: we counted them, by our belief, among the wicked.

﴿أَتَّخَذْنَاهُمْ سِخْرِيًّا﴾ [Sad 63]: i.e., in this world. ﴿أَمْ زَاغَتْ عَنْهُمُ الْأَبْصَارُ﴾, so that we did not see them. Some of them say to each other: O people, ﴿مَا لَنَا لَا نَرَى رِجَالًا كُنَّا نَعُدُّهُمْ مِنَ الْأَشْرَارِ﴾: so-and-so and so-and-so, whom we counted among the wicked. Did we take them in this world as objects of mockery, mocking them and saying "You are the evil ones, you are the tyrants," and the like, while they were not so? Or were they, as we imagined them in this world and counted them among the wicked, but our eyes have now turned away from them in the Fire, and they are now in the Fire while our sight has strayed from them? See how the possibilities go: they are saying, did we take them as mockery in this world, claiming they were wicked when they were not? That is one possibility, and if they were not wicked they would not enter the Fire. Or were they truly wicked, and our saying that they were wicked was a serious statement, and they are now in the Fire, but our eyes have strayed from them? Which is the answer? The first is the truth, not the second.

Therefore Allah the Mighty and Majestic said of them: (﴿أَتَّخَذْنَاهُمْ سِخْرِيًّا﴾ with the sīn vowelled with ḍamma and with kasra; i.e., we used to mock them in this world, and the yā' is the yā' of relative ascription; i.e., are they absent? ﴿أَمْ زَاغَتْ﴾ turned away, ﴿عَنْهُمُ الْأَبْصَارُ﴾ so that we did not see them.)

The answer is to say: you took them as objects of mockery, you ridiculed them, mocked them, and branded them with fault and evil, while they were innocent of it.

He said: (﴿أَمْ زَاغَتْ عَنْهُمُ الْأَبْصَارُ﴾ i.e., their eyes, so we did not see them; and they were the poor among the Muslims, like ʿAmmar, Bilal, Suhayb and Salman.) This is based on the view that the speakers are the disbelievers of Makkah. But if we take the statement in its generality, then every era has its people.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿إِنَّ ذَلِكَ لَحَقٌّ﴾ its occurrence is necessary, and it is ﴿تَخَاصُمُ أَهْلِ النَّارِ﴾ as previously mentioned.) ﴿إِنَّ ذَلِكَ﴾: i.e., the referent of all that has been mentioned of the mutual dispute of the people of the Fire. ﴿لَحَقٌّ﴾: i.e., a fixed and certain matter. This is an emphasis on the report of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, although all of Allah's report is truth, sincerity and certainty. Is "truth" here meant as sincerity or as justice? As sincerity, since it is a report about something that will occur.

And His saying ﴿تَخَاصُمُ أَهْلِ النَّارِ﴾ [Sad 64] is an apposition or explanatory appositive to ﴿لَحَقٌّ﴾. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, took it as the predicate of an omitted subject, saying: (i.e., it is ﴿تَخَاصُمُ أَهْلِ النَّارِ﴾ as previously mentioned): the followers dispute with the leaders. And Allah knows best.

* Student: May Allah reward you well. We mentioned that the women in Paradise and the men are thirty-three years old. But in this world, a woman of thirty-three is not praised at that age; the younger she is, the more desirable she is to the husband. In this world, what is the wisdom of...?
* The Shaykh: By Allah, in any case, if you want to be a sixteen-year-old, you will be a sixteen-year-old, since ﴿فِيهَا مَا تَشْتَهِيهِ الْأَنْفُسُ وَتَلَذُّ الْأَعْيُنُ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 71]. The conditions of the Hereafter are different. If someone came who was sixty cubits tall and seven cubits wide, would he be desirable to people?
* The Student: As of now?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Not desirable. But in Paradise, the people of Paradise have this description: a man sixty cubits tall and seven cubits wide. This body of this size is not familiar in this world, so thirty-three years is a small and suitable age relative to these sizes.
* The Student: So this is due to the size?
* The Shaykh: Regarding size; what matters is proportion. There is no doubt that this is the best thing.
* Student: What is the evidence for thirty-three years?
* The Shaykh: As for the first, it is in the Sahih [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3327) and Muslim (2834/15) from Abu Hurayrah], and I do not know what the author mentioned, but it is consistent with the age of a man.
* Student: (...) If it is said, O Shaykh, that it has been abrogated (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not abrogated. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: it is permissible to flog a person a hundred lashes with a palm-stalk or the like.
* Student: O Shaykh, the hadith: "Whoever swears an oath and sees something better than it..." [Narrated by Muslim (1650/12) from Abu Hurayrah] (...)?
* The Shaykh: And here?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, we say: strike her. Gentleness is better here, because the aim is the upbringing and discipline of the woman, and this is good; but if we said: expiate and do not strike, the purpose would be lost.
* Student: O Shaykh, interpretation (ta'wil), if the person is neither an oppressor nor oppressed?
* The Shaykh: The correct view is that it is prohibited if there is no benefit (maslahah).
* Student: The benefit that returns to the same state, O Shaykh?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 38, verses 45–64 (part 3 of 4)

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. Even if it returns to him, the point is that there is a benefit in it, because sometimes it is meant purely as misdirection, even about something that is not an injustice, and sometimes there is a benefit in it.
* Student: (...) The one who is made to swear sees it otherwise?
* The Shaykh: It does not matter. If a person came, for example, asking me, "How much is your money?" and I said, "My money is, for example, ten," he understands it to be ten riyals, while I have ten million. That is acceptable, and there is nothing wrong with it, since it serves a benefit.
* The Student: Perhaps it becomes apparent afterwards, and he considers it a lie?
* The Shaykh: It does not matter, because I have not wronged him. Perhaps if I say, "I have ten million," he says, "Come on, give me nine million, nine hundred thousand and ninety now." That is a problem, because he would take my money while I watch.

It is said that a man came to Imam Ahmad asking about al-Marwadhi, one of his companions, while al-Marwadhi was present at the lesson. So (Imam Ahmad) said: "Is al-Marwadhi not here? And what is al-Marwazi doing here?" He meant: in this hand of his. What is the purpose of it? Is it a benefit or not? A benefit, there is no (...). There is neither injustice nor a wronged party in it.

* Student: This sentence (...).
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) This is the verse: ﴿And indeed for the righteous is a good return (49), Gardens of Eden, whose doors are opened for them﴾ [Surah Sad 49–50]. ﴿Gardens﴾ is a substitute (badal) of what?
* The Student: A substitute of ﴿a good return﴾, from ﴿good﴾, and ﴿good﴾...?
* The Student: And ﴿good﴾ is a noun.
* The Shaykh: But it is a subject (mubtada').
* The Student: Yes, so this does not allow a badal; I follow.
* The Shaykh: As long as it is the ism of inna, which is one of the nawasikh (particles that change the sentence's grammatical state), it can take a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative). One may say, "Inna Zaydan qā'imun munībān" ("Indeed Zayd is standing, penitent"), and it is permissible to say "qā'iman munībān" is a ḥāl of "Zayd," not of the hidden pronoun in "qā'im."
* Student: And from ﴿lahum﴾?
* The Shaykh: Because the discussion is that the pronoun here is definite, and a ḥāl can be taken from it.
* Student: His saying ﴿reclining (muttaki'īn)﴾.
* The Shaykh: And "lahum" is a pronoun.
* The Student: And it is attached to the omitted element.
* The Shaykh: Even if it were; but the discussion is that the pronoun here is definite, and a ḥāl can be taken from it.
* Student: His saying ﴿reclining﴾ (...). So is the ḥāl (...)?
* The Shaykh: There is no doubt, it is not always so. The ḥāl may be changing, and it may be fixed.
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).
* The Student: Outside the Quran?
* The Shaykh: Outside the Quran, according to the situation.
* Student: Can it be understood from this verse that ﴿Ismail, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl﴾ are with the righteous in the Gardens of Eden?
* The Shaykh: All the righteous. Ismail, al-Yasa', Dhul-Kifl, Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and others.
* The Student: Are the righteous not in the highest gardens, in the highest Firdaws?
* The Shaykh: They are all righteous.
* The Student: But Paradise has degrees?
* The Shaykh: Degrees are known. If you say, "So-and-so is in the palace," this one is in the top of the palace, this one is at its bottom, and this one is in its middle.
* The Student: So the Gardens of Eden include these gardens.
* The Shaykh: All the gardens (...).

* * *

* Student: ﴿Say: I am only a warner, and there is no god except Allah, the One, the Subduer (65), Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾ [Surah Sad 65–66].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Let us take the benefits of what has passed.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And remember Our servants Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, possessors of strength and insight (45). Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: remembrance of the Home (46). And indeed they are, with Us, among the chosen and the excellent﴾ [Surah Sad 45–47].

* From the benefits of these two verses: praise of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub for being people of strength in the worship of Allah and insight into the religion of Allah.
* And from the benefits of this verse, and likewise what is similar to it that has passed: that it is necessary to mention the people of goodness with praise, because in that there are two benefits.
  * The first benefit: reviving the remembrance of these people, so that their virtue becomes clear and they are supplicated for.
  * The second benefit: following them and emulating them in what they were upon, for which they deserved praise.
  Pay attention to this: two benefits. The first: clarifying their virtue and reviving their memory so that one prays for them. The second: taking them as models and emulating them.
* And from the benefits of these two noble verses: Allah the Exalted purified these people with a pure quality, which is remembrance of the Hereafter, such that they are not immersed in the luxury of this world.
* Following from this benefit: whoever Allah has blessed with this quality, which is remembrance of the Hereafter, this is a matter that deserves praise for him, and the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, deserves thanks for it, since He did not make him among those who are folded into the path of the people of this world.
* And from the benefits of these two verses: Allah the Exalted has servants who are chosen. This is shown by His saying ﴿And indeed they are, with Us, among the chosen﴾, because ﴿min﴾ here is either for the category (jins) or for partiality (tab'īd), and it clearly indicates that Allah the Exalted has chosen servants.
* And from its benefits: if the doer has ranks, then the deed also has ranks, because the doer only attains ranks according to his deeds.
  * Following from this benefit is evidence for the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) that faith increases and decreases.
* And from the benefits of these two verses: Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub are among those chosen.
* And from its benefits: those whom Allah has chosen are people of goodness and virtue, by His saying ﴿the chosen, the excellent﴾. He placed the excellent (or the good ones) as a consequence of being chosen.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And remember Ismail, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl, and each is among the excellent (48). This is a reminder. And indeed for the righteous is a good return﴾ [Surah Sad 48–49], to the end.

* In this: praise of Ismail, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl, because Allah commanded that they be mentioned in order to praise them.
* And in it: the virtue of these three messengers: Ismail, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl.
* And in it: that Allah has excellent servants, among whom are these three, by His saying ﴿and each is among the excellent﴾.
* And from its benefits, like the one before it: Allah the Exalted has favour upon some servants which He withholds from others, since He makes these among the chosen excellent ones, while the others are the opposite.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿This is a reminder. And indeed for the righteous﴾, to the end.

* From the benefits of these verses: the Noble Quran is a reminder (dhikr). Allah is remembered through its recitation. It is a reminder by which a person remembers his return and his livelihood. It is a reminder by which he reminds others. We have mentioned this at the beginning of the surah.
* And from the benefits of these verses: giving glad tidings to the righteous that they have a good return, that is, a good place of return. In contrast, those who are not righteous have an evil return, because when Allah ascribes to a thing one of the attributes, He ascribes its opposite to it when that attribute is absent.

If someone says: Why do you not say that if this attribute is absent and the opposite attribute is not established, then why do you not make him intermediate between these two, so that he deserves neither the praise attached to the attribute nor the censure that comes with its opposite?

The answer to that: There is no doubt that matters have two extremes and a middle. The two extremes are opposites, and the middle lies between them. However, the Book and the Sunnah have indicated that righteousness and its opposite are not an extreme and a middle; rather they are two opposing extremes, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Surah Yunus 32]. So when a good return is established for the righteous, then an evil return is for others, and we do not place anything intermediate here, because there is no intermediate between faith and disbelief, or between righteousness and wickedness.

* And from the benefits of these verses: the encouragement to righteousness, through mentioning its reward. Encouragement to a thing is by commanding it, as is evident, and by warning against leaving it, and by praising its doing. In short, the ways of encouraging something are varied, and among them is mentioning its good return.
* And from the benefits of these verses: the affirmation of Gardens for these people, and that they are the good return, by His saying ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. There is no doubt that the best return that humans return to is the Gardens, for in them is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Every believer strives only to reach this great goal.
* From its benefits: that the Gardens are an abode of permanent residence, by His saying ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. The people there are residents who do not depart from them, residents who do not desire any alternative to them. So there are two kinds of residence: residence without departure from them, and the second: the resident does not desire any alternative to them, seeing that it is the place of residence and the most noble place. That is because if he saw that someone else was more noble than him, his bliss would not be complete, because he would see himself as deficient. This is in contrast to the people of the Fire, each of whom sees that no one suffers more than he does, because if he saw someone suffering more than himself he would be consoled by him. Rather, on the contrary, he sees himself as the one suffering most. The people of Paradise do not see that any one of them has a more complete bliss in a way that surpasses him; rather he sees himself in the most complete state of bliss, so that his bliss is not spoiled for him.
* And from the benefits of the verses: that Paradise has doors, by His saying ﴿whose doors are opened for them﴾.
* And from its benefits: the abundance of attendants, which is derived from His saying ﴿opened﴾, and He did not say "open." So the doors are opened for them to welcome them. Whenever they approach a room, the doors are opened for them.
* And from the benefits of these verses: the people of Paradise ask for whatever fruit they desire, by His saying ﴿They call therein for abundant fruit﴾. And in Surah al-Dukhan: ﴿They call therein for every fruit, secure﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan 55].
* And from its benefits, that is, these verses: the people of Paradise have drink, and they call for every kind of drink therein. It has passed in our tafsir (exegesis) that the types of drink are four.
* And from the benefits of these verses: that in Paradise there are pure, chaste spouses who have reached the utmost in beauty, by His saying ﴿And with them are those of restrained gaze﴾ [Surah Sad 52].
* And from its benefits: that these women of restrained gaze have excellent characters and are good, with no rebelliousness (nushūz) at all, by His saying ﴿And with them are those of﴾. In this world, a wife is sometimes with you, and sometimes she becomes upset and goes to her family, so she is not with you. But in Paradise their spouses are always with them. There is no rebelliousness, no anger, and no displeasure, but rather good character as is fitting.
* And from its benefits: the perfect chastity of these women, for they are "those of restrained gaze" toward their husbands, not looking at anyone other than their husbands.
* And in it: the perfect beauty of these women, because they are ﴿those of restrained gaze﴾, that is, they restrict the gazes of their husbands to themselves, so the husband does not look at anyone else, since she has filled his eye and gladdened his heart.
* And from its benefits: that these women, or these spouses, are equals in age and character, so that one of them does not become jealous of the other for being more beautiful or older, or anything similar. This is by His saying ﴿of equal age﴾.
* And from its benefits: that they are addressed with what pleases them and brings light into their hearts, by His saying ﴿This is what you were promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾. This is the opposite of the people of the Fire, who are rebuked: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers with clear proofs?﴾ [Surah Ghafir 50], and similar rebuke. As for these, joy enters their hearts, and it is said to them: ﴿This is what you were promised﴾, which you have taken, reached, and gathered.
* And from the benefits of these verses: the affirmation of the Day of Resurrection, and that it is the Day of Reckoning, by His saying ﴿for the Day of Reckoning﴾.
* And from its benefits: urging people to work, because whenever a person remembers that he will be called to account for his deeds, he will be eager and strive in his work, so that he is not held accountable for anything that he has done.
* And from the benefits of these verses: that these Gardens promised to the righteous are a favour and a bounty from Allah, by His saying ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision﴾.
* And from its benefits: that this provision never runs out and never ends. The fruit is available at all times, the flesh of birds at all times, the drink at all times, the spouses at all times. There is no season of summer without fruit or season of winter without fruit. Everything has no end.
* And from the benefits of these verses: the perfection of the Quran in teaching and conveying, and that it is "mathānī" (oft-repeated): when the righteous and their reward are mentioned, the criminals and their punishment are mentioned. This is why He said: ﴿This, and indeed for the transgressors is an evil return﴾. The transgressors, the opposite of the righteous, have an evil return.
* And from the benefits of these verses: that one who calls to Allah should have a call that is sometimes by encouragement and sometimes by warning. Rather, the best is that his call includes both encouragement and warning. That is because if his call is limited to encouragement, it becomes a cause of feeling secure from the plotting of Allah, and a person persists in disobedience to Allah while hoping in Allah. And if it includes only warning, it becomes a cause of despair of the mercy of Allah and of considering mercy unlikely, and this is harmful. Rather, the caller should combine the two, so as to move people to hope and to fear. This is why Imam Ahmad said: One's fear and hope should be equal; whichever prevails, the other is destroyed.

Some scholars said: Hope and fear are like the two wings of a bird: if one of them drops, the bird falls, and if they are equal, its flight is balanced.

Some scholars said: When doing an act of obedience, a person should give precedence to hope, and when intending an act of disobedience, he should give precedence to fear. That is, at the time of disobedience the side of fear prevails, and at the time of obedience the side of hope prevails. They said: Because when he does an act of obedience, he has done a cause of hope, and when he does an act of disobedience, he has done what causes fear.

Some scholars said: In a state of health, one should give precedence to fear, and in a state of illness, one should give precedence to hope, so that he dies while having a good opinion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Perhaps the intermediate view is the intermediate view: that when a person commits a sin or intends it, he gives precedence to fear, and when he performs an act of obedience or intends it, he gives precedence to hope. This is a good view.

However, the meaning of our saying that we give precedence to hope or to fear is not that he should have nothing of the other side, but rather that he should combine both; the discussion is about which one predominates.

* And from the benefits of these verses: that the transgressors' return is ﴿an evil return﴾, in contrast to the righteous, whose destination is ﴿a good return﴾. As for the transgressors, their return is ﴿an evil return﴾, because their return is to Hell, may Allah protect us. Allah the Exalted mentioned among the types of punishment in this abode what is enough to deter the believer from disobedience.
* And from its benefits: that among the names of the Fire is ﴿Jahannam﴾.
* And from its benefits: that they ﴿burn therein﴾, that is, they fall into its heat, that is, its heat which can never become cool. However, it has been reported that they are sometimes taken around in an extremely cold place, and sometimes in an extremely hot fire.
* From its benefits: praise by censure of this abode. As for Paradise, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And excellent is the home of the righteous﴾ [Surah al-Nahl 30]. As for this one, He said here: ﴿So wretched is the resting place﴾, praising it by censure, ugliness and evil.
* And from the benefits of these verses: that the people of the Fire, may Allah protect us, taste it, that is, the punishment, between boiling water and ghassāq (pus). That is, they are given boiling water to drink, and they are given the pus of the people of the Fire, the ghassāq, may Allah protect us. One of them gulps down this drink ﴿and can hardly swallow it, and death comes to him from every place, but he will not die﴾ [Surah Ibrahim 17].
* And from its benefits, that is, the verses: the variety of punishment for the tyrants, by His saying ﴿and other punishments of similar kinds, in pairs﴾, meaning various categories of punishment. These categories are mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah. Whoever wishes to review them should consult the books written on that subject.
* And from the benefits of these verses: the people of the Fire dispute among themselves, argue, and curse one another. Whenever a group enters, it curses the one that follows: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [Surah al-A'raf 38]. ﴿This is a group rushing in with you; there is no welcome for them. They will surely burn in the Fire﴾ [Surah Sad 59].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 45–64 (part 4 of 4):

* Among its lessons: the followers and the ones they followed who are among the people of the Fire will all be in the Fire, so these followers are not excused for following their masters and the great ones. However, this is not absolute, for the texts have shown that no one is punished until the proof (hujjah) has been established against him. On this basis, the followers mentioned here are understood to be those to whom the proof had reached and to whom the messengers had been sent. They said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers following a religion﴾ [az-Zukhruf 22]. For this reason Allah the Exalted said in surah al-Ahzab: ﴿On the Day when their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!" And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our masters and our elders, and they led us astray from the way." Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great curse﴾ [al-Ahzab 66–68]. This shows that these followers had the proof established against them, and therefore they say: ﴿Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!﴾ [al-Ahzab 66].
* Among the lessons of these verses: the people of the Fire speak to one another and disown one another, and they are neither living nor dead. They are not dead and at rest, nor living in bliss; rather, they are living and being punished.
* Among the lessons of these verses: the follower disowns the one he followed, and vice versa, as the verses of surah al-Baqarah show.
* Among the lessons of these verses: the people of the Fire remember what happened to them in the world, based on His saying: ﴿And they will say, "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the bad?"﴾. This indicates that they remember what was in the world. Likewise, the people of Paradise remember what they had in the world.
Allah the Blessed and Exalted said in surah as-Saffat: ﴿A speaker among them says, "Indeed, I had a companion who used to say, 'Are you really among those who believe? When we die and become dust and bones, will we indeed be recompensed?'" He says, "Would you like to look down?" So he looks and sees him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [as-Saffat 51–55]. He says to his companions who are with him in Paradise: ﴿So he looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [as-Saffat 55]. Whom did he see? His companion. He said to him: ﴿By Allah, you nearly ruined me!﴾ [as-Saffat 56], and he hears this from the highest of the 'Illiyyun, while this one, in the lowest of the lowest, hears it. ﴿By Allah, you nearly ruined me! And if not for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought [to punishment]﴾ [as-Saffat 56–57], i.e., among those brought forth into the punishment, just as you are brought forth into the punishment.
* Among the lessons of this verse: the deficiency of the intellect of the people of the Fire, in that they said: ﴿we used to count them among the bad﴾, because if they do not see them now, then either they are not in the Fire, or those men's eyes have turned away from them. They have stated this in their saying: ﴿Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ [Sad 63]. It is said: the reality is that you are now at fault, either in the world or in the Hereafter. If you took them in mockery, this is a fault of the world; and if your eyes turned away from them, this is a deficiency in the Hereafter.
* Among the lessons of these verses: this dispute that takes place among the people of the Fire is true, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is truth﴾ [Sad 64].
* Branching from this lesson: it is obligatory upon every person not to be deceived by the masters and those who are followed; rather, his concern should be for his own soul.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 38, verse 45–64 (part 1 of 4):

He says: "And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, possessors of strength and of insight" [38:45]. Remember, O Muhammad, and let the one addressed also remember these noble masters. "Remember Our servants Abraham": "Abraham" is a substitute (badal) for "Our servants," a substitute of part from whole, and what is conjoined to it completes the whole.

"Remember Our servants": the word "servants" here refers to the most special of the special, because it is the servanthood of messengership and prophethood. "Abraham" is the imam of the ḥanīfs, whose creed (millah) we have been commanded to follow: "Then We revealed to you, [Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham" [16:123]. "And Isaac," his son, "and Jacob," his grandson, the son of his son.

("Possessors of strength" means people of strength in worship, "and of insight" means insight in religion.) That is, mention them while indicating their strength in religion, because "aydī" is the plural of "yad" (hand), and what is meant by "yad" here is strength. Likewise "al-abṣār" means insight in the religion of God, because they were messengers, and the people most perceptive (abṣar) in the worship of God are the messengers.

(In one reading, "ʿabdanā Ibrāhīm" is an explanation of it, and what follows is conjoined to "ʿabdanā.") That is, it is read in the plural and in the singular. Is this reading canonical (sabʿiyyah) or irregular (shādhdhah)? It is canonical (sabʿiyyah), because the rule is that when the author (may God have mercy on him) says "and in one reading," it is canonical, and when he says "it was read," it is irregular.

Then He says: "Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality" [38:46]. "Akhlaṣnāhum" means: We cleansed them and chose them, because the purification (ikhlāṣ) of a thing is to remove its impurities until it remains pure, and from it comes the purification of religion for God, which is to remove from it the impurities of polytheism.

His statement "with a pure quality" is clarified by His words: it is "the remembrance of the Abode" (dhikrā al-dār). The author has informed us that "dhikrā" is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "it is remembrance." It is permissible for "dhikrā" to be a substitute for "khāliṣah," or an explanatory apposition to it. What is meant by "al-dār" here is the Hereafter.

("The remembrance of the Abode" is the Hereafter; that is, remembering it and working for it. In another reading it is in the genitive construction: "bi-khāliṣati dhikrā al-dār"), and it is explanatory (lil-bayān), meaning the construction here is explanatory, estimated as "min" (of), because the explanatory genitive is estimated as "min," as you say: "a ring of silver" (khātamu fiḍḍah), i.e., of silver; "a garment of silk" (thawbu khazz), i.e., of silk; "a door of wood" (bābu khashab), i.e., of wood, and so on. He says: "the remembrance of the Abode," meaning the Hereafter; that is, remembering it and working for it.

("And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones" [38:47], the chosen, the good ones; "akhyār" is the plural of "khayyir" with shadda.) "And indeed they" — the pronoun refers to the three: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. "With Us" means with God, and the "withness" here is a withness of rank, not of place, because their rank with God is that they are among these.

"Al-muṣṭafā" is a passive participle meaning "the chosen." Here "al-muṣṭafayn" is a masculine sound plural, but there is a difficulty: it is known that the masculine sound plural has the letter before the yā' kasra, as you say: "al-muslimīn," "al-mu'minīn," "al-qānitīn," "al-ṣābirīn," "al-ṣādiqīn." Here the letter before the yā' is fatḥa, and what is known to have fatḥa before the yā' is the dual, as you say: "al-rajulayn," "al-muslimayn," "al-mu'minayn," and so on. So why was the letter before the yā' given fatḥa here?

The grammarians said: because its original form is "al-muṣṭafā" with an alif, and the alif was deleted because the yā' is sākin and the alif is sākin, so it is deleted, as Ibn Mālik said:

"If two sākin letters meet, make what precedes kasra; and if it is a soft letter, its deletion is deserved."

So now an alif and a yā' have met, and the first of them is deleted, which here is the alif, and the fatḥa remains as evidence of it.

"Al-muṣṭafayn" means: in worship, knowledge and messengership. "Al-akhyār" is the plural of "khayr," and "khayyir" is on the pattern "fayʿil," meaning abundant in good. There is no doubt that these three messengers possessed much good, and from their lineage came noble messengers and some of the best nations; from the lineage of Abraham came the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the best of nations and the most honored of them with God.

"And remember Ismāʿīl and al-Yasaʿ" [38:48]. Ismāʿīl, son of Abraham, is mentioned singly because his lineage differs from the lineage of Isaac and Jacob. The lineage of Isaac and Jacob is the Children of Israel, while the lineage of Ismāʿīl is the Arabs, and for this reason he is singled out.

"Al-Yasaʿ," who is a prophet, and the lām is extra (zāʾidah). If the lām is extra, the original form is "Yasaʿ," and he is a prophet, but a prophet and messenger, because every prophet mentioned in the Qur'an is a messenger.

"Dhā al-Kifl": his prophethood is disputed. It was said that he is a prophet, and "al-kifl" means deed and portion, that is, the one of abundant deed and portion. This is according to the view that he is a messenger. As for the view that he is not a messenger, the author said: "It was said: he took responsibility (kafala) for a hundred prophets who fled to him from killing," and the word "it was said" indicates that it is weak. The apparent meaning of "dhā al-kifl" is: the one of deed, the one of great diligence and vigor.

("And all" means all of them), and on this basis the tanwīn in "kull" is a substitute for a noun (all of them are "from the good ones," "akhyār," the plural of "khayyir" with tathqīl). His statement here, "the plural of khayyir with tathqīl," is the same as his earlier statement "the plural of khayyir with tashdīd."

("This is a remembrance" [38:49] for them, with fine praise here, "and indeed for the righteous is a good return," meaning an abode in the Hereafter.) His statement "This is a remembrance" may bear what the author said, namely that "this is a remembrance" for these masters with fine praise; and it may mean that "this is a remembrance" for the people, that is, a reminder for them, as God said at the beginning of the surah: "Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder" [38:1]. This latter is more preponderant. That is, what is mentioned in this surah is a remembrance for whom? For all people.

Then people are divided into the God-fearing and the non-God-fearing: "and indeed for the righteous," and among them are the messengers, indeed they are the masters of the righteous and at their head, "a good return," that is, an abode. Here He said "la-ḥusna" (a good), and there is a difficulty in it, since it is in the accusative with the lām entering upon it.

* Student: What is the grammatical reason for the emphasis of the subject of "inna"?
* The Shaykh: This is the delayed subject of "inna," and "lil-muttaqīn" is the fronted predicate.

("Gardens of Eden" [38:50] is a substitute or explanatory apposition, "a good return.") For this reason it was put in the accusative, though it is in the accusative by kasra standing in for fatḥa. The "gardens" originally means an orchard with many trees, named so because it conceals (yajunnu) whoever is in it, that is, it covers him. What is meant is the abode of bliss that God has prepared for the righteous in the Hereafter. "'Adn" means residence, that is, the gardens in which their inhabitants reside, from which they do not move, and which they do not desire to leave; and each one of the people of Paradise sees that no one has merit over him, and this is the completeness of bliss, because when a person sees that another is better than him, he belittles what God has given him. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Look at those who are below you, and do not look at those who are above you." [Reported by Muslim (2963) from Abū Hurayrah.]

He says: ("Gardens of Eden, whose doors are opened for them" [38:50]), "mufattaḥah" (opened, in the feminine intensive form) rather than "maftūḥah" (opened), because of the multitude of those who open, or the multitude of doors, or both. According to the first, the multitude of openers means they have many servants whose task is to open the doors for them; according to the second, it indicates that its doors are many because of the multitude of those who enter it. It is known that the principal great doors of Paradise are how many? Eight. But there are chambers in the middle of Paradise with rivers flowing beneath them, which have doors, and so the doors are opened for them.

"Reclining therein" [38:51]; that is, in these gardens. Reclining indicates calm, tranquility and freedom from anxiety, and indicates that the person is one of authority who is served and does not serve. His words "therein" mean in the gardens.

The author explained what they recline upon, saying: "on couches," as stated in another verse: "Therein they call for abundant fruit and drink" [38:51]. "Yadʿūna" means they ask for, that is, they say: bring fruit, "abundant," abundant in kind or in individual items, or both? Abundant in kind and in individual items; that is, many kinds and likewise many items, so that whatever you ask for, you obtain it.

"And drink": God has explained that its kinds or types are four: "Therein are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey" [47:15]. These are four kinds of the drink of Paradise.

But notice that these names differ from what is in this world with a great difference. That is, do not think that the water is like the water of this world, or the honey like the honey of this world, or the milk like the milk of this world, or the wine like the wine of this world. No, they differ greatly, because of God's words: "No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes" [32:17]. If it did not differ, we would know this. God said in the sacred hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (3244) and Muslim (2824) from Abū Hurayrah.] O God, make us among its people.

"And with them are those restraining their glances" [38:52]. "Qāṣirāt al-ṭarf": the author said: "withholding the eyes." "Al-ṭarf" means the gaze; that is, they restrict their gaze to their husbands. This is one meaning. The second meaning: restraining the glances of their husbands, so that the husbands do not look at others. The difference between them is clear, but the wording is suitable for both: they restrain their own glances, looking at no one other than their husbands, and they restrain the glances of their husbands, so that the husbands do not look at other women.

Are the women of this world like this? Not at all. When a woman goes out to the market, she begins looking at the men and comparing this man with her husband. Likewise when a man goes out to the market, some people look at women and compare the woman with his wife, and you find that if he sees a woman more beautiful than his wife, his heart becomes occupied with her and he turns away from his wife and loses interest in her. This is from the great wisdom behind the obligation of covering the face. But fools are ignorant. From the great wisdom is that when a man does not see a woman, his gaze does not change regarding his wife; but if he sees a woman like the sun while his wife is like the Suhā star, his heart becomes attached to this woman who is like the sun, and he loses interest in this woman who is like the Suhā, and hardly sees her. Thus it is from the wisdom of God Mighty and Majestic that women were obligated to cover their faces.

("Restraining the glances, of equal age" [38:52], of the same age, and they are young women, daughters of thirty-three years.) "Atrāb" means that they are of one age, young women, daughters of thirty-three years. Likewise the people of Paradise enter Paradise as sons of thirty-three years, and none of them changes; each remains as he is.

As for their being "atrāb," it may be said that they are of equal age, equal in beauty, and equal in everything, so that a person does not incline toward one who surpasses the others, and his gaze upon them is on equal terms.

God said: ("This" which is mentioned, "is what you are promised," in the third person and the second person by iltifāt [shift], "for the Day of Reckoning") — "This is what you are promised" — the author said: "in the third person and the second person"; the second person is "mā tūʿadūn," the third person is "mā yūʿadūn," and both readings are canonical. The author said: "by iltifāt" (shift). Which of them is the shift: the third person or the second person?

* Student: The second person.
* Another student: The third person.
* The Shaykh: The second person, the third person; not the second person nor the third person, the second and the third person, what do we say?
* Students: The second person.
* The Shaykh: "This is a remembrance, and indeed for the righteous is a good return. Gardens of Eden, whose doors are opened for them" [38:49–50]: "them" is third person. "Reclining therein, they call for" [38:51]: "they call" is third person. "And with them" [38:52] is third person. So where is the iltifāt? In the second person: "This is what you are promised" [38:53]; that is, it is said to them: "This is what you are promised," with the pronoun of address; and with the pronoun of the third person it becomes a report from God Mighty and Majestic that what is mentioned is what they are promised on the Day of Resurrection.

("For the Day of Reckoning," that is, because of it.) This is what the author followed: that the lām is causal. But the correct view is that the lām is temporal, as in His words: "So divorce them for their waiting period" [65:1]. So the lām here means "in" (fī), because it is temporal: that is, this is what you are promised on that day, the Day of Reckoning, which is the Day of Resurrection, and it is called "the Day of Reckoning" because people are reckoned on their deeds in it.

He says: "Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end" [38:54]. "Indeed this" refers to what has been mentioned of the bliss of Paradise. "Is Our provision": Our gift. The lām in "la-rizqunā" is for emphasis. "Mā lahu min nafād": "min nafād" is a delayed subject, and the extra "min," extra in wording and extra in meaning, entered upon it; that is, "it has no end," meaning it has no cessation. Is "mā" here Ḥijāzī or do the Tamīmīs and Ḥijāzīs agree on it?

* Student: They agree.
* The Shaykh: They agree. Why? Because the predicate is fronted, and "mā" is not Ḥijāzī except with the order, according to Ibn Mālik's saying:

"... with the persistence of negation and order is established."

So we say: "nafād" is the subject in both dialects. The author said: ("mā lahu min nafād," that is, cessation, and the sentence is a circumstantial clause from "rizqunā," or a second predicate of "inna"; that is, permanently or permanent.) A very concise statement.

("The sentence is a circumstantial clause from 'rizqunā'"), and on this basis the meaning is: "mā lahu min nafād," that is, according to the author's explanation, permanently or permanent? Permanently. Or we say: a second predicate: "Indeed this is Our provision, indeed this has no end," and the estimate is: permanent or permanently? Permanent. So in the sentence there is a chiasmus (laff wa-nashr); is it ordered or unordered? The circumstantial clause from "rizqunā" puts the circumstance first, or another second predicate, namely "permanently," the predicate is delayed, so the order is ordered.

He said: ("This" which is mentioned, "is for the believers," "and indeed for the tyrants") — "This" is a subject which must have a predicate, whose predicate is omitted, as the author estimated, for whom? For the believers. The author says "for the believers," but the correct view is that we estimate "for the God-fearing," because God said: "This is a remembrance, and indeed for the righteous is a good return." So it is better to say: this is for the God-fearing.

As for others, he said: ("And indeed for the tyrants" is a resumed statement.) "And indeed for the tyrants": "tāghīn" is the plural of "ṭāghiyah," and the tyrant (ṭāghī) is one who exceeds the limit. The human limit is to be a servant of God, obeying His command and avoiding His prohibition; whoever does not obey the command is a tyrant, and whoever commits the prohibition is a tyrant. "Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed" [20:43]. So tyranny is exceeding the limit, and the limit for a human is the worship of God; whoever exceeds this limit, by opposing the command or committing the prohibition, is a tyrant.

If someone says: What is the evidence that tughyān means exceeding the limit?
We say: His words: "Indeed, when the water overflowed [tagha al-mā'], We carried you in the sailing ship" [69:11]; that is, it exceeded its limit.

("This, and indeed for the tyrants," is a resumed statement.) "Evil return" [38:55]: that is, the worst return. "Sharra" is in the accusative as the delayed subject of "inna," which is what? "Evil return." He said: "Hell, they will burn therein" [38:56]; this is an explanatory apposition for "evil return," and it is the Fire: Jahannam. The Fire was named by this name because it includes gloom (jahmah) due to its blackness, since there is no light in it, and the depth of its bottom, and we seek refuge with God.

The Prophet ﷺ once heard, while he and his Companions were in Madinah, a thud, meaning the fall of something. He said: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "This is a stone that was thrown into the Fire seventy years ago, and it has been falling into it until now, and has only now reached its bottom." [Narrated by Muslim (2844/31) from Abu Hurayrah.] Seventy years, and it is a large stone with a great sound, falling into the Fire. So its depth is very great, and for this reason it has become dark and black, and Allah forbid. It has also been said that "Jahannam" is not Arabic, and that its origin in Persian is "kahnam," but it was Arabized and became "Jahannam."
* Student: "Kahnam" in Persian?
* The Shaykh: In Persian, yes. And on this view, what we said, that it is derived from "jahama" (darkness and remoteness), does not apply to us; it is then said to be a proper name for the Fire, not derived. Whatever the case, it is one of the names of the Fire; we seek refuge in Allah from it.

﴿يَصْلَوْنَهَا﴾ is a description of "Jahannam," or rather a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because "Jahannam" is definite, and a clause following a definite noun is a circumstantial clause. ﴿يَصْلَوْنَهَا﴾ means: they enter it. But it is not enough to say "they enter it"; rather ﴿يَصْلَوْنَهَا﴾ means they are tormented by its heat (ṣalā), which is its intense heat.

(﴿فَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾ the bed.) As Allah the Exalted says: ﴿أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ الْأَرْضَ مِهَادًا﴾ [An-Naba' 6], and in another verse: ﴿الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ فِرَاشًا﴾ [Al-Baqarah 22]. So "al-mihad" means the bed. ﴿فَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾ means: this is it, ﴿فَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾, because its spreading beneath them is harsh, and its covering is harsh, ﴿لَهُمْ مِنْ فَوْقِهِمْ ظُلَلٌ مِنَ النَّارِ وَمِنْ تَحْتِهِمْ ظُلَلٌ﴾ [Az-Zumar 16]; we seek refuge in Allah.

(﴿هَذَا﴾ [Sad 57], i.e., the punishment implied by what follows, ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾.) It is also permissible for ﴿هَذَا﴾ to be the subject, with the predicate omitted, i.e., "this is what is theirs," ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾. The lām in His saying ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ is the lām of command, and the evidence that it is the lām of command and not the lām of purpose is that it is vowelled with sukūn after the fā', and the lām of command is vowelled with sukūn after fā', wāw and thumma.

﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ means: let them be burned by its heat. Being burned by its heat is "tasting." And the tasting of each thing is according to its nature: in food and drink a person tastes it with the palate of the mouth, while the Fire is tasted by what? By its heat, at whatever part of the body; and cold likewise is tasted by its sting at whatever part of the body.

(﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ حَمِيمٌ﴾ i.e., scalding, burning water, ﴿وَغَسَّاقٌ﴾ with light and emphatic pronunciation.) That is, ﴿غَسَاقٌ﴾ is the light pronunciation, ﴿غَسَّاقٌ﴾ the emphatic pronunciation, (what flows from the pus of the people of the Fire); we seek refuge in Allah.

Now we say: ﴿هَذَا﴾ is the subject, and ﴿حَمِيمٌ وَغَسَّاقٌ﴾ is the predicate and its conjoined element. We have thus departed from what we mentioned before, namely: this is what is theirs of punishment, where we placed the predicate first: "what is theirs of punishment." We have found it better to make ﴿حَمِيمٌ﴾ the predicate and ﴿وَغَسَّاقٌ﴾ conjoined to it, and the clause ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ becomes a parenthetical clause between the subject and the predicate, to hasten their humiliation, since the saying "let them taste the punishment" is undoubtedly a humiliation. Because of this haste, "this" (﴿هَذَا﴾) was placed before the predicate; i.e., the phrase ﴿فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ﴾ was placed first, while the original order of the speech is: this is scalding water and pus, so let them taste it.

Consider the drink: ﴿حَمِيمٌ﴾ is water that is hot, and its heat is not gentle or light. ﴿وَإِنْ يَسْتَغِيثُوا يُغَاثُوا بِمَاءٍ كَالْمُهْلِ﴾ (...) oil, ﴿يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ﴾ [Al-Kahf 29]. First: this drink does not come to them easily. When does it come to them? After they become intensely thirsty, then they call for help, asking Allah to relieve them of this thirst. And when they are given this water, ﴿كَالْمُهْلِ يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ﴾ [Al-Kahf 29], when it approaches their faces to drink it, it roasts them. The scholars said: the flesh of the face falls off. Then when they drink it into their bellies, ﴿وَسُقُوا مَاءً حَمِيمًا فَقَطَّعَ أَمْعَاءَهُمْ﴾ [Muhammad 15], it cuts their insides and their outsides, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Compare this drink with the drink of the people of Paradise: ﴿أَنْهَارٌ مِنْ مَاءٍ غَيْرِ آسِنٍ وَأَنْهَارٌ مِنْ لَبَنٍ لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ طَعْمُهُ وَأَنْهَارٌ مِنْ خَمْرٍ لَذَّةٍ لِلشَّارِبِينَ وَأَنْهَارٌ مِنْ عَسَلٍ مُصَفًّى﴾ [Muhammad 15], and yet they drink whenever they wish. They direct these rivers as they please, without digging channels and without effort; that is, they do not build a wall to stop the water so that it does not flow to right and left, nor do they dig. Ibn al-Qayyim said in the Nuniyyah:

Its rivers flow without a trench, glory be to Him who holds them back from overflowing.

Al-Ghassaq, and we seek refuge in Allah, as soon as you hear its meaning you recoil: the pus of the people of the Fire, the pus that flows from their bodies from their burning. This is a kind of their drink, so their drink is either scalding water that roasts the faces and cuts the bowels, or the pus of the people of the Fire: ﴿يَتَجَرَّعُهُ وَلَا يَكَادُ يُسِيغُهُ وَيَأْتِيهِ الْمَوْتُ مِنْ كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَمَا هُوَ بِمَيِّتٍ وَمِنْ وَرَائِهِ عَذَابٌ غَلِيظٌ﴾ [Ibrahim 17].

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: (﴿وَآخَرُ﴾ [Sad 58], in the plural and singular forms.) ﴿آخَرُ﴾ is singular, ﴿أُخَرُ﴾ is plural; there are therefore two readings, both from the seven canonical readings.

﴿مِنْ شَكْلِهِ﴾ [Sad 58], i.e., of its kind: (i.e., like what was mentioned of scalding water and pus, ﴿أَزْوَاجٌ﴾ i.e., kinds; i.e., their punishment is of various types.)

﴿آخَرُ مِنْ شَكْلِهِ﴾: of its kind, or ﴿أُخَرُ﴾ of its kind, ﴿أَزْوَاجٌ﴾: kinds of punishment by which they are tormented as Allah the Mighty and Majestic willed, and they are humiliated to the utmost degree; they are rebuked and reproached, then they are given hope of coming out. The Fire rises with them until, when they approach its gates, ﴿كُلَّمَا أَرَادُوا أَنْ يَخْرُجُوا مِنْهَا أُعِيدُوا فِيهَا﴾ [As-Sajdah 20]. And this is from the severity of the torment, my brothers. If a prisoner who is imprisoned approaches the door thinking he will leave, and then is sent back, this is more painful for him than if he remained in his place. They are subjected to great varieties of punishment that do not occur to the mind nor come to the imagination. O Allah, save us from the Fire.

(﴿وَآخَرُ مِنْ شَكْلِهِ أَزْوَاجٌ﴾ i.e., kinds; i.e., their punishment is of various types.
